school-c12-accountancy-a.title: Class 12 Accountancy — Partnership (Part A)
school-c12-accountancy-a.description: Class 12 Accountancy, partnership firms chapter by chapter: basics, goodwill, change in ratio, admission, retirement/death and dissolution.

courses.title: Partnership: Basic Concepts
courses.summary: Partnership deed, the default rules of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, Profit & Loss Appropriation Account, interest on capital and drawings, fixed vs fluctuating capitals, guarantee of profit and past adjustments — with full solved examples.
outcomes: Learners can state the default rules that apply when there is no partnership deed
Learners can prepare a Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
Learners can calculate interest on drawings by the product and average-period methods
Learners can prepare fixed and fluctuating capital accounts
Learners can treat guarantee of profit and past adjustments

scenes.text: Riya and Kabir open a bakery together and agree to share profits.
Their uncle says: write down everything — capital, ratio, salary, interest — in a deed.
Kabir asks: what if we forget to write something?

steps.title: What is a partnership?
steps.body:
A **partnership** is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Section 4).

Essential features:
- At least **two persons**; the maximum is **50** (Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 under the Companies Act 2013)
- An **agreement** (oral or written)
- A **business** carried on with a motive of **sharing profits**
- **Mutual agency** — each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners
- **Unlimited liability** of partners

steps.title: Partnership deed — what it contains
steps.body: A **partnership deed** is the written agreement. It usually covers: name and address of firm and partners, nature of business, capital of each partner, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salary/commission to partners, interest on partners' loans, rules for admission, retirement and death, method of valuing goodwill, and how disputes are settled.

steps.title: When there is NO deed (or the deed is silent)
steps.body:
The Act's default rules apply:
- Profits and losses shared **equally**
- **No interest on capital**
- **No interest on drawings**
- **No salary or commission** to any partner
- **Interest on a partner's loan @ 6% p.a.** — and it is a **charge** against profit (paid even if there is a loss)

steps.title: Solved example 1 — no deed
steps.body:
Asha and Bina have no deed. Asha contributed ₹2,00,000 capital, Bina ₹1,00,000. Asha also lent ₹50,000 to the firm. Profit before interest on loan = ₹63,000. Asha claims interest on capital and a 2:1 share.

**Step 1:** No deed → no interest on capital; profit shared equally.
**Step 2:** Interest on Asha's loan = 50,000 × 6% = ₹3,000 (a charge).
**Step 3:** Divisible profit = 63,000 − 3,000 = ₹60,000 → Asha ₹30,000, Bina ₹30,000. Asha also gets ₹3,000 interest on loan.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — loss year
steps.body: Same firm, but profit before interest on loan is only ₹2,000. Interest on loan ₹3,000 is still paid because it is a charge. Net result = loss of ₹1,000, shared equally (₹500 each).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving interest on capital when the deed is silent — not allowed.
- Treating interest on partner's **loan** as an appropriation — it is a **charge** to Profit & Loss Account.
- Using capital ratio as profit ratio when no deed exists — the default is **equal**.

statements.s: Without a deed, profits are shared in capital ratio.
Interest on a partner's loan is allowed at 6% p.a. even without a deed.
A partner is entitled to salary if he works more, even without a deed.
A partnership can be formed by an oral agreement.
statements.why: Agreement may be oral or written; written is advisable.

quiz.q: Maximum number of partners in a firm under current rules is:
quiz.why: The maximum number of partners in a firm is 50, under the Companies Act 2013 and the rules made under it. A firm with more partners must be registered as a company.

quiz.q: Interest on partner's loan in the absence of a deed is:
quiz.why: If the partnership deed is silent, a partner who lends money to the firm is entitled to interest on the loan at 6% p.a.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feature of partnership?
quiz.why: A partnership firm is not a separate legal entity from its partners. The firm and the partners are legally the same, which is why liability is unlimited.

quiz.q: When the deed is silent, interest on capital is:
quiz.why: If the deed does not provide for it, no interest on capital is allowed to partners. It must be agreed in the deed.

quiz.q: Interest on partner's loan is debited to:
quiz.why: Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit, so it is debited to the Profit & Loss Account before profit is divided. Interest on capital is an appropriation.

scenes.text: Year one: the bakery earns ₹1,20,000 net profit.
Riya: "First interest on capital, then Kabir's salary, then we split the rest 3:2."
They prepare a Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.

steps.title: What goes in the Appropriation Account
steps.body:
The **P&L Appropriation Account** is an extension of the P&L Account. It shows how net profit is distributed.

**Debit side (appropriations):** interest on capital, salary/commission to partners, transfer to reserve, and finally the share of profit to each partner.
**Credit side:** net profit (from P&L A/c), interest on drawings.

Items like rent paid to a partner and interest on partner's loan are **charges** — they go to the P&L Account, not here.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A and B share 3:2. Capitals ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000; interest on capital 10% p.a.; B's salary ₹2,000 per month; net profit ₹1,20,000.

**Step 1:** IoC: A ₹20,000; B ₹10,000.
**Step 2:** B's salary = ₹24,000.
**Step 3:** Total appropriations = ₹54,000 → divisible profit ₹66,000.
**Step 4:** A = 66,000 × 3/5 = ₹39,600; B = ₹26,400.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — insufficient profit
steps.body:
Same data but net profit is only ₹24,000 and interest on capital is an **appropriation**. Interest due = ₹30,000 > profit. So the whole profit is shared in the ratio of interest due (20,000 : 10,000 = 2:1): A ₹16,000, B ₹8,000. No salary or further share is given.

If the deed says interest on capital is a **charge**, it is allowed in full (₹30,000) and the resulting loss of ₹6,000 is shared 3:2.

steps.title: Commission on profit after charging commission
steps.body:
Profit before commission ₹1,10,000; manager-partner gets 10% of profit **after** charging such commission.
Commission = 1,10,000 × 10/110 = **₹10,000**. (Check: 1,10,000 − 10,000 = 1,00,000 and 10% of that is 10,000.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting interest on partner's loan in the Appropriation A/c.
- Forgetting to credit interest on drawings to the Appropriation A/c.
- Allowing salary when profit is already exhausted by interest on capital (appropriation case).
- Using 10% of profit **before** commission when the question says **after**.

activity.prompt: Profit before commission ₹2,20,000. Partner X gets commission of 10% of net profit AFTER charging such commission. Find X's commission (₹).

quiz.q: Interest on drawings is shown on the ___ side of the P&L Appropriation A/c.
quiz.why: Interest charged on drawings is an income to the firm, so it is shown on the credit side of the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.

quiz.q: Rent paid to a partner for using his building is:
quiz.why: Rent paid to a partner for using his building is a business expense, so it is a charge to the Profit & Loss A/c and not an appropriation of profit.

quiz.q: Profit ₹50,000; IoC (appropriation) due A ₹40,000, B ₹20,000. A gets:
quiz.why: Interest on capital due is 40,000 + 20,000 = 60,000, which exceeds the profit of ₹50,000. So the profit is shared in the ratio of interest due, 2 : 1. A gets 50,000 × 2/3 ≈ ₹33,333.

quiz.q: Transfer to general reserve appears on:
quiz.why: A transfer to general reserve is an appropriation of profit, so it is shown on the debit side of the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.

quiz.q: Commission 5% on profit after charging it; profit before commission ₹2,10,000. Commission =
quiz.why: Commission is 5% of profit after charging it, so commission = profit before commission × 5/105 = 2,10,000 × 5/105 = ₹10,000.

scenes.text: Kabir withdraws ₹5,000 at the start of every month for home expenses.
The deed says interest on drawings is 12% p.a.
"Do I pay interest for 12 months on every rupee?" Not quite.

steps.title: Why charge interest on drawings?
steps.body:
Drawings reduce the funds available to the firm, so the deed may charge interest on them. It is charged only for the period the money stayed out of the business, from the date of drawing to the end of the accounting year.

**Product method** (dates vary): Interest = Sum of (amount × months outstanding) × rate × 1/12.

steps.title: Average-period shortcut (equal amounts, equal intervals, full year)
steps.body:
- Beginning of each month → **6½ months**
- Middle of each month → **6 months**
- End of each month → **5½ months**
- Beginning of each quarter → **7½ months**
- End of each quarter → **4½ months**
- Date unknown (total given) → **6 months**

steps.title: Solved example 1 — monthly
steps.body:
₹5,000 at the **beginning** of each month, 12% p.a. Total ₹60,000.
Interest = 60,000 × 12/100 × 6.5/12 = **₹3,900**.
If withdrawn at the **end** of each month: 60,000 × 12% × 5.5/12 = **₹3,300**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — product method
steps.body:
Year ends 31 March. Drawings: ₹10,000 on 1 July, ₹6,000 on 1 October; rate 10%.
**Step 1:** Months to 31 March: 1 July → 9 months; 1 October → 6 months.
**Step 2:** Products: 90,000 + 36,000 = 1,26,000.
**Step 3:** Interest = 1,26,000 × 10% × 1/12 = **₹1,050**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Charging interest for 12 months on all drawings.
- Mixing up beginning (6½) and end (5½) of month.
- Forgetting that interest on drawings is a **gain to the firm**: debit partner, credit P&L Appropriation.
- Charging interest when the deed is silent — not allowed.

activity.prompt: A partner withdrew ₹4,000 at the END of every month for a full year. Rate 9% p.a. Interest on drawings = ? (₹)

quiz.q: Equal drawings at the middle of every month: average period is
quiz.why: If equal amounts are drawn in the middle of every month, the average period is 6 months (the average of 11.5, 10.5 … 0.5 months is 6).

quiz.q: Drawings at the beginning of each quarter: average period
quiz.why: Drawings at the start of each quarter are outstanding for 12, 9, 6 and 3 months. The average is (12 + 9 + 6 + 3)/4 = 7½ months.

quiz.q: ₹12,000 drawn on 1 October, year ends 31 March, rate 10%. Interest =
quiz.why: From 1 October to 31 March is 6 months. Interest = 12,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹600.

quiz.q: Total drawings ₹30,000, dates not given, rate 8%. Interest =
quiz.why: When dates are not given, the amount is assumed to be drawn evenly, so the average period is 6 months. Interest = 30,000 × 8% × 6/12 = ₹1,200.

quiz.q: Journal entry for interest on drawings:
options: Partner's Capital/Current Dr, To Interest on Drawings
Interest on drawings Dr, To Cash
quiz.why: Interest on drawings is charged to the partner, so the partner's account is debited, and the credit goes to Interest on Drawings (income to the firm).

scenes.text: Riya likes to keep her capital steady at ₹2,00,000.
Kabir's capital keeps changing with every profit and withdrawal.
Their accountant shows them two methods.

steps.title: The two methods
steps.body:
**Fixed capital method:** two accounts per partner — a **Capital A/c** (changes only for fresh capital or withdrawal of capital) and a **Current A/c** (all adjustments: interest, salary, profit share, drawings). The current account may show a debit or credit balance.

**Fluctuating capital method:** only one **Capital A/c**; all adjustments go into it, so the balance keeps changing. This is the default if the question does not say capitals are fixed.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — fixed capital
steps.body:
A's capital ₹1,00,000 (fixed). During the year: IoC ₹10,000, salary ₹12,000, profit share ₹30,000, drawings ₹20,000, interest on drawings ₹500.
Current A/c: Cr 10,000 + 12,000 + 30,000 = 52,000; Dr 20,000 + 500 = 20,500 → **credit balance ₹31,500**. Capital A/c stays ₹1,00,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — fluctuating
steps.body: Same data, fluctuating method: Capital A/c closing = 1,00,000 + 52,000 − 20,500 = **₹1,31,500**.

steps.title: Opening capital from closing capital
steps.body: If interest on capital must be calculated on **opening** capital but only closing capitals are given: Opening capital = Closing capital + Drawings − Share of profit − IoC − Salary (or + share of loss). Work backwards.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Posting drawings to the Capital A/c under the fixed method — they go to Current A/c.
- Thinking a capital account under fixed method can show a debit balance — normally it cannot; a current account can.
- Calculating IoC on closing capital when the question says opening capital.

activity.prompt: Under the FIXED capital method, where is each item recorded?

quiz.q: Under the fixed capital method, salary to partner is credited to:
quiz.why: Under the fixed capital method the capital balance does not change, so the partner's salary is credited to the Current Account, along with other adjustments.

quiz.q: Which account may show a debit balance under fixed capital method?
quiz.why: Under the fixed capital method, the Current Account can have a debit balance, if drawings and charges exceed the credits. The Capital Account is fixed and normally has a credit balance.

quiz.q: If nothing is stated, capitals are assumed to be:
quiz.why: If the question does not say whether capitals are fixed, they are assumed to be fluctuating, the default method.

quiz.q: Closing capital ₹1,50,000; drawings ₹20,000; profit share ₹40,000. Opening capital =
quiz.why: Opening capital = closing capital + drawings − profit share = 1,50,000 + 20,000 − 40,000 = ₹1,30,000.

quiz.q: Number of accounts per partner in fixed capital method:
quiz.why: With fixed capitals, each partner has two accounts: a Capital Account and a Current Account.

lessons.title: Guarantee of profit and past adjustments

story.title: A promise to a new partner

scenes.text: Meena joins with a 1/6 share and is promised at least ₹20,000 a year.
The firm earns ₹90,000; her share is only ₹15,000.
Who makes up the ₹5,000 gap?

steps.title: Guarantee of profit
steps.body: A minimum profit may be guaranteed to a partner. If the actual share is less, the **deficiency** is borne by the guaranteeing partner(s) — in the agreed ratio, or in their profit-sharing ratio if nothing is said.

steps.title: Past adjustments
steps.body:
If an item (interest on capital, salary, interest on drawings) was **omitted or wrongly given** after accounts are closed, we do not reopen the accounts. We pass one **adjustment entry** through partners' capital/current accounts.

Method (table): (1) amounts that should have been credited/debited, (2) reverse the wrong profit distribution, (3) net effect per partner.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — omitted interest on capital
steps.body:
A's capital ₹60,000, B's ₹40,000; IoC 5% omitted; profits shared equally.
IoC: A ₹3,000, B ₹2,000 (total ₹5,000). This ₹5,000 would have reduced profit, so each bears ₹2,500.
Net: A +3,000 − 2,500 = **+₹500**; B +2,000 − 2,500 = **−₹500**.
Entry: **B's Capital A/c Dr ₹500, To A's Capital A/c ₹500**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making the guaranteed partner bear part of his own deficiency.
- In past adjustments, forgetting to reverse the profit effect — the net amount is what matters.
- Passing the adjustment through P&L Appropriation (accounts are already closed).

activity.prompt: X, Y, Z share 2:2:1. Z is guaranteed ₹25,000 by X alone. Profit ₹1,00,000. What is X's final share (₹)?

quiz.q: Deficiency of a guaranteed partner is borne (if not specified) by guarantors in:
quiz.why: If the guarantee does not say how the deficiency is shared, it is borne by the guaranteeing partners in their mutual profit-sharing ratio.
Past adjustments (errors or omissions) are corrected with a single adjustment entry through the partners' Capital/Current Accounts, without reopening the old Profit & Loss Appropriation Account.

quiz.q: C has 1/5 share, guaranteed ₹30,000; profit ₹1,00,000. Deficiency =
quiz.why: C's share is 1/5 of ₹1,00,000 = ₹20,000, but ₹30,000 is guaranteed. The deficiency is 30,000 − 20,000 = ₹10,000.

quiz.q: If omitted interest on drawings is now charged, the partner with more drawings will usually:
quiz.why: Interest on drawings is a charge to each partner. The partner who drew more is debited more, so will usually lose when it is corrected.

quiz.q: In a guarantee case, the firm's total profit distributed:
quiz.why: A guarantee only moves profit between the partners. The firm's total profit and its total distribution do not change.

questions.q: Without a partnership deed, partners share profit:
questions.why: If there is no partnership deed, the Partnership Act says partners share profit equally, whatever their capital or time given.

questions.q: Interest on partner's loan without a deed is allowed at:
questions.why: Without a deed, interest on a partner's loan to the firm is allowed at 6% p.a.

questions.q: Which item is a charge, not an appropriation?
questions.why: Rent paid to a partner is a business expense and therefore a charge against profit. Salary, interest on capital and transfers to reserve are appropriations out of profit.

questions.q: Average period for equal drawings at the end of each month:
questions.why: Equal drawings at the end of each month stay outstanding for 11, 10, … 0 months, an average of 5½ months.

questions.q: Under fixed capital method, drawings are debited to:
questions.why: With fixed capitals, drawings are debited to the partner's Current Account, as the Capital Account does not change.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Interest on capital is not allowed when the firm suffers a loss (appropriation case). Reason (R): Interest on capital, as an appropriation, is allowed only out of profits.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Interest on capital is an appropriation of profit, so it can be allowed only if there is profit, and not when the firm has made a loss. So R explains A.

questions.q: Profit ₹36,000. IoC (appropriation) due: P ₹30,000, Q ₹15,000. P receives:
questions.why: Interest on capital due is 30,000 + 15,000 = 45,000, which exceeds profit of ₹36,000. So profit is shared in the ratio of interest due, 2 : 1, and P gets 36,000 × 2/3 = ₹24,000.

questions.q: ₹3,000 drawn at the beginning of each month for 12 months at 10%. Interest =
questions.why: Drawings at the start of each month total 3,000 × 12 = 36,000 with an average period of 6.5 months. Interest = 36,000 × 10% × 6.5/12 = ₹1,950.

questions.q: Commission 10% of net profit after charging it; profit before commission ₹3,30,000. Commission =
questions.why: Commission is 10% of net profit after charging it, so commission = 3,30,000 × 10/110 = ₹30,000.

questions.q: Case: X and Y (capitals ₹80,000 and ₹40,000) share equally. IoC 10% was omitted. The adjustment entry is:
questions.why: Interest at 10% would be ₹8,000 for X and ₹4,000 for Y, a total of ₹12,000 that is shared equally (6,000 each). X was due net +2,000 and Y net −2,000, so Y's account is debited ₹2,000 and X's credited.

questions.q: A, B, C share 2:2:1. C guaranteed ₹30,000 by A and B equally. Profit ₹1,00,000. A gets:
questions.why: C's share is 1/5 of 1,00,000 = 20,000, so C is short by 10,000 of the guarantee. A and B bear 5,000 each. A's share = 2/5 × 1,00,000 − 5,000 = 40,000 − 5,000 = ₹35,000.

questions.q: Drawings ₹5,000 on 1 June, ₹8,000 on 1 December; year ends 31 March; rate 12%. Interest by product method:
Closing capital ₹1,10,000; drawings ₹30,000; profit share ₹50,000; IoC was on opening capital @10%. Opening capital (before IoC) is X where X + 0.1X + 50,000 − 30,000 = 1,10,000. X =
questions.why: Closing capital = opening capital + interest on capital + profit share − drawings, so X + 0.1X + 50,000 − 30,000 = 1,10,000. This gives 1.1X = 90,000 and X ≈ ₹81,818.

questions.q: Mutual agency means:
options: Partners are agents of each other and of the firm
questions.why: Mutual agency means each partner acts as an agent of the other partners and of the firm, and the firm is bound by acts of any partner done in the course of business.

questions.q: Under fluctuating capital method, salary to partner is credited to:
questions.why: Under the fluctuating capital method there is only one account per partner, the Capital Account, so salary and all adjustments are credited to it.

questions.q: Case: Profit ₹60,000 before interest on loan. A has lent ₹1,00,000, no deed. Profit available for sharing equally:
questions.why: With no deed, interest on A's loan is 6% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹6,000, a charge against profit. Profit left for sharing = 60,000 − 6,000 = ₹54,000.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

courses.title: Goodwill: Nature and Valuation
courses.summary: What goodwill is, factors affecting it, and its valuation by the average profit, weighted average, super profit and capitalisation methods.
outcomes: Learners can explain goodwill and the factors that affect it
Learners can value goodwill by simple and weighted average profit methods
Learners can value goodwill by the super profit method
Learners can value goodwill by capitalisation of average and super profits

lessons.title: Nature of goodwill and factors affecting it

scenes.text: Two sweet shops have identical ovens and buildings.
One has queues every evening; the other is empty.
The extra earning power of the busy one is its goodwill.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Goodwill** is the value of a firm's reputation that enables it to earn **more than normal profits** compared with similar firms. It is an **intangible asset** (not fictitious) — it has value, can be sold with the business, but cannot be seen or touched.

steps.title: Factors affecting goodwill
steps.body:
- Nature of business (stable demand, low risk)
- Location
- Efficiency of management
- Market situation (monopoly / limited competition)
- Special advantages (licences, patents, cheap power, long contracts)
- Quality of products and customer relations

steps.title: When is goodwill valued in a partnership?
steps.body: Whenever the profit-sharing arrangement changes: change in profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement, death, dissolution (if business sold), and amalgamation of firms.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — classify
steps.body: Which raise goodwill? (a) Shop near a railway station → raises; (b) Frequent change of management → lowers; (c) Exclusive import licence → raises; (d) Many new competitors → lowers.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — purchased goodwill
steps.body: A firm buys a business with net assets ₹5,00,000 for ₹6,20,000. Purchased goodwill = 6,20,000 − 5,00,000 = **₹1,20,000**. Only **purchased** goodwill is recorded in books (AS 26 does not allow self-generated goodwill to be recorded).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling goodwill a fictitious asset — it is intangible.
- Recording self-generated goodwill in the books.
- Thinking goodwill is only valued at sale — it is needed for every reconstitution.

activity.prompt: Does each factor usually increase or decrease goodwill?

quiz.why: Goodwill is an intangible asset: it has value but no physical form, and it is not a current or fictitious asset.

quiz.q: Which goodwill can be recorded in books?
quiz.why: Under AS 26 only purchased goodwill (paid for) is recorded in the books. Self-generated goodwill is not recorded because its cost cannot be measured reliably.
Goodwill arises because the business can earn more than the normal profit (super profit) due to reputation, location and good customers, not simply because of large assets or capital.
Goodwill is the price paid in excess of the net assets acquired: 4,50,000 − 3,80,000 = ₹70,000.

quiz.q: Goodwill is NOT required to be valued on:
quiz.why: Goodwill must be valued when profit-sharing or the partners change, for example on admission, retirement or change in ratio. A change in a partner's drawings does not affect profit sharing.

scenes.text: A buyer looks at the firm's last three years: ₹40,000, ₹50,000, ₹60,000.
Profits are rising — should the latest year count more?
Simple average vs weighted average.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**Simple average:** Goodwill = Average profit × Number of years' purchase.
**Weighted average:** use when profits show a trend; give higher weights to recent years. Weighted average profit = Σ(profit × weight) / Σ weights.

Before averaging, **normalise** profits: add back abnormal losses, deduct abnormal gains, adjust for under/over-valued items, and deduct expected managerial remuneration if not charged.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — weighted
steps.body:
Same profits, weights 1, 2, 3 (latest = 3).
Products: 40,000 + 1,00,000 + 1,80,000 = 3,20,000; Σw = 6.
Weighted average = ₹53,333 (approx.) → Goodwill at 2 years = **₹1,06,667** (approx.).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — normalising
steps.body: Profit of year 2 (₹50,000) included an abnormal gain of ₹5,000 from sale of land. Normal profit of year 2 = ₹45,000. New average = (40,000+45,000+60,000)/3 = ₹48,333 → Goodwill (2 yrs) = ₹96,667.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not removing abnormal gains/losses before averaging.
- Giving the highest weight to the oldest year.
- Multiplying by number of years in the data instead of number of years' purchase.

activity.prompt: Profits for 4 years: ₹30,000, ₹40,000, (₹10,000 loss), ₹60,000. Goodwill = 3 years' purchase of average profit. Goodwill (₹)?

quiz.q: Weighted average is preferred when profits:
options: Show a rising or falling trend
quiz.why: Weighted average gives more importance to recent years, so it is preferred when profits show a rising or falling trend.
Goodwill under the average profit method = average profit × number of years' purchase = 60,000 × 3 = ₹1,80,000.

quiz.q: An abnormal loss of ₹8,000 in one year should be:
options: Added back to that year's profit
quiz.why: An abnormal loss is not expected to repeat, so it is added back to that year's profit to show the normal profit for valuing goodwill.

options: Number of years for which buyer pays for future excess earnings
quiz.why: 'Years' purchase' is the number of years for which a buyer is willing to pay for the expected future (excess) profits. It is the multiplier applied to average profit or super profit to get goodwill.

scenes.text: Similar firms earn 10% on capital employed.
Our firm earns ₹55,000 on ₹4,00,000 — more than ₹40,000 normal.
The ₹15,000 extra is super profit.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Capital employed** = Total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − Outside liabilities.
**Normal profit** = Capital employed × Normal rate of return / 100.
**Super profit** = Average actual profit − Normal profit.
**Goodwill** = Super profit × Number of years' purchase.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Capital employed ₹4,00,000; normal rate 10%; average profit ₹55,000; 3 years' purchase.
Normal profit = ₹40,000; Super profit = ₹15,000; Goodwill = **₹45,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — finding capital employed
steps.body: Assets: ₹6,00,000 (including goodwill ₹50,000); creditors ₹1,00,000; bank loan ₹50,000. Capital employed = 6,00,000 − 50,000 − 1,50,000 = **₹4,00,000**.

steps.title: No super profit?
steps.body: If average profit ≤ normal profit, super profit is nil or negative → goodwill is **nil** under this method.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including goodwill in capital employed.
- Using latest profit instead of average profit.
- Forgetting to deduct outside liabilities from assets.

activity.prompt: Capital employed ₹5,00,000; normal rate 12%; average profit ₹78,000; goodwill = 2 years' purchase of super profit. Goodwill (₹)?

quiz.why: Super profit is the profit earned over and above what a normal business would earn on the same capital: average profit − normal profit.
Normal profit = capital employed × normal rate of return = 3,00,000 × 10% = ₹30,000.

quiz.q: Average profit ₹50,000, normal profit ₹40,000, 4 years' purchase. Goodwill =
quiz.why: Super profit = 50,000 − 40,000 = 10,000. Goodwill by the super profit method = super profit × years' purchase = 10,000 × 4 = ₹40,000.
Capital employed is the capital used in the business, which excludes goodwill because goodwill is the very thing being valued (including it would be circular).

quiz.q: If average profit < normal profit, goodwill by super profit method is:
quiz.why: If average profit is less than normal profit, there is no super profit, so goodwill by the super profit method is nil.

story.title: What should the business be worth?

scenes.text: If 10% is normal, a firm earning ₹55,000 "should" have ₹5,50,000 of capital.
It actually employs only ₹4,00,000.
The gap ₹1,50,000 is goodwill.

steps.title: Two versions
steps.body:
**(a) Capitalisation of average profit:**
Capitalised value = Average profit × 100 / NRR
Goodwill = Capitalised value − Capital employed (net assets).

**(b) Capitalisation of super profit:**
Goodwill = Super profit × 100 / NRR.

Both give the same answer for the same data.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — average profit
steps.body:
Average profit ₹55,000; NRR 10%; net assets ₹4,00,000.
Capitalised value = 55,000 × 100/10 = ₹5,50,000 → Goodwill = **₹1,50,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — super profit
steps.body:
Same data: normal profit = ₹40,000; super profit = ₹15,000.
Goodwill = 15,000 × 100/10 = **₹1,50,000** ✓ (matches).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — hidden net assets
steps.body: Total assets ₹7,00,000 (incl. fictitious ₹20,000), liabilities ₹1,80,000 → net assets ₹5,00,000. Average profit ₹60,000, NRR 12% → capitalised value ₹5,00,000 → Goodwill = **nil**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by the rate as a whole number (÷10 instead of ×100/10).
- Subtracting total assets instead of net assets.
- Including fictitious assets (e.g. P&L debit balance) in net assets.

activity.prompt: Match the method to its formula

quiz.q: Average profit ₹40,000; NRR 8%; net assets ₹4,00,000. Goodwill (capitalisation) =
quiz.why: Capitalised value of average profit = 40,000 × 100/8 = 5,00,000. Goodwill = capitalised value − net assets = 5,00,000 − 4,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.

quiz.q: Super profit ₹12,000; NRR 12%. Goodwill by capitalising super profit =
quiz.why: Goodwill by capitalising super profit = super profit × 100/NRR = 12,000 × 100/12 = ₹1,00,000.

quiz.q: Capitalised value of a business means:
options: Capital needed to earn its average profit at normal rate
quiz.why: The capitalised value is the amount of capital that would be needed to earn the firm's average profit at the normal rate of return: average profit × 100/NRR.
Net assets are total assets (excluding goodwill) less outside liabilities, which is the same as capital employed.

options: The same goodwill for same data
quiz.why: The two capitalisation methods (of average profit and of super profit) are mathematically equivalent, so they give the same goodwill for the same data.

questions.q: Goodwill is classified as:
questions.why: Goodwill is an intangible asset: it has value but no physical form. It is not current, a liability or a fictitious asset.

questions.q: Self-generated goodwill under AS 26 is:
questions.why: Under AS 26 only purchased goodwill is recorded in the books. Self-generated goodwill is not recorded, since its cost cannot be measured reliably.

questions.q: Which does NOT affect goodwill?
questions.why: Goodwill depends on factors such as management efficiency, location and market situation. The number of partners' children has no effect on the earning capacity of the firm.

questions.q: Profits ₹20,000, ₹30,000, ₹40,000; 2 years' purchase of average. Goodwill =
Normal profit is calculated on:
questions.why: Normal profit is the return that is normally expected on the capital employed, i.e. capital employed × normal rate of return.

questions.q: Assertion: Weighted average method gives more importance to recent profits. Reason: Recent profits better indicate future earning capacity.
questions.why: Both are true. The weighted average gives more weight to recent profits because they better show future earning capacity, so R explains A.

questions.q: Capital employed ₹2,00,000; NRR 15%; average profit ₹45,000; 3 years' purchase. Goodwill =
Average profit ₹36,000; NRR 12%; net assets ₹2,50,000. Goodwill by capitalisation =
Weights 1,2,3,4 on profits 10k, 20k, 30k, 40k. Weighted average profit =
Case: Profits ₹50k, ₹60k, ₹70k. Year 3 included abnormal gain ₹10k. Goodwill = 2 years' purchase of average normal profit =
questions.why: The abnormal gain of ₹10,000 is removed from year 3, so the profit is 60,000. Average = (50,000 + 60,000 + 60,000)/3 = 56,667. Goodwill = 56,667 × 2 ≈ ₹1,13,333.

questions.q: Total assets ₹8,00,000 (incl. goodwill ₹1,00,000); liabilities ₹2,00,000; NRR 10%; avg profit ₹80,000. Super profit =
Super profit ₹18,000, NRR 12%, 5 years' purchase. Goodwill by super profit method vs capitalisation of super profit:
questions.why: By super profit method: 18,000 × 5 = ₹90,000. By capitalisation of super profit: 18,000 × 100/12 = ₹1,50,000. The two methods usually give different values.

questions.q: Capitalised value ₹6,00,000; goodwill ₹1,20,000; NRR 10%. Average profit and net assets are:
questions.why: Average profit = capitalised value × NRR = 6,00,000 × 10% = ₹60,000. Net assets = capitalised value − goodwill = 6,00,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹4,80,000.

questions.q: Goodwill by capitalisation of super profit is ₹75,000 at NRR 12%. Super profit is:
questions.why: Goodwill = super profit × 100/NRR, so super profit = goodwill × NRR/100 = 75,000 × 12% = ₹9,000.

questions.q: If expected managerial remuneration ₹12,000 has not been charged, average profit should be:
questions.why: Remuneration that will be payable to managers in future is a real cost, so it must be deducted. The average profit should be reduced by ₹12,000 to show the true future profit.

questions.q: Goodwill needs valuation at:
questions.why: Goodwill has to be valued at every reconstitution of the firm, such as admission, retirement, death or change in profit-sharing ratio, as the partners' shares change.

courses.title: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio among Existing Partners
courses.summary: Sacrificing and gaining ratios, treatment of goodwill, revaluation of assets and liabilities, and accumulated profits/reserves when existing partners change their ratio.
outcomes: Learners can compute sacrificing and gaining ratios
Learners can pass goodwill adjustment entries
Learners can prepare a Revaluation Account
Learners can distribute reserves and accumulated profits/losses

scenes.text: A and B shared 3:2; now they agree to share equally.
A gives up part of his share; B gains it.
The gainer must compensate the sacrificer.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Sacrificing ratio** = Old share − New share (positive for partners who give up).
**Gaining ratio** = New share − Old share (positive for partners who gain).

In a change among existing partners, total sacrifice = total gain.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
X:Y:Z = 3:2:1 → new 2:2:2 (equal).
X: 3/6 − 2/6 = 1/6 sacrifice; Y: 2/6 − 2/6 = 0; Z: 2/6 − 1/6 = 1/6 gain. Only Z compensates X.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting the wrong way (a negative sacrifice means the partner actually gains).
- Not taking LCM before subtracting fractions.
- Assuming every partner sacrifices.

activity.prompt: P:Q = 5:3 → new ratio 1:1. P's sacrifice as a fraction — enter as decimal (e.g. 0.125).

quiz.why: Sacrificing ratio is the ratio in which partners give up their share, calculated as old share − new share.
B's old share is 1/3 and the new share is 1/2, so B gains 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. (A sacrifices 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6.)

quiz.q: In change of ratio, total sacrifice equals:
quiz.why: The shares only move between existing partners, so the total sacrificed equals the total gained.
A's share goes from 2/5 to 1/3 and B's from 2/5 to 1/3, so both sacrifice (1/15 each). C's share rises from 1/5 to 1/3, so C gains.

quiz.q: If a partner's new share > old share, he:
quiz.why: A partner whose new share is bigger than the old share gains profit share (he is a gaining partner) and has to compensate the sacrificing partners.

lessons.title: Treatment of goodwill on change in ratio

scenes.text: Firm's goodwill is valued at ₹50,000.
B gains 1/10, A sacrifices 1/10.
B must pay A for that slice of goodwill.

steps.title: Rule (AS 26 approach)
steps.body:
Goodwill is **not raised** in the books. The gaining partner's capital is **debited** and the sacrificing partner's capital is **credited** by their share of goodwill.

Entry: **Gaining Partner's Capital/Current A/c Dr, To Sacrificing Partner's Capital/Current A/c.**

If goodwill already exists in books, first write it off in the **old** ratio.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A:B 3:2 → 1:1; goodwill ₹50,000. A sacrifices 1/10 → ₹5,000. Entry: B's Capital Dr ₹5,000, To A's Capital ₹5,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — existing goodwill
steps.body: Same firm, goodwill ₹20,000 already in books. Step 1: write off in old ratio: A Dr 12,000, B Dr 8,000, To Goodwill 20,000. Step 2: adjust ₹50,000 valuation as in example 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting goodwill to a Goodwill A/c (raising goodwill) — not allowed under AS 26.
- Writing off existing goodwill in the new ratio.
- Using the full goodwill value instead of the sacrificed fraction.

activity.prompt: X:Y:Z 3:2:1 → equal. Goodwill ₹60,000. Amount Z pays X (₹)?

quiz.q: On change in ratio, goodwill is adjusted through:
quiz.why: On a change in profit-sharing ratio, goodwill is adjusted through the partners' capital (or current) accounts, with no cash needed. No separate Goodwill A/c is opened.
The gaining partner pays for the extra share, so his capital account is debited and the sacrificing partners' capital accounts are credited.

quiz.q: Existing goodwill in books is written off in:
quiz.why: Goodwill already in the books belongs to the old partners, who created it, so it is written off in the old ratio.
A's share goes from 1/2 to 3/5, a gain of 1/10. A pays 1/10 × 1,00,000 = ₹10,000 to B: A's capital is debited and B's credited.
AS 26 does not allow self-generated goodwill to be recorded. Only purchased goodwill may appear in the books.

scenes.text: The building bought years ago is now worth ₹20,000 more.
Some stock is damaged.
Old partners must get the gain or bear the loss in OLD ratio.

steps.title: Revaluation Account
steps.body:
A nominal account showing increase/decrease in assets and liabilities.
- **Debit:** decrease in assets, increase in liabilities, unrecorded liability
- **Credit:** increase in assets, decrease in liabilities, unrecorded asset
Balance = gain/loss → transferred to old partners in **old ratio**.

(Alternatively, partners may decide not to change book values and pass a single adjustment entry using sacrificing/gaining ratio.)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A:B 3:2. Building appreciated ₹20,000; stock reduced ₹5,000; provision for doubtful debts ₹1,000 created.
Revaluation: Cr 20,000; Dr 5,000 + 1,000 → **gain ₹14,000** → A ₹8,400, B ₹5,600.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — liabilities
steps.body: Creditors ₹40,000 to be reduced to ₹38,000 (gain ₹2,000); outstanding rent ₹3,000 unrecorded (loss ₹3,000). Net loss ₹1,000 shared in old ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crediting a decrease in assets.
- Sharing revaluation profit in new ratio.
- Forgetting unrecorded assets/liabilities.

activity.prompt: Debit or credit side of Revaluation A/c?

quiz.why: Profit or loss on revaluation belongs to the period before the change, so it is shared by the partners in the old ratio.

quiz.q: Increase in liability is shown on Revaluation A/c:
quiz.why: An increase in liabilities is a loss, so it is debited to the Revaluation Account. A decrease in liabilities is a gain and is credited.
The Revaluation Account records gains and losses from revaluation, so it is a nominal account.
The loss on depreciating machinery is 10% of 50,000 = ₹5,000, which is debited to the Revaluation Account.
Bringing an unrecorded asset into the books is a gain, so the Revaluation Account is credited (and the asset debited).

scenes.text: General Reserve ₹30,000 and P&L credit balance ₹10,000 are in the books.
They were earned under the old ratio.
So they go to old partners in old ratio.

steps.title: Treatment
steps.body:
Undistributed reserves and accumulated profits (General Reserve, P&L credit balance, Workmen Compensation Reserve in excess of liability, Investment Fluctuation Reserve in excess) are credited to old partners in **old ratio**. Accumulated losses (P&L debit balance, deferred revenue expenditure such as advertisement suspense) are debited in **old ratio**.

Entry: General Reserve A/c Dr, P&L A/c Dr, To Partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A:B 3:2; General Reserve ₹30,000. A gets ₹18,000; B ₹12,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — keep reserve in books
steps.body: If partners want the reserve to remain in books, pass one adjustment: compute effect = reserve × sacrifice/gain. A sacrifices 1/10 of ₹30,000 = ₹3,000 → B's Capital Dr ₹3,000, To A's Capital ₹3,000.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — Workmen Compensation Reserve
steps.body: WCR ₹15,000; claim ₹6,000. Transfer ₹6,000 to Provision for WC claim; excess ₹9,000 to partners in old ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Distributing reserves in new ratio.
- Distributing the whole WCR when there is a claim.
- Forgetting that P&L debit balance is a loss to be debited.

activity.prompt: A:B:C 2:2:1. General Reserve ₹50,000 and P&L debit balance ₹10,000. Net amount credited to C (₹)?

quiz.q: General reserve on change in ratio is credited in:
quiz.why: A general reserve was built up from profits earned by the old partners in the old ratio, so it is credited to them in the old ratio.

options: Debited to partners in old ratio
quiz.why: A debit balance of Profit & Loss is an accumulated loss from the past, so it is written off by debiting the partners in the old ratio.

quiz.q: WCR ₹20,000; claim ₹25,000. Shortfall ₹5,000 is debited to:
quiz.why: If the claim (₹25,000) is more than the provision (₹20,000), the shortfall of ₹5,000 is an extra liability and a loss, so the Revaluation A/c is debited.

quiz.q: Reserves belong to old partners because:
options: They were earned in the old ratio
quiz.why: Reserves were earned by the old partners in the old profit-sharing ratio, so they belong to the old partners.

quiz.q: Advertisement suspense (deferred revenue) on change in ratio is:
options: Debited to partners in old ratio
quiz.why: Advertisement suspense is a past expense that has not been written off, so it is a loss of the old period. The old partners are debited in the old ratio.

questions.q: Sacrificing ratio is calculated as:
questions.why: The sacrificing ratio is calculated as old ratio − new ratio. New − old gives the gaining ratio.

questions.q: On change in PSR, reserves are distributed in:
questions.why: On a change in profit-sharing ratio, existing reserves are distributed among the partners in the old ratio, as they were earned in that ratio.

questions.q: Revaluation A/c is credited with:
questions.why: The Revaluation Account is credited with gains such as an increase in the value of assets or a decrease in liabilities.

questions.q: A:B 3:1 → 1:1. A's sacrifice =
questions.why: A's old share is 3/4 and the new share is 1/2, so A sacrifices 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.q: Goodwill on change in ratio is adjusted by debiting:
questions.why: Goodwill is adjusted by debiting the gaining partner's capital account, since he receives extra profit share. The sacrificing partners' capital accounts are credited.

questions.q: Assertion: A partner who gains on change in ratio must compensate the sacrificing partner. Reason: He acquires a share of future profits including goodwill.
questions.why: Both are true. The partner who gains acquires a larger share of future profits, including the goodwill, so he must compensate those who sacrificed.

questions.q: A:B 3:2 → 2:3; goodwill ₹1,00,000. Entry:
questions.why: B's share goes from 2/5 to 3/5, a gain of 1/5. B pays 1/5 × 1,00,000 = ₹20,000 to A: B's capital is debited and A's credited.

questions.q: Machinery up ₹12,000, stock down ₹4,000, creditors up ₹2,000. Revaluation result:
questions.why: Gains: machinery up 12,000. Losses: stock down 4,000 and creditors up 2,000. Net = 12,000 − 4,000 − 2,000 = a gain of ₹6,000.

questions.q: X:Y:Z 4:3:2 → 2:3:4. Who gains and by how much?
questions.why: Old shares are 4/9, 3/9, 2/9 and new shares are 2/9, 3/9, 4/9. Z gains 4/9 − 2/9 = 2/9 and X sacrifices 2/9; Y is unchanged.

questions.q: Case: P:Q 1:1 → 3:2. General reserve ₹40,000 to remain in books. Adjustment:
questions.why: If the reserve stays in the books, P's gain of 1/10 must still be adjusted: 1/10 × 40,000 = ₹4,000, so P's capital is debited and Q's credited.

questions.q: WCR ₹30,000; claim ₹12,000; A:B 2:1. A is credited:
questions.why: The provision (₹30,000) is more than the claim (₹12,000), so the excess of ₹18,000 is a gain credited to Revaluation A/c. A's share is 2/3 of 18,000 = ₹12,000.

questions.q: A:B:C share 1:1:1 and change to 2:2:1; goodwill ₹90,000 (not in books). Which entry records the goodwill adjustment?
A, B and C share profits 1:1:1 and change to 2:2:1. Goodwill is valued at ₹90,000 and is not in the books. Considering only the goodwill adjustment, A's account is:
questions.why: A's share rises from 1/3 to 2/5, a gain of 2/5 − 1/3 = 1/15. A compensates the sacrificing partner: 1/15 × ₹90,000 = ₹6,000, so A's account is debited ₹6,000.

questions.q: Deferred revenue expenditure of ₹15,000 is written off when A:B 3:2. A is debited:
questions.why: Deferred revenue expenditure is a past loss, so it is written off in the old ratio: A's share is 3/5 × 15,000 = ₹9,000 (debit).

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason to revalue on change in ratio?
questions.why: Revaluation is done so that gains and losses from changes in asset and liability values go to the old partners. An increase in drawings is a partner's personal matter and not a reason for it.

courses.title: Admission of a Partner
courses.summary: New profit-sharing ratio, sacrificing ratio, treatment of goodwill (premium, hidden goodwill), revaluation, reserves and adjustment of capitals on the admission of a new partner.
outcomes: Learners can calculate new and sacrificing ratios in every type of question
Learners can record premium for goodwill brought in cash or not brought
Learners can find hidden goodwill
Learners can adjust capitals on the basis of the new partner's capital or vice versa

lessons.title: New ratio and sacrificing ratio on admission

scenes.text: A and B (3:2) admit C for a 1/5 share.
From whom does C's 1/5 come?
It depends on what the question says.

steps.title: Four common cases
steps.body:
1. **Only new partner's share given** → old partners sacrifice in old ratio. Remaining share (1 − new share) divided in old ratio.
2. **New partner takes shares from each old partner** (given amounts) → subtract each from old share.
3. **Old partners surrender a fraction of their own shares** → new share of old partner = old × (1 − fraction).
4. **New ratio of all partners directly given** → sacrifice = old − new.

steps.title: Solved example 1 (case 1)
steps.body: A:B 3:2; C gets 1/5. Remaining 4/5 → A = 4/5 × 3/5 = 12/25; B = 8/25; C = 5/25. **New ratio 12:8:5**. Sacrificing ratio = old ratio 3:2.

steps.title: Solved example 3 (case 3)
steps.body: A surrenders 1/3 of his share and B 1/4 of his in favour of C. A gives 3/5 × 1/3 = 1/5; B gives 2/5 × 1/4 = 1/10. New: A 2/5 = 4/10, B 3/10, C 3/10 → **4:3:3**; sacrifice 2:1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming sacrifice is always in old ratio (not true in cases 2–3).
- Leaving the new ratio unsimplified or in fractions with different denominators.
- Confusing "1/3 of his share" with "1/3 share".

activity.prompt: A:B = 2:1. C is admitted for 1/4 share. What is A's new share? Enter as decimal.

quiz.q: A:B 1:1; C admitted for 1/3. New ratio:
quiz.why: C takes 1/3, leaving 2/3 for A and B to share equally (as 1:1), so each gets 1/3. The new ratio is 1:1:1.

quiz.q: If only new partner's share is given, sacrificing ratio =
quiz.why: If only the new partner's share is stated, it is taken as coming from the old partners in their old ratio, so the sacrificing ratio equals the old ratio.

quiz.q: A:B 3:2; C takes 1/5 entirely from A. New ratio:
quiz.why: A's new share is 3/5 − 1/5 = 2/5, B's remains 2/5 and C has 1/5. The new ratio is 2:2:1.

quiz.q: A:B 5:3; new ratio A:B:C 4:3:1. Sacrificing ratio A:B =
quiz.why: A's share goes from 5/8 to 4/8, a sacrifice of 1/8. B's share stays 3/8, so B sacrifices nothing. The sacrificing ratio is 1:0.

quiz.q: Sacrificing ratio is used to distribute:
quiz.why: The sacrificing ratio is used to share the premium (goodwill) brought in by the new partner among the old partners who gave up a share.

lessons.title: Goodwill on admission — premium and hidden goodwill

scenes.text: C brings ₹30,000 as premium for goodwill.
A and B gave up shares — they get the premium.
But what if C brings no premium?

steps.title: Treatment (AS 26)
steps.body:
**(a) Premium brought in cash:** Cash/Bank Dr, To Premium for Goodwill A/c; then Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr, To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs (sacrificing ratio).
**(b) Premium not brought (or partly):** New Partner's Current/Capital A/c Dr, To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs.
**(c) Premium paid privately:** no entry.
**(d) Existing goodwill:** write off in old ratio first.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — premium in cash
steps.body: A:B 3:2; C brings ₹30,000 premium for 1/5 share (sacrifice in old ratio). A gets ₹18,000, B ₹12,000 credited to capitals.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — hidden goodwill
steps.body:
A and B's capitals (after all adjustments) ₹50,000 and ₹40,000. C brings ₹40,000 for 1/4 share.
**Step 1:** Total capital implied by C's contribution = 40,000 × 4 = ₹1,60,000.
**Step 2:** Actual total capital = 50,000 + 40,000 + 40,000 = ₹1,30,000.
**Step 3:** Hidden goodwill = ₹30,000 → C's share = 30,000 × 1/4 = ₹7,500 → C's Current A/c Dr 7,500, To A and B in sacrificing ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Raising goodwill at full value in books (not allowed).
- Distributing premium in new ratio instead of sacrificing ratio.
- In hidden goodwill, forgetting to include the new partner's own capital in the actual total.

activity.prompt: X and Y (capitals ₹70,000 and ₹50,000). Z brings ₹60,000 for 1/3 share. Hidden goodwill of the firm (₹)?

quiz.q: Premium for goodwill brought by new partner is shared by old partners in:
quiz.why: The premium brought by the new partner compensates old partners for what they sacrifice, so it is shared in the sacrificing ratio.

quiz.q: Premium paid privately to old partners:
quiz.why: A premium paid privately outside the firm does not pass through the firm's books, so no entry is made in the books.

quiz.q: Firm goodwill ₹60,000; C gets 1/4 share; C cannot bring premium. Entry:
options: C Current Dr 15,000 to sacrificing partners
quiz.why: C's share of goodwill is 1/4 × 60,000 = ₹15,000. If C cannot bring it in cash, C's current account is debited and the sacrificing partners are credited.

quiz.q: Existing goodwill on admission is written off in:
quiz.why: Goodwill already in the books belongs to the old partners and is written off in the old ratio.

quiz.q: C brings ₹50,000 for 1/5; others' capitals total ₹1,50,000. Hidden goodwill =
quiz.why: C's 50,000 for 1/5 implies the firm's total capital is 50,000 × 5 = 2,50,000. Actual capital is 1,50,000 + 50,000 = 2,00,000, so hidden goodwill is ₹50,000.

scenes.text: On C's admission, stock is revalued and a reserve exists.
Old gains and losses belong to A and B.
Then capitals are made proportionate to the new ratio.

steps.title: Revaluation and reserves
steps.body: Exactly as in change of ratio: Revaluation profit/loss and reserves/accumulated profits go to **old partners in old ratio**. The new partner gets nothing from them.

steps.title: Capital adjustment
steps.body:
**(i) Based on new partner's capital:** Total capital = New partner's capital ÷ his share; each old partner's required capital = total × new share. Surplus is withdrawn / deficiency brought in (or via current accounts).
**(ii) New partner's capital based on old partners' adjusted capitals:** Total = combined adjusted capital of old partners ÷ their combined new share; new partner's capital = total × his share.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — method (i)
steps.body: New ratio 3:2:1; C brings ₹30,000 for 1/6. Total = ₹1,80,000 → A should have ₹90,000, B ₹60,000. If A's adjusted capital is ₹1,00,000 → withdraw ₹10,000; if B's is ₹50,000 → bring ₹10,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — method (ii)
steps.body: A and B adjusted capitals ₹1,20,000 + ₹80,000 = ₹2,00,000; C admitted for 1/5. Old partners hold 4/5 → total = 2,00,000 × 5/4 = ₹2,50,000 → C brings **₹50,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving the new partner a share in revaluation profit.
- Adjusting capitals before all goodwill/revaluation/reserve entries are passed.
- Dividing by old ratio instead of new shares.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for solving an admission question
items: Record capital and premium brought by new partner
Prepare Revaluation A/c and share in old ratio
Distribute reserves/accumulated profits in old ratio
Adjust capitals and prepare the new Balance Sheet

quiz.q: Revaluation loss on admission is borne by:
quiz.why: A revaluation loss (or gain) relates to the time before the new partner joined, so it is shared by the old partners in the old ratio.

quiz.q: C brings ₹40,000 for 1/4 share. Total capital of firm =
quiz.why: C brings ₹40,000 for 1/4 share, so the total capital is 40,000 × 4 = ₹1,60,000.

quiz.q: Old partners' adjusted capitals ₹3,00,000 for 3/4 share. New partner's capital =
quiz.why: The old partners' capital of 3,00,000 represents 3/4, so total capital = 3,00,000 × 4/3 = 4,00,000. The new partner brings 1/4 of it = ₹1,00,000.

quiz.q: Does the new partner get a share in General Reserve existing at admission?
quiz.why: The general reserve was built up by the old partners, so the new partner has no claim on the existing reserve. It is shared among the old partners in the old ratio.

quiz.q: Excess capital of an old partner after adjustment is:
options: Withdrawn in cash or credited to current A/c
quiz.why: If an old partner's adjusted capital is more than needed, the excess is withdrawn in cash or credited to his current account.

lessons.title: Full admission problem and balance sheet

scenes.text: A big 6-mark question appears in the exam.
It needs ratios, premium, revaluation and new balance sheet.
Follow a fixed order and it falls into place.

steps.title: Solved problem
steps.body:
A and B share 3:2. Capitals ₹60,000 and ₹40,000; General Reserve ₹10,000. C admitted for 1/5 share, brings ₹30,000 capital and ₹10,000 premium. Building appreciated by ₹5,000.

**Step 1:** New ratio 12:8:5; sacrificing 3:2.
**Step 2:** Premium ₹10,000 → A 6,000, B 4,000.
**Step 3:** Revaluation gain ₹5,000 → A 3,000, B 2,000.
**Step 4:** Reserve ₹10,000 → A 6,000, B 4,000.
**Step 5:** Capitals: A = 60,000 + 6,000 + 3,000 + 6,000 = **₹75,000**; B = 40,000 + 4,000 + 2,000 + 4,000 = **₹50,000**; C = **₹30,000**.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Total capitals ₹1,55,000. Cash increased by ₹40,000; building ₹5,000 higher; reserve removed. The balance sheet totals must match — always tally liabilities and assets.

steps.title: Exam presentation
steps.body: Show working notes for ratios, then Revaluation A/c, Partners' Capital A/cs (columnar), then Balance Sheet. Columnar capital accounts save time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding premium to the new partner's capital.
- Forgetting to remove the reserve from the balance sheet after distributing it.
- Showing goodwill in the new balance sheet when AS 26 forbids it.

activity.prompt: In the solved problem, if the building had DEPRECIATED by ₹5,000 instead, what would A's closing capital be (₹)?

quiz.q: A and B share profits 3:2. C joins for a 1/5 share and brings ₹10,000 as goodwill premium. A and B sacrifice in their old ratio. B's share of the premium is:
quiz.why: The premium goes to the sacrificing partners in their sacrificing ratio, here the old ratio 3:2. B gets 2/5 × ₹10,000 = ₹4,000 (A gets ₹6,000).

quiz.q: Columnar capital accounts are useful because:
options: They show all partners side by side
quiz.why: Columnar capital accounts show all the partners' entries side by side in one account, which makes adjustments easier to see.

quiz.q: After distributing general reserve, it appears in the new balance sheet:
quiz.why: Once the general reserve has been distributed to the old partners' capital accounts, it no longer appears in the new balance sheet.

quiz.q: C's capital account is credited with premium brought?
options: No — premium goes to old partners
quiz.why: The premium brought by C goes to the old (sacrificing) partners' capital accounts, not to C's own capital account.

quiz.q: Total of new capitals in the problem:
quiz.why: The new capitals in the problem add up to 75,000 + 50,000 + 30,000 = ₹1,55,000.

questions.q: When only new partner's share is given, old partners sacrifice in:
questions.why: If only the new partner's share is given, the old partners are taken to sacrifice in their old ratio.

questions.q: Premium for goodwill is credited to:
questions.why: The premium for goodwill is brought by the new partner and credited to the sacrificing partners, since they give up part of their share.

questions.q: Revaluation profit on admission goes to:
questions.why: Revaluation profit relates to the period before admission, so it goes to the old partners in the old ratio.

questions.q: A:B 1:1; C admitted for 1/4. New ratio:
questions.why: C gets 1/4, leaving 3/4 for A and B equally, so each gets 3/8. C's share is 2/8, and the new ratio is 3:3:2.

questions.q: A:B 3:2; C takes 1/10 from A and 1/10 from B. New ratio:
questions.why: A's share is 3/5 − 1/10 = 5/10, B's is 2/5 − 1/10 = 3/10 and C's is 2/10. The new ratio is 5:3:2.

questions.q: Assertion: Premium paid privately is not recorded. Reason: It does not pass through the firm's books.
questions.why: Both are true. A premium paid privately does not pass through the firm's books, so it is not recorded there.

questions.q: A:B 2:1; C admitted for 1/4; goodwill of firm ₹80,000; C brings premium in cash. A receives:
questions.why: C's premium is 1/4 × 80,000 = ₹20,000. The sacrificing ratio equals the old ratio 2:1, so A gets 2/3 × 20,000 ≈ ₹13,333.

questions.q: A surrenders 1/4 of his share, B 1/2 of his, in favour of C. A:B 2:1. C's share =
questions.why: A gives up 1/4 of 2/3 = 1/6 and B gives up 1/2 of 1/3 = 1/6. C's share is 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3.

questions.q: C brings ₹60,000 for 1/4; A and B adjusted capitals ₹1,00,000 and ₹50,000. Hidden goodwill =
questions.why: C's ₹60,000 for 1/4 implies total capital of 2,40,000. Actual = 1,00,000 + 50,000 + 60,000 = 2,10,000, so hidden goodwill is ₹30,000.

questions.q: Case: A, B share 3:2 with adjusted capitals ₹90,000 and ₹60,000. C joins for 1/4 and must bring capital in proportion. C brings:
questions.why: A and B have 1,50,000 and this represents 3/4 of the total capital. The total is 1,50,000 × 4/3 = 2,00,000, so C brings 1/4 of it = ₹50,000.

questions.q: New ratio 5:3:2; C brings ₹40,000 capital. A's adjusted capital ₹1,10,000. A must:
questions.why: Total capital = 40,000 ÷ 2/10 = 2,00,000. A's 5/10 share needs 1,00,000. A has 1,10,000, so A withdraws the excess ₹10,000.

questions.q: A:B 3:2; C admitted for 1/5 share; C brings ₹20,000 premium but A and B decide goodwill already in books ₹25,000 to be written off. A's total debit for write-off:
questions.why: Goodwill already in the books (₹25,000) is written off in the old ratio 3:2. A bears 3/5 × 25,000 = ₹15,000.

questions.q: A:B 4:1; new ratio A:B:C 3:1:1. Premium ₹50,000 brought by C. A gets:
questions.why: A's share falls from 4/5 to 3/5 (a sacrifice of 1/5), while B's remains 1/5. Only A sacrifices, so A receives the whole premium of ₹50,000.

questions.q: A and B capitals ₹50,000 each, ratio 1:1. C brings ₹50,000 for 1/4 share and no premium; hidden goodwill credited to A and B. A's credit:
questions.why: Total capital implied by C's ₹50,000 for 1/4 is 2,00,000. Actual capital is 1,50,000, so hidden goodwill is 50,000. C's share of it is 12,500, shared 1:1, so A is credited ₹6,250.

questions.q: New partner's share of revaluation loss is:
questions.why: The new partner has no share in the revaluation loss because the loss relates to the time before he joined. It is borne by the old partners only.

questions.q: Which ratio is used to distribute accumulated losses on admission?
questions.why: Accumulated losses belong to the period before the new partner joined, so they are written off by the old partners in the old ratio.

courses.title: Retirement and Death of a Partner
courses.summary: Gaining ratio, goodwill adjustment, revaluation and reserves on retirement/death, settling the amount due, and profit up to the date of death with the executor's account.
outcomes: Learners can compute new and gaining ratios on retirement
Learners can adjust the retiring partner's share of goodwill
Learners can calculate the amount due and record its settlement
Learners can compute a deceased partner's profit share till death by time and sales basis

scenes.text: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires.
A and B will now share his 1/5.
Their gain decides who pays C for goodwill.

steps.title: Gaining ratio
steps.body:
**Gaining ratio = New share − Old share** of each continuing partner.
If nothing is said, continuing partners take the retiring share in their **old ratio** → gaining ratio = their old ratio.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A:B:C 2:2:1; C retires; nothing stated. New A:B = 1:1; gaining ratio 1:1.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A:B:C 3:2:1; C retires; A and B agree to share 1:1 in future. A: 1/2 − 3/6 = 0; B: 1/2 − 2/6 = 1/6. **Only B gains** — B alone compensates C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sacrificing ratio (that is for admission).
- Assuming gain is always in old ratio when a new ratio is given.

activity.prompt: P:Q:R = 5:3:2. R retires; P and Q will share 1:1. What is Q's gain? (decimal)

quiz.why: The gaining ratio is calculated as new ratio − old ratio. It shows how much each continuing partner gains when a partner retires.

quiz.q: If new ratio of continuing partners is not given, gaining ratio =
quiz.why: If the new ratio of the continuing partners is not given, they are assumed to share the retiring partner's share in their old ratio, so the gaining ratio equals their old ratio.

quiz.q: A:B:C 1:1:1; C retires. New ratio A:B:
quiz.why: A and B were sharing equally with C. After C retires they continue sharing in the ratio of their old shares, 1:1.
The gaining ratio is used to share the retiring partner's goodwill among the gaining partners, who pay for the share they acquire.

quiz.q: A:B:C 3:2:1 → A:B 3:2 after C retires. A's gain =
quiz.why: A's old share is 3/6 = 1/2 and the new share is 3/5. A gains 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10.

lessons.title: Goodwill, revaluation and reserves on retirement

scenes.text: Firm's goodwill is ₹60,000; C had 1/5.
Land has risen in value; a reserve exists.
C must get his share of all of it before leaving.

steps.title: Entries
steps.body:
**Goodwill:** Gaining partners' Capital A/cs Dr (gaining ratio), To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c (his share of goodwill). Existing goodwill written off in old ratio first.
**Revaluation:** gain/loss to **all partners in old ratio** (including retiring).
**Reserves & accumulated profits:** to all partners in **old ratio**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A:B:C 2:2:1, C retires; goodwill ₹50,000. C's share = ₹10,000. Gaining ratio 1:1 → A Dr 5,000, B Dr 5,000, To C 10,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A:B:C 3:2:1 → A:B 1:1 (only B gains 1/6). Goodwill ₹36,000. C's share ₹6,000; **B Dr ₹6,000, To C ₹6,000**. A not affected.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Debiting continuing partners in new ratio instead of gaining ratio.
- Excluding the retiring partner from revaluation profit.
- Raising full goodwill in books.

activity.prompt: X:Y:Z 2:2:1. Z retires; X and Y continue 3:2. Goodwill ₹1,00,000. Amount debited to X for goodwill (₹)?

quiz.q: Revaluation profit on retirement is credited to:
quiz.why: Revaluation profit or loss belongs to all the partners, including the retiring one, in the old ratio, as it arose while they were partners.

quiz.q: Retiring partner's share of goodwill is borne by:
quiz.why: The retiring partner's share of goodwill is borne by the gaining partners, in the ratio in which they gain, as they get the benefit of his share.

quiz.q: General reserve on retirement goes to:
quiz.why: The general reserve belongs to all the partners and is credited to them (including the retiring one) in the old ratio.
C's share of goodwill = 1/4 × 80,000 = ₹20,000.

quiz.q: If a continuing partner's share falls on retirement of another, that partner is:
quiz.why: If a continuing partner's share falls, he is giving up a part of the profit, so he sacrifices and is credited.

lessons.title: Amount due to the retiring partner and its settlement

scenes.text: C's capital after all adjustments is ₹82,000.
The firm pays ₹20,000 now; the rest becomes a loan.
It is repaid in instalments with interest.

steps.title: Calculating the amount due
steps.body:
Amount due = Capital balance + Share of goodwill + Share of revaluation gain + Share of reserves + Interest on capital/salary till date − Drawings − Interest on drawings − Share of losses.

Settlement: paid in cash, or transferred to **Retiring Partner's Loan A/c** (Section 37: if not settled, he may claim 6% p.a. interest or share of profit attributable to his money, at his option).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: C's capital ₹60,000; goodwill share ₹10,000; revaluation gain ₹4,000; reserve ₹8,000. Amount due = **₹82,000**. Paid ₹20,000 → C's Capital Dr 82,000, To Bank 20,000, To C's Loan 62,000.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — instalments
steps.body: Loan ₹60,000 repaid in 3 equal annual instalments + 10% interest on balance. Year 1: interest 6,000; pay 20,000 + 6,000 = 26,000. Year 2: interest 4,000; pay 24,000. Year 3: interest 2,000; pay 22,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting drawings when computing amount due.
- Charging interest on the original loan every year instead of on the outstanding balance.

activity.prompt: Retiring partner's loan ₹90,000 repaid in 3 equal annual instalments plus 12% interest on the outstanding balance. Total payment at end of year 1 (₹)?

quiz.q: Unpaid amount due to retiring partner is transferred to:
quiz.why: If the retiring partner is not paid in full, the unpaid amount is transferred to his Loan Account, which is paid later with interest.

quiz.q: Under Section 37, if not settled, retiring partner may claim interest at:
quiz.why: If the amount due is not settled, under Section 37 the retiring partner may claim interest at 6% p.a. or a share of profits earned.
Drawings are amounts already taken out by the partner, so they reduce the amount due to him. Goodwill, reserve share and revaluation gain increase it.

quiz.q: Loan ₹40,000; two equal instalments + 10% interest. First payment:
quiz.why: Each equal instalment is 20,000, plus interest on the full balance 10% × 40,000 = 4,000 for the first payment. First payment = 24,000.

quiz.q: Interest on retiring partner's loan is:
quiz.why: Interest on the retiring partner's loan is a charge against profit, debited to the Profit & Loss Account, and not an appropriation of profit.

scenes.text: Partner D dies on 30 June; the year ends on 31 March.
His estate is entitled to his profit share up to the date of death.
Payment goes to his executor (legal representative).

steps.title: What changes on death
steps.body:
All retirement adjustments apply (goodwill, revaluation, reserves) PLUS:
- **Profit up to date of death** — by time basis or sales (turnover) basis
- Amount due credited to **Deceased Partner's Executor's A/c**

Entry for profit share: **Profit & Loss Suspense A/c Dr, To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c** (or debit continuing partners in gaining ratio).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — time basis
steps.body:
Last year's profit ₹60,000; D's share 1/4; death on 30 June (3 months from 1 April).
Share = 60,000 × 3/12 × 1/4 = **₹3,750**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sales basis
steps.body:
Last year: sales ₹4,00,000, profit ₹40,000 (10%). Sales from 1 April to date of death ₹1,20,000. D's share 1/3.
Profit till death = 1,20,000 × 10% = ₹12,000 → D's share = **₹4,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 12 months instead of months till death.
- Applying last year's profit ratio to sales without computing the rate.
- Crediting the amount to "Deceased Partner's Loan" instead of Executor's A/c.

activity.prompt: Average profit of last 3 years ₹72,000. Partner (share 1/3) dies 4 months after the start of the year. His share of profit till death (time basis, ₹)?

quiz.q: Deceased partner's balance is transferred to:
quiz.why: The amount due to a deceased partner is transferred to his Executor's (or legal representative's) Account, from which it is paid.

quiz.q: Profit till death on time basis uses:
options: Months from start of year to death
quiz.why: On the time basis, the profit up to the date of death is the profit of the year × (months from the start of the year to death)/12.

options: Debited with deceased partner's share of profit
quiz.why: The deceased partner's share of profit up to death is estimated and debited to the Profit & Loss Suspense A/c, and credited to his capital account.

quiz.q: Sales till death ₹2,00,000; profit rate 15%; share 1/2. Share =
quiz.why: Profit till death = 2,00,000 × 15% = 30,000. The deceased's share is 1/2 × 30,000 = ₹15,000.

quiz.q: Goodwill on death is adjusted in:
quiz.why: As in retirement, goodwill share of the deceased partner is borne by the surviving partners in the gaining ratio.

questions.q: On retirement, goodwill is debited to continuing partners in:
questions.why: On retirement, the retiring partner's goodwill share is debited to the continuing partners in the gaining ratio, since they gain from his share.

questions.q: Revaluation on retirement is shared in:
questions.why: Revaluation profit or loss is shared in the old ratio among all partners, including the retiring partner, as it relates to the past.

questions.q: Amount due to a deceased partner is credited to:
questions.why: The amount due to a deceased partner is credited to his executor's account, and from this the executors are paid.

questions.q: A:B:C 1:1:1; C retires. Gaining ratio:
questions.why: A and B continue and share equally as before, so each gains 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. The gaining ratio is 1:1.

questions.q: Retiring partner's unpaid amount carries interest (if not agreed) at:
questions.why: Under Section 37, a retiring partner whose dues are not settled may claim interest at 6% p.a. (or a share of profit).

questions.q: Assertion: Retiring partner gets a share in revaluation profit. Reason: Revaluation reflects changes in value during his time as partner.
questions.why: Both are true. Revaluation shows changes in value during his time as a partner, so the retiring partner shares in the profit or loss, and R explains A.

questions.q: A:B:C 5:3:2; C retires; A and B share 3:2. Gaining ratio:
questions.why: A gains 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10 and B gains 2/5 − 3/10 = 1/10, so the gaining ratio is 1:1.

questions.q: Goodwill ₹90,000; C (1/3) retires; A and B gain 1:2. B is debited:
questions.why: C's goodwill share is 1/3 × 90,000 = 30,000. A and B gain in the ratio 1:2, so B bears 2/3 × 30,000 = ₹20,000.

questions.q: Profit last year ₹1,20,000; partner (1/5) dies on 31 July; year starts 1 April. Share (time basis):
questions.why: The year starts on 1 April, so death on 31 July is 4 months in. Share = 1,20,000 × 4/12 × 1/5 = ₹8,000.

questions.q: Case: D's capital ₹50,000; goodwill share ₹12,000; revaluation loss share ₹2,000; drawings ₹5,000; profit till death ₹3,000. Amount due:
questions.why: Amount due = capital 50,000 + goodwill 12,000 − revaluation loss 2,000 − drawings 5,000 + profit 3,000 = ₹58,000.

questions.q: Loan ₹1,20,000 repaid in 4 equal annual instalments with 10% interest on balance. Total interest over the period:
questions.why: Instalments of 30,000 each. Interest on the balance at 10%: 12,000 + 9,000 + 6,000 + 3,000 = ₹30,000.

questions.q: Sales last year ₹5,00,000, profit ₹50,000. Sales till death ₹1,50,000. Deceased share 2/5. His share:
questions.why: Last year's profit is 10% of sales (50,000/5,00,000). Profit till death = 1,50,000 × 10% = 15,000. The deceased's share is 2/5 × 15,000 = ₹6,000.

questions.q: A:B:C 4:3:2; C retires; his share taken by A and B equally. New ratio A:B:
questions.why: C's share is 2/9, split equally between A and B (1/9 each). A's new share is 4/9 + 1/9 = 5/9 and B's is 3/9 + 1/9 = 4/9, so 5:4.

questions.q: A:B:C 3:2:1; B retires. A and C share 2:1 in future. Gaining ratio A:C:
questions.why: A's gain is 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6 and C's gain is 1/3 − 1/6 = 1/6. Both gain equally, so the ratio is 1:1.

questions.q: Executor's A/c is a:
questions.why: The Executor's Account is the account of a person (the deceased partner's legal representative), so it is a personal account.

questions.q: Retiring partner's share of accumulated losses is:
questions.why: Accumulated losses belong to all partners, so the retiring partner's share is debited to his capital account (reducing his amount due).

courses.title: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
courses.summary: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm, modes of dissolution, settlement of accounts under Section 48, and the Realisation Account with complete solved problems.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish dissolution of partnership from dissolution of the firm
Learners can list the modes of dissolution
Learners can apply the order of settlement under Section 48
Learners can prepare Realisation, Partners' Capital and Cash/Bank accounts

scenes.text: After ten years Riya and Kabir decide to close the bakery.
This is dissolution of the FIRM, not just a change in partners.
The law lists how a firm can be dissolved.

steps.title: Partnership vs firm
steps.body:
**Dissolution of partnership:** relationship among partners changes (admission, retirement, death, change in ratio) but the **firm continues**.
**Dissolution of firm:** relationship among **all** partners ends; business closes; assets realised and liabilities paid.

steps.title: Modes of dissolution of a firm
steps.body:
- **By agreement** (Sec 40)
- **Compulsory** (Sec 41): all/all but one partner insolvent, or business becomes illegal
- **On happening of contingencies** (Sec 42): expiry of term, completion of venture, death/insolvency of a partner (subject to contract)
- **By notice** (Sec 43) in a partnership at will
- **By court** (Sec 44): partner of unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach, transfer of interest, perpetual losses, just and equitable grounds

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A partner becomes of unsound mind → another partner may apply to court → **dissolution by court**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: The firm's business (say, a banned product) becomes illegal → **compulsory dissolution**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying every dissolution of partnership dissolves the firm.
- Confusing "by notice" (partnership at will) with "by court".

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the mode of dissolution
pairs: Partner at will gives written notice

quiz.q: On dissolution of partnership, the firm:
quiz.why: Dissolution of partnership means the partners' relationship ends, but the firm may continue under a new arrangement. Dissolution of the firm is when it closes.

quiz.q: Insolvency of all partners leads to:
quiz.why: If all the partners (or all but one) become insolvent, the firm is dissolved compulsorily by law.

quiz.q: Dissolution by court can happen when a partner:
quiz.why: A court can order dissolution if a partner becomes of unsound mind, among other grounds such as permanent incapacity or persistent breaches.
A partnership at will, with no fixed term, can be dissolved by a partner giving notice to the others.

quiz.q: Which section deals with settlement of accounts?
quiz.why: Section 48 of the Partnership Act deals with the mode of settlement of accounts between the partners after dissolution.

scenes.text: Assets fetch ₹90,000.
Outsiders, partners' loans, capitals — in what order?
Section 48 sets the order.

steps.title: Order of payment
steps.body:
Losses (including capital deficiencies) are paid first out of profits, then out of capital, then by partners individually in profit-sharing ratio.

Assets (including sums contributed by partners) are applied in this order:
1. **Debts of the firm to third parties** (outside liabilities)
2. **Partners' loans/advances** (as distinguished from capital), rateably
3. **Partners' capitals**, rateably
4. Surplus, if any, divided in profit-sharing ratio

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Assets realised ₹1,00,000. Creditors ₹50,000; A's loan ₹10,000; capitals A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000 (PSR 1:1).
**Step 1:** Pay creditors ₹50,000 → ₹50,000 left.
**Step 2:** Repay A's loan ₹10,000 → ₹40,000 left.
**Step 3:** Capitals total ₹50,000 but only ₹40,000 remains → loss ₹10,000 shared 1:1 (₹5,000 each).
**Step 4:** Pay A ₹25,000 and B ₹15,000. Total ₹40,000 ✓.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Partner's private debts vs firm's debts: firm's property is first used for firm's debts; a partner's private property is first used for his private debts; any surplus may then go to the other side.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying partners' capitals before partners' loans.
- Paying partners before outsiders.

activity.prompt: Order of applying the firm's assets on dissolution (Section 48)
items: Distribute any surplus in profit-sharing ratio

quiz.q: First claim on the firm's assets on dissolution belongs to:
quiz.why: On dissolution, the firm's assets are first applied to pay outside creditors (external liabilities).
Partners' loans are paid after outside creditors but before partners' capital, since a loan is a liability of the firm to the partner.

quiz.q: Losses on dissolution are first met from:
quiz.why: Losses on dissolution are first met out of profits, then out of capital, and finally by the partners from their private assets.

quiz.q: Surplus after paying capitals is shared in:
