scenes.text: Sweet Bites made a profit but cannot pay salaries.
Profit is not cash: customers have not paid yet.
A Cash Flow Statement shows where cash came from and went.

steps.title: Meaning (AS 3)
steps.body:
A **cash flow statement** shows inflows and outflows of **cash and cash equivalents** during a period.
**Cash** = cash in hand + demand deposits with banks.
**Cash equivalents** = short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value — generally with original maturity of **three months or less** (e.g. treasury bills, commercial paper, short-term deposits).
Movements between cash and cash equivalents are **not** cash flows.

steps.title: Three activities
steps.body:
- **Operating:** principal revenue-producing activities (cash from customers, payments to suppliers and employees, income tax paid)
- **Investing:** acquisition/disposal of long-term assets and investments not part of cash equivalents (buy/sell machinery, purchase of shares of other companies, interest and dividend **received** by a non-financial company)
- **Financing:** changes in size/composition of owners' capital and borrowings (issue of shares/debentures, repayment of loans, interest **paid**, dividend **paid**)

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Classify (non-financial company): purchase of building → investing outflow; issue of debentures → financing inflow; payment to creditors → operating outflow; dividend received → investing inflow; interest on debentures paid → financing outflow.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — financial company
steps.body: For a bank/finance company, interest and dividend received and interest paid are **operating** activities (it is their main business). Dividend paid is still financing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating purchase of a 6-month deposit as a cash equivalent (maturity > 3 months).
- Classifying interest paid by a manufacturing company as operating.
- Treating conversion of debentures into shares as a cash flow — it is a non-cash transaction.

activity.prompt: Classify for a manufacturing company

quiz.q: Cash equivalents generally have original maturity of:
quiz.why: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments with an original maturity of 3 months or less.

quiz.q: Dividend paid by a company is a/an ___ activity.
quiz.why: A dividend paid is a payment to the providers of capital (owners), so it is a financing activity.

quiz.q: Interest received by a non-financial company:
quiz.why: For a non-financial company, interest received is a return on investment, so it is shown under investing activities.
Purchase of goodwill (a long-term asset) is a cash outflow under investing activities.
Bonus shares involve no cash, so they are a non-cash transaction and are not shown in the cash flow statement.

lessons.title: Cash from operating activities — indirect method

scenes.text: Start with profit before tax.
Add back non-cash items, remove non-operating items.
Then adjust for working-capital changes.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Net profit before tax and extraordinary items** (= Profit for the year + provision for tax (current year) + proposed dividend if deducted + transfers to reserves, etc.)
2. **Add:** depreciation, amortisation (goodwill, patents), loss on sale of non-current assets, interest paid (finance cost), writing off of discount on issue.
**Less:** profit on sale of non-current assets, interest/dividend received.
= **Operating profit before working capital changes**
3. **Working capital:** increase in current assets (−), decrease in current assets (+); increase in current liabilities (+), decrease in current liabilities (−).
4. **Less:** income tax paid → **Net cash from operating activities.**

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
PBT ₹1,00,000; depreciation ₹20,000; loss on sale of machinery ₹5,000; increase in trade receivables ₹15,000; decrease in inventory ₹10,000; increase in trade payables ₹8,000; tax paid ₹25,000.
Operating profit before WC = 1,25,000; WC adjustments = −15,000 + 10,000 + 8,000 = +3,000 → 1,28,000; less tax → **₹1,03,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — finding PBT
steps.body:
Surplus (P&L balance) rose from ₹50,000 to ₹80,000; transfer to general reserve ₹20,000; provision for tax made ₹30,000.
PBT = 30,000 (increase) + 20,000 + 30,000 = **₹80,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding an increase in trade receivables.
- Forgetting to add back transfer to reserve and tax provision to get PBT.
- Including interest received in operating profit for a non-financial company.

activity.prompt: PBT ₹2,00,000; depreciation ₹30,000; profit on sale of land ₹10,000; increase in inventory ₹25,000; decrease in trade payables ₹5,000; tax paid ₹50,000. Net cash from operating activities (₹)?

quiz.q: Depreciation in the indirect method is:
quiz.why: Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so under the indirect method it is added back to net profit to get cash from operations.
An increase in trade receivables means sales that have not yet brought in cash, so it is deducted from operating profit.

quiz.q: Profit on sale of machinery is:
quiz.why: Profit on sale of machinery is included in profit but the cash from the sale belongs in investing activities, so it is deducted from operating profit.

quiz.q: Increase in outstanding expenses (current liability) is:
quiz.why: An increase in outstanding expenses means expenses were charged but not paid in cash, so it is added to operating profit.

quiz.q: Interest on debentures (finance cost) in operating section:
quiz.why: Interest paid is classified under financing activities, so the interest expense (finance cost) is added back to profit in operating activities.

scenes.text: New machinery bought; an old one sold.
Shares issued; a loan repaid; dividend paid.
Each goes to its own section.

steps.title: Finding hidden figures
steps.body:
Use the asset account: Opening + Purchases − Book value of sales − Depreciation = Closing.
Cash from sale = Book value ± profit/loss.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Machinery: opening ₹2,00,000; closing ₹2,50,000; depreciation ₹30,000; machinery of book value ₹30,000 sold at a loss of ₹5,000.
Purchases = 2,50,000 + 30,000 + 30,000 − 2,00,000 = **₹1,10,000**. Sale proceeds = **₹25,000**.
Investing: −1,10,000 + 25,000 = **−₹85,000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — financing
steps.body:
Equity shares: 4,00,000 → 5,00,000 (issued for cash); 10% debentures: 2,00,000 → 1,40,000 (redeemed at par); interest paid ₹20,000; dividend paid ₹40,000.
Financing = +1,00,000 − 60,000 − 20,000 − 40,000 = **−₹20,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting depreciation when finding purchases.
- Showing book value instead of sale proceeds as investing inflow.
- Showing dividend paid under operating.

activity.prompt: Machinery opening ₹5,00,000, closing ₹6,00,000, depreciation for year ₹60,000, no sales. Purchase of machinery (₹)?

quiz.q: Sale proceeds of an asset with book value ₹40,000 sold at a profit of ₹6,000:
quiz.why: Sale proceeds = book value + profit = 40,000 + 6,000 = ₹46,000.
Redemption of debentures for cash repays a long-term borrowing, which is a financing outflow.
Purchase of long-term investments uses cash for long-term assets, so it is an investing outflow.

options: Not shown in cash flow statement
quiz.why: Issuing shares for machinery involves no cash flow, so it is a non-cash transaction and is not shown in the cash flow statement.
Repayment of a long-term loan is a payment to a lender, so it is a financing outflow.

scenes.text: Operating, investing and financing — together.
Their total = change in cash and cash equivalents.
Check against opening and closing cash.

steps.title: Solved problem
steps.body:
Using earlier figures:
**A. Operating:** ₹1,03,000
**B. Investing:** purchase of machinery (80,000); sale of machinery 25,000 → (₹55,000)
**C. Financing:** issue of shares 50,000; repayment of loan (40,000); interest paid (6,000); dividend paid (20,000) → (₹16,000)
**Net increase** = 1,03,000 − 55,000 − 16,000 = **₹32,000**.
Opening cash & equivalents ₹18,000 → closing **₹50,000** ✓.

steps.title: Presentation
steps.body: Use brackets for outflows. Show "Net cash from (used in) operating/investing/financing activities" as subtotals. End with: Net increase/(decrease), add opening cash and cash equivalents, closing cash and cash equivalents.

steps.title: Objectives and uses
steps.body: Helps assess ability to generate cash, meet obligations and pay dividends; explains difference between profit and cash; aids short-term planning; required by AS 3 for companies (except some small companies).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not tallying the final figure with the Balance Sheet cash.
- Double-counting interest (adding back in operating AND showing as operating outflow).

activity.prompt: Operating ₹1,50,000; investing (₹90,000); financing (₹20,000); opening cash ₹15,000. Closing cash and cash equivalents (₹)?

quiz.q: Total of the three activities equals:
options: Net change in cash and cash equivalents
quiz.why: The total of cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities equals the net change in cash and cash equivalents.
By convention, cash outflows are shown in brackets, so inflows and outflows can be told apart.

quiz.q: Cash flow statement is prepared as per:
quiz.why: The cash flow statement is prepared as per AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements).
Net change = 80,000 − 1,00,000 + 50,000 = +30,000. The outflow from investing is deducted.
A cash flow statement shows the cash inflows and outflows, which explains why profit can differ from the cash actually available.

questions.q: Cash flow statement is governed by:
questions.why: The cash flow statement is prepared as per AS 3.

questions.q: Purchase of machinery is:
questions.why: Buying machinery acquires a long-term asset, so it is an investing activity (an outflow).

questions.q: Dividend paid is:
questions.why: A dividend paid is a payment to owners who provided capital, so it is a financing activity.

questions.q: Depreciation is added back because it is:
questions.why: Depreciation is charged in arriving at profit but involves no cash payment, so it is added back as a non-cash expense.

questions.q: Decrease in trade payables is:
questions.why: A decrease in trade payables means more cash was paid to suppliers than expenses charged, so it is deducted from operating profit.

questions.q: Assertion: Interest paid by a manufacturing company is a financing activity. Reason: It is a cost of obtaining financial resources.
questions.why: Both are true. Interest paid is the cost of obtaining financial resources (borrowings), so it is treated as a financing activity.

questions.q: Purchase of a treasury bill maturing in 60 days is:
questions.why: A treasury bill maturing in 60 days (3 months or less) is a cash equivalent, so buying it is just a conversion of cash and not a cash flow.

questions.q: Surplus rose ₹40,000; transfer to reserve ₹10,000; tax provision ₹20,000. PBT:
questions.why: The surplus rose by 40,000 after setting aside reserve (10,000) and tax (20,000), so PBT = 40,000 + 10,000 + 20,000 = ₹70,000.

questions.q: Opening machinery 3,00,000; closing 3,50,000; depreciation 40,000; asset of BV 20,000 sold. Purchases:
questions.why: Machinery purchases = closing 3,50,000 + depreciation 40,000 + book value of machinery sold 20,000 − opening 3,00,000 = ₹1,10,000.

questions.q: Case: PBT 1,50,000; depreciation 25,000; interest paid 10,000; dividend received 5,000; increase in receivables 20,000; tax paid 40,000. Cash from operations:
questions.why: PBT 1,50,000 + depreciation 25,000 + interest paid 10,000 (financing) − dividend received 5,000 (investing) = 1,80,000. Less increase in receivables 20,000 = 1,60,000, less tax paid 40,000 = ₹1,20,000.

questions.q: Case: Investment (BV ₹50,000) sold at 10% profit; new investment bought ₹80,000. Net investing:
questions.why: The investment sold at 10% profit brings 55,000 inflow. The new investment is an outflow of 80,000. Net investing = 55,000 − 80,000 = (₹25,000).

questions.q: For a finance company, interest received is:
questions.why: For a finance company, lending and earning interest are the main business, so interest received is an operating activity.

questions.q: Case: Debentures 5,00,000 → 3,00,000 redeemed at 5% premium; interest paid 35,000; shares issued at 10% premium ₹2,00,000 (face). Net financing:
questions.why: Shares: 2,00,000 + 10% premium = +2,20,000; debentures redeemed 2,00,000 at 5% premium = −2,10,000; interest −35,000. Net = −₹25,000.

questions.q: Net increase in cash ₹12,000; closing cash ₹40,000. Opening cash:
questions.why: Opening cash = closing cash − net increase = 40,000 − 12,000 = ₹28,000.

questions.q: Conversion of debentures into equity shares:
questions.why: Converting debentures into equity shares involves no cash, so it is a non-cash transaction and is not shown in the cash flow statement.

questions.q: Income tax paid is generally classified as:
questions.why: Income tax paid is generally classified as an operating activity unless it can be specifically tied to investing or financing.

courses.title: Revision & Practice — Class 12 Accountancy

outcomes: Learners can recall every key formula and rule quickly
Learners can avoid the most common exam errors
Learners can attempt mixed questions under time pressure

scenes.text: Riya has one hour left to revise partnership.
She keeps a one-page sheet of rules and ratios.

steps.title: Defaults (no deed)
steps.body: Equal profit share · no interest on capital · no interest on drawings · no salary · interest on partner's loan 6% p.a. (charge)

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body: Sacrificing = Old − New (admission/change) · Gaining = New − Old (retirement/death/change) · New partner's share only given → sacrifice in old ratio

steps.title: Goodwill
steps.body: Average profit × years · Super profit = Avg − Normal; × years · Capitalisation: Avg × 100/NRR − Net assets · Super profit × 100/NRR · Hidden goodwill = implied total capital − actual total capital

steps.title: Interest on drawings average periods
steps.body: Beginning of month 6½ · middle 6 · end 5½ · beginning of quarter 7½ · end of quarter 4½ · unknown dates 6

steps.title: Dissolution order (Sec 48)
steps.body: Outside debts → partners' loans → partners' capitals → surplus in PSR

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: Always write working notes for ratios first. Use columnar capital accounts. Tally the balance sheet.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body: Wrong ratio for the wrong item (old vs new vs sacrificing vs gaining) is the #1 error — make a table: item → ratio.

quiz.q: Interest on drawings at beginning of each quarter: period
quiz.why: Drawings at the beginning of each quarter remain for 12, 9, 6 and 3 months. The average period is (12 + 9 + 6 + 3)/4 = 7½ months.

options: New partner's capital implies higher total capital than actual
quiz.why: Hidden goodwill arises when the capital brought by the new partner implies a higher total capital for the firm than the actual capital.

quiz.q: Partner's loan on dissolution is paid:
quiz.why: On dissolution, a partner's loan is paid after outside creditors but before partners' capital.
Reserves existing at admission were earned by the old partners, so they belong to the old partners in the old ratio.

quiz.q: Deficiency of guaranteed partner borne by guarantors (unspecified) in:
quiz.why: If the guarantee does not say how the deficiency is shared, the guarantors bear it in their own profit-sharing ratio.

scenes.text: Six journal patterns cover most share questions.
Four cover most debenture questions.

steps.title: Share capital
steps.body: Paid-up = called-up − calls in arrears · forfeiture: Share Capital Dr (called-up) [+ Securities Premium Dr if unpaid], To unpaid calls, To Forfeiture (received) · Capital reserve = forfeited amount on reissued shares − discount on reissue

steps.title: Pro-rata
steps.body: Excess application money adjusts to allotment (then calls); defaulter owes allotment − his excess

steps.title: Securities premium (Sec 52) uses
steps.body: Bonus shares · preliminary expenses · issue expenses/discount · premium on redemption · buy-back. Never dividend.

steps.title: Debentures
steps.body: Issue at discount / redeem at premium: Bank Dr, Loss on Issue Dr, To Debentures, To Premium on Redemption. Write off loss: Securities Premium first, then Statement of P&L. Interest on face value; TDS deducted.

steps.title: Schedule III heads
steps.body: Shareholders' funds · Non-current liabilities · Current liabilities | Non-current assets · Current assets

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body: Debiting Securities Premium on forfeiture when premium was already received; crediting Securities Premium for premium payable on redemption.

cards.back: Added to share capital in notes

quiz.q: Forfeited share balance on reissued shares after discount goes to:
quiz.why: After meeting the discount on reissue, the balance left in the Share Forfeiture Account is a capital profit, transferred to Capital Reserve.

quiz.q: Premium on redemption of debentures is a:
quiz.why: Premium on redemption of debentures is an amount the company must pay later, so it is a liability.

quiz.q: Max interest on calls in arrears (Table F):
quiz.why: Under Table F, interest on calls in arrears is charged at a rate not exceeding 10% p.a.
Unpaid dividend is a liability for amounts that are due to shareholders, shown under Other Current Liabilities.

quiz.q: Shares at discount allowed only as:
quiz.why: A company may issue shares at a discount only as sweat equity shares (to employees or directors). Otherwise a discount is prohibited by Section 53.

scenes.text: Four families, fifteen formulas.
Learn them as pairs: formula + meaning.

steps.title: Liquidity
steps.body: Current = CA/CL · Quick = (CA − inventories − prepaid)/CL

steps.title: Solvency
steps.body: Debt-equity = LTD/SHF · Total assets to debt = TA/LTD · Proprietary = SHF/TA · Interest coverage = PBIT/interest

steps.title: Activity
steps.body: Inventory TO = COGS/avg inventory · Receivables TO = credit revenue/avg (debtors + B/R) · Payables TO = credit purchases/avg (creditors + B/P) · WC TO = revenue/WC

steps.title: Profitability
steps.body: GP% · Operating ratio = (COGS + op. exp.)/revenue · Operating profit% = 100 − OR · NP% = PAT/revenue · ROI = PBIT/capital employed

steps.title: Analysis tools
steps.body: Comparative (horizontal; % change on previous year) · Common-size (vertical; P&L base = revenue from operations, BS base = total assets)

cards.back: Total assets − current liabilities (= SHF + non-current liabilities)

quiz.why: Interest coverage ratio is PBIT divided by interest, since it measures how easily operating profit covers the interest.
In a common-size balance sheet, the base (100%) is total assets (or total of equity and liabilities).
Operating profit ratio = 100% − operating ratio = 100 − 75 = 25%.
Debt-equity measures the long-term financial structure and the ability to meet long-term obligations, so it is a solvency ratio.
Inventory turnover is calculated as cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory, so the numerator is COGS.

scenes.text: Three sections, one reconciliation.
End figure must equal the Balance Sheet cash.

steps.title: Operating (indirect)
steps.body: PBT + depreciation/amortisation + loss on sale + finance cost − profit on sale − interest/dividend received = operating profit before WC; ± WC changes (CA up −, CA down +, CL up +, CL down −); − tax paid

steps.title: Investing
steps.body: Purchase/sale of PPE, intangibles, long-term investments; interest & dividend received (non-financial co.)

steps.title: Financing
steps.body: Issue/redemption of shares & debentures (incl. premium), borrowings raised/repaid, interest paid, dividend paid

steps.title: Cash equivalents
steps.body: Highly liquid, original maturity ≤ 3 months; movements within cash & cash equivalents are not cash flows

steps.title: PBT from balance sheets
steps.body: Increase in Surplus + transfers to reserves + current-year tax provision + (interim/final dividend paid if deducted)

cards.front: Profit on sale of machinery in operating section?

quiz.why: An increase in inventory uses up cash, so it is deducted from operating profit in the cash flow statement.
Premium paid on redemption of debentures is a payment related to the repayment of borrowings, so it is a financing outflow.
Purchase of patents is the acquisition of a long-term asset, so it is an investing outflow.
Money raised by issuing debentures is borrowing, so it is a financing inflow.
A fixed deposit with a 2-month maturity (3 months or less) is a cash equivalent, so it is not treated as a separate investment.

questions.q: Mock A1 · Without a deed, interest on capital is:
questions.why: If the partnership deed does not provide for it, partners are not allowed any interest on capital.

questions.q: Mock A2 · Securities premium cannot be used for:
questions.why: Securities premium may be used for bonus shares, buy-back and writing off issue expenses or discount, but not for paying dividends.

questions.q: Mock A3 · A:B 3:2; C gets 1/5 from A. New ratio:
questions.why: C takes 1/5 from A, so A's share is 3/5 − 1/5 = 2/5, B's stays 2/5, and C has 1/5. The new ratio is 2:2:1.

questions.q: Mock A4 · Current ratio 2.5; quick ratio 1.5; CL ₹40,000. Inventory:
questions.why: Current ratio − quick ratio = inventory/CL = 2.5 − 1.5 = 1. So inventory = 1 × 40,000 = ₹40,000.

questions.q: Mock A5 · Avg profit ₹50,000; NRR 10%; net assets ₹4,00,000. Goodwill (capitalisation):
Mock A6 · Forfeited 100 shares (₹10 called, ₹6 paid); reissued at ₹8 fully paid. Capital reserve:
questions.why: The amount forfeited is 100 × 6 = ₹600. Discount on reissue at ₹8 for a ₹10 share = 100 × 2 = ₹200. Capital reserve = 600 − 200 = ₹400.

questions.q: Mock A7 · Case: PBT ₹80,000; depreciation ₹12,000; increase in debtors ₹6,000; increase in creditors ₹4,000; tax paid ₹20,000. Cash from operations:
questions.why: Start with PBT 80,000, add depreciation 12,000 = 92,000. Less increase in debtors 6,000 and add increase in creditors 4,000 = 90,000. Less tax paid 20,000 = ₹70,000.

questions.q: Mock A8 · Loan ₹60,000 to retiring partner, 3 equal annual instalments + 10% on balance. Second payment:
questions.why: Each instalment is 20,000. Before the second payment the balance is 40,000, so interest is 10% × 40,000 = 4,000. Second payment = 24,000.

questions.q: Mock A9 · Assertion: Debentures issued as collateral carry no interest. Reason: No money is received for them.
questions.why: Both are true. Collateral debentures bring no money to the company, so there is no loan on them and no interest is paid.

questions.q: Mock A10 · Revenue ₹6,00,000 at cost + 20%; avg inventory ₹50,000. Inventory turnover:
questions.why: Cost + 20% means COGS = 6,00,000 × 100/120 = 5,00,000. Inventory turnover = 5,00,000/50,000 = 10 times.

questions.q: Mock B1 · Dividend paid in cash flow statement:
questions.why: Dividend paid goes to the company's owners (providers of capital), so it is shown under financing activities.

questions.q: Mock B2 · Revaluation profit on retirement credited to:
questions.why: Revaluation profit on retirement belongs to all partners, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio.

questions.q: Mock B3 · Interest on debentures in Statement of P&L:
questions.why: Interest on debentures is a cost of borrowing, so it is shown under Finance Costs.

questions.q: Mock B4 · Drawings ₹2,000 at end of each month, 12% p.a. Interest:
questions.why: Drawings of ₹24,000 in a year (2,000 × 12) have an average period of 5½ months for end-of-month drawings. Interest = 24,000 × 12% × 5.5/12 = ₹1,320.

questions.q: Mock B5 · Applications 24,000 for 16,000 shares pro rata, application ₹2. Excess adjusted:
questions.why: The company allots 16,000 of the 24,000 applied for, so 8,000 shares' applications are excess. The excess money adjusted is 8,000 × 2 = ₹16,000.

questions.q: Mock B6 · Equity ₹10,00,000; 12% debentures ₹5,00,000; PAT ₹1,40,000; tax ₹60,000. ROI:
Mock B7 · Case: X:Y:Z 2:2:1. Z retires; X, Y share 1:1; goodwill ₹75,000. X is debited:
questions.why: Z's share is 1/5, so Z's goodwill is 1/5 × 75,000 = 15,000. X and Y gain equally (gaining ratio 1:1), so X is debited ₹7,500.

questions.q: Mock B8 · 3,000 debentures of ₹100 at 3% discount redeemable at 7% premium. Loss on issue:
questions.why: Discount on issue = 3% × 3,00,000 = 9,000. Premium on redemption = 7% × 3,00,000 = 21,000. Loss on issue = 9,000 + 21,000 = ₹30,000.

questions.q: Mock B9 · Realisation: assets BV ₹1,50,000 realised ₹1,30,000; creditors ₹40,000 paid ₹38,000; expenses ₹2,000. Loss:
questions.why: Debit side: assets 1,50,000 + creditors paid 38,000 + expenses 2,000 = 1,90,000. Credit side: creditors 40,000 + realised 1,30,000 = 1,70,000. Loss = ₹20,000.

questions.q: Mock B10 · Machinery opening ₹4,00,000, closing ₹4,80,000; depreciation ₹50,000; machine BV ₹40,000 sold at profit ₹5,000. Purchases and sale proceeds:
questions.why: Machinery purchases = closing 4,80,000 + depreciation 50,000 + BV of the sold machine 40,000 − opening 4,00,000 = 1,70,000. Sale proceeds = 40,000 + 5,000 profit = ₹45,000.

school-c12-biology-a.title: Class 12 Biology — Part A (Ch 1–6)
school-c12-biology-a.description: Class 12 Biology chapter by chapter: reproduction in flowering plants and humans, reproductive health, inheritance, molecular basis of inheritance and evolution — explained fully with examples, common mistakes and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
courses.summary: Stamen and pollen, pistil and embryo sac, pollination and outbreeding devices, double fertilisation, endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit, apomixis and polyembryony.
outcomes: Learners can describe microsporogenesis and the structure of pollen
Learners can describe megasporogenesis and the 7-celled embryo sac
Learners can compare pollination types and agents
Learners can explain double fertilisation and post-fertilisation events
Learners can explain apomixis and its value

lessons.title: The stamen, microsporangium and pollen grain

scenes.text: Diya brushes a lily and her sleeve turns yellow. Her grandmother says, 'That's the flower's pollen — its male side.'
Under the school microscope each speck is a tough, sculpted pollen grain built inside the anther.

steps.title: Pre-fertilisation: the stamen
steps.body: A flower is the reproductive organ of an angiosperm. The **stamen** (male) has a filament and an anther. A typical anther is **bilobed and dithecous** (two thecae) and in cross-section looks **tetragonal** with **four microsporangia** — two in each lobe — which become pollen sacs.

steps.title: Wall of the microsporangium (outside → inside)
steps.body:
- **Epidermis** – protection
- **Endothecium** – helps dehiscence (opening) of the anther
- **Middle layers** (1–3)
- **Tapetum** – innermost; its dense, often multinucleate cells **nourish** developing pollen

At the centre lies **sporogenous tissue**.

steps.title: Microsporogenesis and the pollen grain
steps.body:
Each sporogenous cell can act as a **pollen mother cell (PMC, 2n)**. It divides by **meiosis** to form a **microspore tetrad** (4 haploid cells). Microspores separate and mature into pollen grains.

- **Exine**: hard outer wall of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known (survives high temperature, strong acids and alkalis; no enzyme is known to degrade it). Gaps called **germ pores** have no sporopollenin.
- **Intine**: thin inner wall of cellulose and pectin.
- A mature grain has a large **vegetative cell** (food reserve, irregular nucleus) and a small spindle-shaped **generative cell**. In over 60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this **2-celled** stage; in the rest the generative cell divides first to give two male gametes (3-celled stage).

steps.title: Solved: count the products
steps.body:
Q: An anther has 4 microsporangia, each with 100 PMCs. How many pollen grains form?

Step 1: each PMC undergoes meiosis → 4 microspores.
Step 2: 4 × 100 = 400 per microsporangium.
Step 3: 400 × 4 = **1600 pollen grains**.

steps.title: Solved: why are fossil pollen grains common?
steps.body:
Step 1: the exine is made of sporopollenin.
Step 2: sporopollenin resists heat, acids, alkalis and enzymes.
Step 3: so pollen walls survive in sediments for millions of years — useful to scientists studying past climates.

steps.title: Pollen in daily life
steps.body: Pollen of some plants (e.g. Parthenium, carrot grass) causes allergies and bronchial problems. Pollen tablets are sold as food supplements. Viability varies: rice and wheat pollen lose viability within about 30 minutes, some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae stay viable for months. Pollen can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C in **pollen banks** for crop breeding.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the tapetum protective — it is **nutritive**.
- Saying a PMC divides by mitosis to form microspores — it is **meiosis**.
- Saying pollen is always 3-celled when shed — most are 2-celled.

activity.prompt: Match the anther wall layer to its job

quiz.q: A typical angiosperm anther has how many microsporangia?
quiz.why: A typical anther is bilobed and each lobe has two microsporangia, so there are four microsporangia (two per lobe).
Pollen mother cells (diploid) divide by meiosis to form a tetrad of four haploid microspores, which become pollen grains.
The outer wall of the pollen grain, the exine, is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known.
Germ pores are the places on the pollen wall where sporopollenin is absent, and the pollen tube comes out through them.

quiz.q: The innermost wall layer of a microsporangium is
quiz.why: The tapetum is the innermost wall layer of the microsporangium and nourishes the developing pollen grains.

quiz.q: Most angiosperm pollen is shed at the
quiz.why: In over 60% of angiosperms the pollen is shed at the 2-celled stage (vegetative and generative cell); in the rest it is shed at the 3-celled stage.

lessons.title: The pistil, ovule and embryo sac

scenes.text: Kabir opens a young pea pod: a row of tiny green beads hangs inside. Each bead is an ovule.
Inside every ovule a microscopic 7-celled embryo sac waits — the female gametophyte.

steps.title: Pistil and ovule
steps.body:
The **gynoecium** may be **monocarpellary** (one pistil) or **multicarpellary**, either **syncarpous** (fused, e.g. Papaver) or **apocarpous** (free, e.g. Michelia). Each pistil has stigma, style and ovary; the ovary holds ovules on the **placenta**.

Parts of an ovule: **funicle** (stalk), **hilum** (junction with funicle), one or two **integuments** leaving an opening, the **micropyle**; the opposite end is the **chalaza**. Inside is the **nucellus** with the **embryo sac**.

steps.title: Megasporogenesis
steps.body: A single **megaspore mother cell (MMC, 2n)** in the micropylar region of the nucellus undergoes **meiosis** → 4 megaspores. In most flowering plants **one is functional and three degenerate** — the embryo sac forms from a single megaspore, so this is **monosporic** development.

steps.title: Female gametophyte
steps.body:
The functional megaspore nucleus divides **mitotically three times** (free-nuclear divisions) → 8 nuclei. Cell walls then form:

- **Micropylar end**: the **egg apparatus** = 2 **synergids** + 1 **egg cell**. Synergids have a thickened **filiform apparatus** that guides the pollen tube.
- **Chalazal end**: 3 **antipodal** cells.
- **Centre**: a large **central cell** with 2 **polar nuclei**.

So a typical embryo sac is **8-nucleate and 7-celled**.

steps.title: Solved: counting divisions
steps.body:
Q: How many meiotic and mitotic divisions form one embryo sac from an MMC?

Step 1: MMC → 4 megaspores: **1 meiosis**.
Step 2: functional megaspore → 8 nuclei: 2 → 4 → 8 = **3 mitotic divisions**.

steps.title: Solved: ploidy table
steps.body:
Q: Give the ploidy of nucellus, MMC, functional megaspore and egg.

Nucellus 2n (sporophyte tissue); MMC 2n; megaspore n (after meiosis); egg n (formed by mitosis from a haploid nucleus).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the embryo sac is 8-celled — it has 8 nuclei but **7 cells** (two polar nuclei share one central cell).
- Placing antipodals at the micropylar end.
- Calling the nucellus haploid.

activity.prompt: Order the events from MMC to mature embryo sac
items: Megaspore mother cell differentiates in the nucellus
First mitosis gives a 2-nucleate embryo sac
Two more mitoses give 8 free nuclei
Walls form: 7 cells including egg apparatus and antipodals

quiz.why: The egg apparatus lies at the micropylar end of the embryo sac and consists of the egg cell and two synergids.

quiz.q: The filiform apparatus is found in
quiz.why: The synergids have a special cellular thickening called the filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube into the synergid.
A typical embryo sac is 8-nucleate but 7-celled, because the two polar nuclei lie together in one large central cell.
Monosporic development means the embryo sac forms from only one of the four megaspores (the functional megaspore).
The nucellus is part of the ovule's sporophytic tissue, so it is diploid (2n).
A syncarpous pistil has fused carpels, as in Papaver. Michelia has free carpels (apocarpous).

lessons.title: Pollination: types, agents and outbreeding devices

scenes.text: In the desert, a moth lays eggs inside a Yucca flower and, while doing so, carries its pollen to the stigma.
The plant gets pollinated; the moth larvae get seeds to eat — neither can complete its cycle without the other.

steps.title: Kinds of pollination
steps.body:
**Pollination** = transfer of pollen to a stigma.

- **Autogamy**: within the same flower. Chasmogamous flowers open; **cleistogamous** flowers never open and are invariably autogamous (e.g. *Viola*, *Oxalis*, *Commelina*, which bear both types).
- **Geitonogamy**: to another flower of the **same plant** — functionally cross-pollination but genetically like autogamy.
- **Xenogamy**: to a flower of a **different plant** — brings genetically different pollen.

steps.title: Agents
steps.body:
- **Wind**: light, non-sticky pollen; well-exposed stamens; large feathery stigma; often one ovule per ovary; numerous flowers packed in an inflorescence (e.g. the corn cob's 'tassels' are stigmas and styles). Common in grasses.
- **Water**: rare, about 30 genera, mostly monocots — *Vallisneria*, *Hydrilla*, marine sea-grasses like *Zostera*. In *Vallisneria* female flowers reach the surface on long stalks; male flowers/pollen float to them. Many aquatic plants (water hyacinth, water lily) are actually pollinated by insects or wind.
- **Animals**: bees are the dominant insect pollinators; also butterflies, moths, beetles, birds (sunbirds, hummingbirds), bats. Such flowers are large, colourful, fragrant, rich in nectar; pollen is sticky. Floral rewards are nectar and pollen; some insects are **pollen/nectar robbers**.

steps.title: Outbreeding devices (to discourage self-pollination)
steps.body:
- Pollen release and stigma receptivity **not synchronised**
- Anther and stigma at **different positions**
- **Self-incompatibility**: a genetic mechanism that stops self-pollen from germinating or growing
- **Unisexual flowers**: *monoecious* plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy but **not** geitonogamy; *dioecious* plants (papaya) prevent both

steps.title: Pollen–pistil interaction and artificial hybridisation
steps.body: The pistil recognises compatible pollen (chemical signalling) and lets it germinate; the pollen tube grows through the style into the ovule via the micropyle into a synergid. Breeders use **emasculation** (removing anthers before they shed pollen) and **bagging** (covering with butter-paper bags) to ensure only chosen pollen reaches the stigma; then re-bag after dusting.

steps.title: Solved: identify the type
steps.body:
Q: A flower of a maize plant is pollinated by pollen from another flower on the same plant. Which type?

Step 1: different flower → not autogamy.
Step 2: same plant → **geitonogamy**.
Step 3: genetically it is like self-pollination because all flowers of one plant share the same genotype.

steps.title: Solved: why emasculation isn't needed in papaya
steps.body: Papaya is dioecious: female plants bear only pistillate flowers, so there are no anthers to remove — only **bagging** is required.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking monoecy prevents all selfing — it still allows geitonogamy.
- Saying all aquatic plants are water-pollinated.
- Mixing up cleistogamy (closed, self) and chasmogamy (open).

activity.prompt: Which agent pollinates this flower?

items.text: Light, dry pollen; feathery stigma; grass

quiz.why: Cleistogamous flowers never open, so the anthers and stigma are enclosed and pollination is always within the same flower (autogamy).
In geitonogamy, pollen comes from another flower of the same plant, so it is genetically the same as autogamy.

quiz.q: Which prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy?
quiz.why: In dioecious plants male and female flowers are on separate plants, which prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
Emasculation is the removal of anthers from a bisexual flower bud before they burst, to prevent self-pollination in breeding.
Vallisneria is pollinated by water. Water lily and lotus are mostly insect-pollinated, and water hyacinth is pollinated by insects.
Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that stops pollen of the same flower or plant from fertilising the ovules, which promotes outbreeding.

lessons.title: Double fertilisation, endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit

scenes.text: Rehan drinks coconut water and eats the white kernel. His teacher asks, 'Both are endosperm — why does one look like water?'
Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm (thousands of nuclei, no walls); the kernel is the cellular endosperm that forms later.

steps.title: Double fertilisation
steps.body:
The pollen tube releases **two male gametes** into a synergid.

- Gamete 1 + egg → **zygote (2n)** — this is **syngamy**.
- Gamete 2 + two polar nuclei → **primary endosperm nucleus (PEN, 3n)** — **triple fusion**.

Two fusions in one embryo sac = **double fertilisation**, unique to flowering plants. The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC).

steps.title: Endosperm and embryo
steps.body:
Endosperm develops **before** the embryo so the embryo has food. Most commonly the PEN divides repeatedly without walls (**free-nuclear endosperm**), then walls form (cellular).

- Endosperm fully used up before maturity in pea, groundnut, beans (**non-albuminous** seeds).
- Persists in castor, coconut, wheat, maize, barley (**albuminous** seeds).
- Remnant nucellus in a seed is **perisperm** (black pepper, beet).

The zygote divides after some endosperm has formed. Proembryo → globular → heart-shaped → mature embryo.

**Dicot embryo**: embryonal axis + 2 cotyledons; **epicotyl** ends in plumule (shoot tip); **hypocotyl** ends in radicle (root tip) covered by a root cap.
**Monocot embryo** (grass): one shield-shaped cotyledon, the **scutellum**; shoot apex covered by **coleoptile**, radicle and root cap enclosed in **coleorhiza**.

steps.title: Seed and fruit
steps.body:
Ovule → **seed** (integuments → seed coat; micropyle remains as a small pore for O₂ and water during germination). Ovary → **fruit** (wall → pericarp). As seeds mature they dry (10–15% moisture) and may become **dormant**.

- **False fruits**: thalamus also forms part (apple, strawberry, cashew).
- **Parthenocarpic fruits**: develop without fertilisation, seedless (banana); can be induced with growth hormones.
- Seeds can stay viable for very long: a lupine (*Lupinus arcticus*) seed estimated ~10,000 years old germinated; a ~2000-year-old date palm (*Phoenix dactylifera*) seed from King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea also germinated.

steps.title: Solved: ploidy puzzle
steps.body:
Q: If a plant's leaf cell has 24 chromosomes, how many are in its egg, PEN, endosperm and zygote?

Step 1: leaf = 2n = 24 ⇒ n = 12.
Step 2: egg = n = **12**; zygote = 2n = **24**.
Step 3: PEN and endosperm = 3n = **36**.

steps.title: Solved: why is a cashew a 'false fruit'?
steps.body:
Step 1: a true fruit develops only from the ovary.
Step 2: in cashew, the fleshy edible part comes from the **thalamus** (receptacle), with the true fruit (nut) attached.
Step 3: hence it is a false fruit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing triple fusion as fusion of three male gametes — it is 1 male gamete + 2 polar nuclei.
- Calling endosperm 2n.
- Confusing perisperm (nucellus, 2n) with endosperm (3n).

statements.s: The primary endosperm nucleus is triploid.
Groundnut is an albuminous seed.
Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm.
Apple is a true fruit.
Banana is parthenocarpic.

quiz.why: Syngamy is the fusion of a male gamete with the egg, which forms the zygote.

options: the cotyledon of a grass embryo
quiz.why: The scutellum is the single shield-shaped cotyledon of the embryo in grass family seeds (monocots).
Perisperm is the persistent remnant of the nucellus found in some seeds, for example black pepper and beet.
After fertilisation, the integuments of the ovule harden to form the seed coat.
In monocot seeds, the coleorhiza is the protective sheath that encloses the radicle and root cap.
The primary endosperm nucleus divides first, before the zygote, so that food is ready to nourish the developing embryo.

scenes.text: Every season, farmer Ramesh buys new hybrid maize seed. If he sows seeds from his own hybrid crop, the next generation segregates and yields fall.
If hybrids could make seeds by apomixis, the seed would be a genetic copy and the hybrid vigour would be kept year after year.

steps.title: Apomixis
steps.body:
**Apomixis** = forming seeds **without fertilisation** — asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. Found in some species of **Asteraceae** and **grasses**.

Ways: a diploid egg cell forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation; or some nucellar/integument cells divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

steps.title: Polyembryony
steps.body: When **more than one embryo** occurs in a seed. Common in many *Citrus* and mango varieties, where nucellar cells form extra embryos. Such nucellar embryos are genetically identical to the parent.

steps.title: Solved: why apomixis interests breeders
steps.body:
Step 1: hybrid seeds must be produced every year by controlled crossing, so they are expensive.
Step 2: seeds collected from hybrids segregate in the next generation, losing hybrid characters.
Step 3: if apomixis genes were introduced into hybrids, their seeds would be clones, so farmers could reuse them. Scientists are working to understand the genetics of apomixis for this reason.

steps.title: Solved: are nucellar embryos clones?
steps.body:
Step 1: the nucellus is maternal sporophytic tissue (2n).
Step 2: no meiosis or fertilisation is involved.
Step 3: so the embryos are **genetically identical** to the mother plant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing apomixis (seed without fertilisation) with parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilisation).
- Saying all polyembryonic embryos come from the zygote.

items.back: More than one embryo in a seed (e.g. Citrus, mango)
Develops from nucellus cells; a clone of the parent

quiz.why: Apomixis, the formation of seeds without fertilisation, is common in some members of the Asteraceae and grass families.
Polyembryony, the presence of more than one embryo in a seed, is common in Citrus and mango, where nucellar cells give extra embryos.
Nucellar embryos form from the diploid nucellus without meiosis or fertilisation, so they are clones of the mother plant.

quiz.q: Banana fruit without seeds is an example of
quiz.why: A fruit that develops without fertilisation, and so has no seeds, is called parthenocarpic. Banana is an example.

quiz.q: Main benefit of apomixis in hybrids
options: hybrid traits are retained in seeds
quiz.why: Hybrid seeds produced by apomixis do not undergo meiosis and fertilisation, so the hybrid traits are kept in each generation without segregation.

questions.q: The male reproductive organ of a flower is the
questions.why: The stamen, made of the filament and anther, is the male reproductive part of a flower. The pistil is the female part.

questions.q: Exine of pollen is made of
questions.why: The pollen exine is made of sporopollenin, a very tough polymer that resists acids, alkalis and enzymes.

questions.q: Number of nuclei in a typical embryo sac
questions.why: A typical embryo sac has 8 nuclei: the egg, 2 synergids, 3 antipodals and 2 polar nuclei. It looks 7-celled because the polar nuclei share one cell.

questions.q: Triple fusion produces a nucleus that is
questions.why: In triple fusion, one male gamete (n) fuses with the two polar nuclei (n + n), which gives the 3n primary endosperm nucleus.

questions.q: Which seed is non-albuminous?
questions.why: Pea seeds are non-albuminous: the endosperm is fully used up by the developing embryo, so the mature seed has none. Castor, wheat and maize keep endosperm.

questions.q: Wind-pollinated flowers usually have
questions.why: Wind-pollinated flowers usually have large, feathery stigmas to catch airborne pollen, with light, non-sticky pollen.

questions.q: Assertion: Geitonogamy is genetically similar to autogamy. Reason: in geitonogamy pollen comes from the same plant.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. In geitonogamy the pollen comes from the same plant, so the genes are the same as in autogamy, which is why they are genetically alike.

questions.q: Leaf cells of a plant have 16 chromosomes. Its endosperm cells have
questions.why: Leaf (somatic) cells are diploid, 2n = 16, so n = 8. Endosperm cells are triploid, 3n = 24.

questions.q: Case: A breeder wants to cross two varieties of a bisexual flower. The correct sequence is
questions.why: For a controlled cross, remove anthers first (emasculation), bag the flower, then dust it with the pollen of the other variety, and bag it again to prevent unwanted pollen.

questions.q: Monoecious plants like maize prevent
questions.why: In monoecious plants like maize, male and female flowers are separate but on the same plant. This prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.

questions.q: The 2-celled pollen grain contains
options: a vegetative and a generative cell
questions.why: A 2-celled pollen grain has a large vegetative cell and a smaller generative cell, which later divides to form two male gametes.

questions.q: If an MMC undergoes meiosis and the functional megaspore 3 mitoses, the number of megaspores degenerating is
questions.why: A megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores. Only one remains functional (and forms the embryo sac), so three degenerate.

questions.q: A false fruit among these
questions.why: Apple is a false fruit because the thalamus (the flower stalk end) contributes to the fruit as well as the ovary. In true fruits like mango and tomato the fruit develops only from the ovary.

questions.q: Which statement about the filiform apparatus is correct?
options: It is on the egg and forms the zygote
It is on synergids and guides the pollen tube
It is on antipodals and stores food
questions.why: The filiform apparatus is a thickening on the synergids that guides the pollen tube into the embryo sac.

questions.q: Perisperm and endosperm differ in ploidy as
questions.why: Perisperm is left from the diploid nucellus (2n), while endosperm develops from the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (3n).

questions.q: Case: Seeds from a farmer's F₁ hybrid crop give a variable, lower-yielding crop. The best explanation is
questions.why: F₁ hybrid seeds do not breed true, since the next generation (F₂) shows segregation of characters, giving variable, lower-yielding plants.

questions.q: Number of pollen grains from 10 microspore mother cells
questions.why: Each microspore mother cell gives 4 microspores by meiosis, so each becomes a pollen grain: 10 × 4 = 40.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Human Reproduction
courses.summary: Male and female reproductive systems, spermatogenesis and oogenesis, the menstrual cycle, fertilisation and implantation, pregnancy and embryonic development, parturition and lactation — factual and exam-ready.
outcomes: Learners can describe the male and female reproductive systems
Learners can compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis with chromosome numbers
Learners can explain the phases and hormones of the menstrual cycle
Learners can trace development from zygote to birth
Learners can explain parturition and lactation
courses.guardianNote: Covers the human reproductive systems, gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle, fertilisation, pregnancy, birth and lactation as in the Class 12 biology syllabus. Factual, medically accurate and non-explicit (diagrams described in words only); suitable for 16–18-year-old science students.

story.title: Why biology class is not embarrassing

scenes.text: When the chapter on reproduction begins, a few students giggle. Their teacher says, 'This is how every one of us came to be. Let's learn it like scientists.'
The class starts with the male system — organs, ducts and glands, each with a clear job.

steps.title: Testes
steps.body:
The **testes** (primary male sex organs) lie outside the abdomen in a pouch, the **scrotum**, which keeps them about **2–2.5 °C below** body temperature — needed for sperm production.

Each testis has about **250 compartments (testicular lobules)**, each with 1–3 coiled **seminiferous tubules**. Their lining has:

- **Spermatogonia** (male germ cells) that produce sperm by meiosis-based development
- **Sertoli cells** that nourish germ cells

Between tubules are **interstitial (Leydig) cells** that secrete **androgens** (e.g. testosterone), plus immunologically competent cells.

steps.title: Accessory ducts and glands
steps.body:
Duct path: seminiferous tubules → **rete testis** → **vasa efferentia** → **epididymis** (on the back of each testis) → **vas deferens** (goes up into the abdomen, loops over the urinary bladder) → joins the duct of the seminal vesicle → **ejaculatory duct** → **urethra**, which opens to the outside through the penis.

Glands: paired **seminal vesicles**, a **prostate** and paired **bulbourethral glands**. Their secretions form the **seminal plasma**, rich in fructose, calcium and some enzymes. The bulbourethral secretion also helps lubrication.

steps.title: Solved: trace a sperm's route
steps.body:
Q: List the structures a sperm passes through from where it forms to exit.

Seminiferous tubule → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra → urethral meatus.

steps.title: Solved: why is the scrotum outside the body?
steps.body:
Step 1: spermatogenesis needs a slightly lower temperature.
Step 2: the scrotum holds the testes outside the abdominal cavity, about 2–2.5 °C cooler.
Step 3: if the testes fail to descend, sperm production is affected — a reason doctors check this in newborn boys.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Leydig cells nourish sperm — they secrete androgens; **Sertoli** cells nourish.
- Mixing up the order epididymis → vas deferens.
- Thinking the prostate produces sperm — it adds fluid only.

activity.prompt: Arrange the male duct system in order (sperm path)

quiz.why: Leydig cells (interstitial cells) lie between the seminiferous tubules and secrete androgens, mainly testosterone.
The scrotum keeps the testes about 2–2.5 °C below body temperature, which is needed for normal sperm production.
Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules give support and nourishment to the developing germ cells.
Seminal plasma contains fructose (an energy source for sperm), calcium and enzymes.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a male accessory gland?
quiz.why: The prostate, seminal vesicles and bulbourethral glands are male accessory glands. Bartholin's glands are female glands near the vaginal opening.

quiz.q: Number of testicular lobules per testis (approx.)
quiz.why: Each testis has about 250 testicular lobules, each holding one to three seminiferous tubules.

lessons.title: The female reproductive system and mammary glands

scenes.text: Asha's textbook diagram looks complicated. She turns it into a 'map' — two ovaries, two tubes, one uterus, a cervix and a birth canal.
Once each part has a job attached, the diagram becomes easy to draw and label.

steps.title: Ovaries and oviducts
steps.body:
**Ovaries** (primary female sex organs, 2–4 cm long) produce the female gamete (ovum) and hormones. Each ovary has a stroma of peripheral **cortex** and inner **medulla**, with ovarian follicles at various stages.

Each **oviduct (fallopian tube)**, about 10–12 cm, has: a funnel-shaped **infundibulum** with finger-like **fimbriae** (collect the ovum at ovulation) → the wider **ampulla** → the narrow **isthmus**, which joins the uterus.

steps.title: Uterus, cervix, vagina and external genitalia
steps.body:
The **uterus (womb)** is a single, inverted pear-shaped organ. Its wall has three layers: outer **perimetrium**, thick muscular middle **myometrium** (strong contractions during childbirth) and inner glandular **endometrium** (changes in each menstrual cycle). The uterus opens into the **vagina** through the narrow **cervix**; the cervical canal and vagina together form the **birth canal**.

The external genitalia (collectively the vulva) include the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen and clitoris. The hymen may be torn by many ordinary activities such as sport or cycling, or may persist — its presence or absence is **not** a reliable indicator of anything about a person's sexual history.

steps.title: Mammary glands
steps.body: Paired mammary glands contain glandular tissue and fat. Glandular tissue of each breast has 15–20 **mammary lobes** with clusters of cells called **alveoli** that secrete milk. Milk passes: alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → **mammary ampulla** → **lactiferous duct** → out of the nipple.

steps.title: Solved: where is the ovum caught?
steps.body:
Step 1: at ovulation the ovum is released from the ovary surface.
Step 2: the **fimbriae** of the infundibulum sweep it into the oviduct.
Step 3: it travels towards the ampulla, where fertilisation usually occurs.

steps.title: Solved: uterine layers and their functions
steps.body: Perimetrium – outer covering; myometrium – smooth muscle, contracts during childbirth; endometrium – lining that thickens each cycle and supports implantation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fertilisation happens in the uterus — usually in the **ampulla** of the oviduct.
- Mixing up myometrium and endometrium.
- Believing myths about the hymen — it is not a test of anything.

activity.prompt: Match the part with its role
pairs: Lining for implantation; sheds in menstruation

quiz.why: Fertilisation normally takes place in the ampulla (the wider region) of the oviduct, where the sperm meets the egg.

quiz.q: Which uterine layer sheds during menstruation?
quiz.why: The endometrium, the glandular inner lining of the uterus, is shed in menstruation. The myometrium is the muscular layer.
The birth canal is formed by the cervical canal and the vagina together.
An ovary is a small, almond-sized organ about 2–4 cm long.
Milk passes through the alveoli, then the mammary tubules and ducts, and finally leaves the breast via the lactiferous duct at the nipple.
Fimbriae are finger-like projections at the edge of the infundibulum, the funnel-shaped end of the oviduct, that help collect the ovum after ovulation.

scenes.text: A student is puzzled: a man produces millions of sperm each day, but usually only one egg is released a month. Why so different?
The answer lies in how meiosis is shared out — equally in spermatogenesis, very unequally in oogenesis.

steps.title: Spermatogenesis (from puberty)
steps.body:
Spermatogonia (2n, 46 chromosomes) multiply by mitosis. Some become **primary spermatocytes (2n)** → **meiosis I** → two **secondary spermatocytes (n, 23)** → **meiosis II** → four **spermatids (n)**.

**Spermiogenesis**: spermatids transform into **spermatozoa**. Sperm heads stay embedded in Sertoli cells and are finally released — **spermiation**.

Hormones: hypothalamic **GnRH** → pituitary **LH** (acts on Leydig cells → androgens, which stimulate spermatogenesis) and **FSH** (acts on Sertoli cells → factors that help spermiogenesis).

steps.title: Structure of a sperm
steps.body: Head (haploid nucleus capped by the **acrosome**, filled with enzymes that help fertilisation), neck, **middle piece** (many mitochondria → energy for swimming) and tail. A human ejaculate releases about 200–300 million sperm; for normal fertility at least 60% should have normal shape and size, and at least 40% should show vigorous motility.

steps.title: Oogenesis (begins before birth)
steps.body:
In the foetal ovary, oogonia form; no more are formed or added after birth. They enter meiosis I and **arrest in prophase I** as **primary oocytes**, each in a primary follicle. Many degenerate; at puberty about **60,000–80,000** primary follicles remain in each ovary.

Primary follicle → secondary follicle → tertiary follicle (fluid-filled cavity, the **antrum**). The primary oocyte completes meiosis I unequally → large **secondary oocyte** + tiny **first polar body**. The tertiary follicle becomes the mature **Graafian follicle**; the secondary oocyte forms the **zona pellucida** around it. At **ovulation** the secondary oocyte is released. Meiosis II completes only when a sperm enters → **ovum** + second polar body.

steps.title: Solved: products of meiosis
steps.body:
Q: How many sperm come from 100 primary spermatocytes, and how many ova from 100 primary oocytes?

Sperm: 100 × 4 = **400**. Ova: 100 × 1 = **100** (the rest of the divisions give polar bodies).

steps.title: Solved: chromosome numbers
steps.body: Spermatogonium 46; primary spermatocyte 46; secondary spermatocyte 23; spermatid 23; sperm 23; secondary oocyte 23; first polar body 23.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a secondary oocyte is released after completing meiosis II — meiosis II finishes only after sperm entry.
- Calling spermiation the formation of sperm — that is spermiogenesis; spermiation is **release**.
- Thinking new oogonia form after birth.

activity.prompt: Belongs to spermatogenesis or oogenesis?

quiz.q: Meiosis II in a human secondary oocyte completes
quiz.why: The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II. Meiosis II is completed only after a sperm enters it.

quiz.q: Number of chromosomes in a human secondary spermatocyte
quiz.why: A primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes. After meiosis I, each secondary spermatocyte is haploid with 23 chromosomes.
In males FSH acts on the Sertoli cells, stimulating them to help in spermatogenesis. LH acts on Leydig cells.
The acrosome at the head of the sperm holds enzymes that help the sperm penetrate the layers around the ovum.

quiz.q: Release of sperm from Sertoli cells is
quiz.why: Spermiation is the release of mature sperm from the Sertoli cells into the lumen of the seminiferous tubules.

quiz.q: A fluid-filled cavity in the tertiary follicle
quiz.why: The antrum is the fluid-filled cavity that forms in the tertiary follicle.

scenes.text: Neha tracks her period on a calendar app. Her biology chapter explains what is actually happening inside each week.
Hormones from the brain and ovaries run the cycle like a relay team — LH, FSH, oestrogen and progesterone.

steps.title: Overview
steps.body: The **menstrual cycle** is the reproductive cycle in female primates; on average about **28/29 days**. The first menstruation at puberty is **menarche**; cycles stop around 50 years of age at **menopause**. Cycles can be irregular due to stress, poor health and other causes, especially in the first years after menarche.

steps.title: Phases
steps.body:
- **Menstrual phase** (3–5 days): the endometrium and its blood vessels break down and flow out. Occurs only if the released ovum is **not fertilised**. Missing a period can indicate pregnancy (or other causes).
- **Follicular (proliferative) phase**: primary follicles grow into a Graafian follicle; the endometrium regenerates. FSH and LH from the pituitary rise gradually; growing follicles secrete **oestrogens**.
- **Ovulation** (about day 14): LH and FSH peak mid-cycle; the rapid **LH surge** causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte.
- **Luteal (secretory) phase**: the ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which secretes large amounts of **progesterone**, essential to maintain the endometrium for implantation. Without fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium breaks down → the next menstruation. During pregnancy, menstrual cycles stop.

steps.title: Solved: which hormone, which day?
steps.body:
Q: In a 28-day cycle, which hormone peaks around day 14 and what does it trigger?

Step 1: LH surge occurs mid-cycle.
Step 2: it triggers ovulation — rupture of the Graafian follicle.

steps.title: Solved: why does menstruation start?
steps.body:
Step 1: no fertilisation → corpus luteum degenerates.
Step 2: progesterone level drops.
Step 3: the endometrium cannot be maintained and is shed — menstruation.

steps.title: Practical health facts
steps.body: Periods are a normal, healthy body process. Use clean pads, cups or tampons and change them regularly; dispose of them hygienically. Mild cramps are common; very heavy bleeding, severe pain or periods missing for months should be discussed with a doctor. This is general education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ovulation releases a mature ovum — it releases a **secondary oocyte**.
- Swapping the hormones: progesterone (corpus luteum) maintains the endometrium; LH surge triggers ovulation.
- Thinking the cycle is always exactly 28 days.

activity.prompt: Arrange the events of a menstrual cycle without fertilisation
items: Follicles grow; oestrogen rises; endometrium regenerates

quiz.q: Ovulation is triggered by a surge of
quiz.why: A surge of luteinising hormone (LH) in the middle of the cycle triggers the release of the egg from the follicle (ovulation).
After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone, which maintains the endometrium for a possible pregnancy.
The first menstruation, at the start of puberty in girls, is called menarche.
The menstrual phase, when the uterine lining is shed, typically lasts about 3–5 days.
During pregnancy the corpus luteum, and later the placenta, keep making hormones (such as progesterone) that maintain the uterine lining, so menstrual cycles stop.
The follicular phase is also called the proliferative phase, because the endometrium grows (proliferates) under the influence of oestrogen from the developing follicles.

story.title: From one cell to a baby

scenes.text: A new baby cousin arrives. Arjun wonders how a single cell became a complete human in about nine months.
The journey: fertilisation → cleavage → blastocyst → implantation → organ formation → birth.

steps.title: Fertilisation and sex of the baby
steps.body:
Sperm deposited in the female tract swim to the **ampullary region** of the oviduct. Fertilisation happens only if ovum and sperm arrive there together. Sperm contact the **zona pellucida**, which then changes to block entry of additional sperm. The acrosome's secretions help the sperm enter; meiosis II in the oocyte completes; haploid nuclei fuse → **diploid zygote**.

Sex: the ovum always carries X; a sperm carries X or Y. X sperm → XX (female); Y sperm → XY (male). So the chromosome from the **father's sperm** determines the baby's sex.

steps.title: Cleavage and implantation
steps.body: The zygote divides by mitosis (cleavage) while moving down the isthmus → 2, 4, 8, 16 **blastomeres**. With 8–16 blastomeres it is a **morula**, which becomes a **blastocyst**: outer **trophoblast** and an **inner cell mass**. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium and the blastocyst becomes embedded — **implantation** → pregnancy. The inner cell mass contains **stem cells** that can give rise to all tissues and organs.

steps.title: Placenta and development
steps.body:
Finger-like **chorionic villi** and uterine tissue interdigitate to form the **placenta**: it supplies O₂ and nutrients, removes CO₂ and wastes, and is connected to the embryo by the **umbilical cord**. It is also an endocrine tissue producing **hCG, hPL, oestrogens and progestogens**; late in pregnancy the ovary secretes **relaxin**.

The inner cell mass forms **ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm**. Milestones: heart forms by the end of month 1; limbs and digits by the end of month 2; most major organ systems by the end of 12 weeks (first trimester); first movements and appearance of hair usually in month 5; by the end of 24 weeks (second trimester) fine hair covers the body, eyelids separate and eyelashes form. Pregnancy (gestation) lasts about 9 months.

steps.title: Parturition and lactation
steps.body:
Birth is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism. Signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta cause mild uterine contractions — the **foetal ejection reflex** — which triggers release of **oxytocin** from the maternal pituitary. Oxytocin causes stronger contractions, which stimulate more oxytocin (positive feedback) until the baby is delivered, followed by the placenta.

**Lactation**: milk production begins towards the end of pregnancy. The first milk, **colostrum**, contains antibodies (IgA) that protect the newborn. Breastfeeding during the initial months is recommended by doctors for a healthy baby.

steps.title: Solved: who decides the baby's sex?
steps.body:
Step 1: mother's eggs all carry X.
Step 2: father's sperm carry X or Y in equal proportions.
Step 3: the sperm that fertilises the egg decides — so blaming a mother for a baby's sex is scientifically wrong.

steps.title: Solved: hormone of pregnancy test kits
steps.body: Home pregnancy kits detect **hCG** in urine. hCG is produced by the developing placenta/trophoblast after implantation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying implantation happens in the oviduct — it occurs in the **uterine endometrium**.
- Calling relaxin a placental hormone — in the syllabus it is from the ovary in late pregnancy.
- Mixing morula (solid ball) and blastocyst (with cavity and inner cell mass).

activity.prompt: Put the developmental milestones in order

events.text: Fertilisation forms a zygote in the ampulla

quiz.why: Fertilisation usually takes place in the ampulla, the wider upper part of the oviduct, not in the uterus.

quiz.q: The sex of the baby is determined by
quiz.why: The egg always carries an X chromosome, but a sperm carries either X or Y. So the sex of the baby depends on which sperm fertilises the egg.

quiz.q: The inner cell mass gives rise to
quiz.why: In the blastocyst, the inner cell mass (embryoblast) gives rise to the embryo. The outer layer, the trophoblast, helps form the placenta.
Pregnancy test kits detect hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin), a hormone made by the developing placenta.
During childbirth, uterine contractions stimulate more oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions. This is a positive feedback loop (the foetal ejection reflex).
Colostrum, the first milk, is rich in IgA antibodies that protect the newborn from infections, giving passive immunity.

questions.q: Primary male sex organs
questions.why: The testes are the primary male sex organs because they produce sperm (gametes) and the male hormone testosterone.

questions.q: Usual site of fertilisation
questions.why: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the oviduct (fallopian tube), where sperm meet the egg.

questions.q: Leydig cells secrete
questions.why: Leydig cells in the testes secrete androgens, mainly testosterone. LH and FSH are made by the pituitary.

questions.q: Menstruation occurs when
questions.why: If the ovum is not fertilised, the corpus luteum degenerates, hormone levels fall, and the endometrium is shed as menstruation.

questions.q: Number of sperm from one primary spermatocyte
questions.why: A primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis to form four spermatids, each of which matures into a sperm, giving 4 sperm.

questions.q: The structure that blocks polyspermy
questions.why: After the first sperm touches the zona pellucida, the layer changes and blocks other sperm, preventing polyspermy.

questions.q: Assertion: Human secondary oocyte completes meiosis II only after sperm entry. Reason: Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both facts are true but the reason doesn't explain why meiosis II needs sperm entry.

questions.q: Which hormone is NOT produced by the placenta?
questions.why: Relaxin is described in the syllabus as coming from the ovary late in pregnancy, whereas hCG, hPL and progestogens are made by the placenta.

questions.q: Case: A woman has a regular 28-day cycle. Around which day is ovulation most likely?
questions.why: In a regular 28-day cycle, the LH surge triggers ovulation around the middle of the cycle, about day 14.

questions.q: The morula has
options: an inner cell mass and cavity
questions.why: The morula is a solid ball of cells with 8–16 blastomeres. It forms before the blastocyst, which has a cavity and an inner cell mass.

questions.q: At puberty each ovary has about
questions.why: At puberty, each ovary contains about 60,000–80,000 primary follicles, since many follicles degenerate between birth and puberty.

questions.q: Sertoli cells are stimulated by
questions.why: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells in males, stimulating them to help sperm formation.

questions.q: A primary spermatocyte and a spermatid have chromosome numbers
questions.why: A primary spermatocyte is diploid (46 chromosomes). After meiosis, the spermatid is haploid (23 chromosomes).

questions.q: Case: In a pregnant woman, which structure takes over hormone production to maintain the endometrium?
options: corpus luteum and later the placenta
questions.why: In early pregnancy the corpus luteum supports the endometrium with hormones, and later the placenta takes over this job.

questions.q: By the end of the first trimester
options: most major organ systems are formed
questions.why: By the end of the first trimester (about 12 weeks), most major organ systems of the foetus have formed, including the heart, which starts earlier.

questions.q: Which correctly pairs a cell with its function?
questions.why: Sertoli cells nourish the developing germ cells. The other pairs are mismatched: the acrosome holds enzymes, Leydig cells make androgens, and the middle piece has mitochondria for energy.

questions.q: Oxytocin during parturition acts through
questions.why: Oxytocin is part of a positive feedback loop: stronger contractions cause more oxytocin release, which causes still stronger contractions until birth.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Reproductive Health
courses.summary: Reproductive health and national programmes, contraceptive methods, MTP under Indian law, sexually transmitted infections and their prevention, infertility and assisted reproductive technologies.
outcomes: Learners can define reproductive health and list strategies to improve it
Learners can classify contraceptive methods and explain how they work
Learners can state key facts about MTP in India
Learners can explain STI prevention and why early treatment matters
Learners can distinguish IVF, ZIFT, IUT, GIFT, ICSI and IUI
courses.guardianNote: Covers reproductive health, contraception methods, medical termination of pregnancy under Indian law, sexually transmitted infections and assisted reproductive technologies, as in the Class 12 biology syllabus. Factual, evidence-based and non-explicit; it encourages informed, responsible decisions and seeking qualified medical help. Suitable for 16–18-year-old science students.

story.title: A health camp in the village

scenes.text: A mobile health van visits Sita's village. Nurses talk about safe motherhood, adolescent health and why girls should not marry early.
Reproductive health, the WHO explains, means total well-being — physical, emotional, behavioural and social — in all aspects of reproduction.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Reproductive health** (WHO) = total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A reproductively healthy society has people with physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects.

steps.title: Indian programmes and strategies
steps.body:
India was among the first countries to start action plans at a national level towards a reproductively healthy society — **family planning** programmes from **1951**. Improved and broader programmes now run as **Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH)** programmes.

Strategies include:
- Awareness through audio-visual and print media, and **sex education in schools** so that young people get correct information and avoid myths
- Information on reproductive organs, adolescence, safe hygienic practices, STIs and AIDS
- Educating couples about birth control, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care, breastfeeding, and equal opportunities for boys and girls
- **Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination** to stop female foeticide
- Mass child immunisation
- Research on contraceptives (e.g. **Saheli**, a once-a-week non-steroidal oral pill developed at CDRI, Lucknow)

steps.title: Solved: why ban sex determination?
steps.body:
Step 1: amniocentesis tests foetal cells in amniotic fluid; it can reveal genetic disorders — and the sex of the foetus.
Step 2: misuse for sex determination led to female foeticide and a skewed sex ratio.
Step 3: so India legally bans its use for sex determination while permitting genuine medical use.

steps.title: Solved: indicators of improved reproductive health
steps.body: Better facilities and awareness have led to: reduced maternal and infant mortality rates, early detection and cure of STIs, assistance for infertility, better post-natal care, and increasing numbers of couples with small families.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Defining reproductive health only as 'absence of disease' — it is total well-being.
- Saying amniocentesis itself is banned — its use for **sex determination** is banned.

statements.s: Reproductive health includes emotional and social well-being.
India started national family planning programmes in 1951.
Amniocentesis may legally be used to choose a baby's sex in India.
Saheli is a once-a-week oral contraceptive.

quiz.why: The WHO defines reproductive health as total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social.
RCH stands for Reproductive and Child Health Care, a national programme that aims to improve mother and child health.
Amniocentesis is legally banned for determining the sex of the foetus, to prevent female foeticide. It is still allowed to detect genetic disorders.
Saheli, a non-steroidal oral contraceptive pill for women, was developed at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a goal of RCH?
quiz.why: Sex-selective abortion is illegal and is not a goal of the RCH programme, which promotes safe motherhood, child immunisation and STI awareness.

lessons.title: Contraception and medical termination of pregnancy

scenes.text: A counsellor at a family-health clinic explains many contraceptive options to a married couple who want to space their children.
An ideal method is user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with few side-effects.

steps.title: Natural and barrier methods
steps.body:
- **Natural**: periodic abstinence (avoiding intercourse around days 10–17 of the cycle, when ovulation is expected), withdrawal, and **lactational amenorrhoea** (no ovulation during intense breastfeeding — reliable only up to about 6 months after birth). These have no side-effects but high failure rates.
- **Barriers**: condoms (for males and females; made of thin rubber/latex) prevent sperm meeting the ovum and **also protect against STIs and AIDS**; diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults (reusable) cover the cervix. Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are often used with barriers.

steps.title: IUDs, hormones and surgery
steps.body:
- **Intra-uterine devices** (inserted by doctors/trained nurses): non-medicated (Lippes loop), **copper-releasing** (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) — copper ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity; **hormone-releasing** (Progestasert, LNG-20) make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperm. IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperm in the uterus. Ideal for women who want to delay or space pregnancies.
- **Oral pills**: progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations taken daily for 21 days; inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus. **Saheli** is taken once a week.
- **Injections/implants** (under the skin) work similarly with longer action.
- **Emergency contraception**: certain pills or an IUD **within 72 hours** of unprotected intercourse.
- **Surgical (sterilisation)** — terminal, usually not reversible: **vasectomy** (part of the vas deferens removed or tied) and **tubectomy** (part of the fallopian tube removed or tied).

steps.title: Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)
steps.body: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is **MTP** (induced abortion). In India it was legalised by the **MTP Act, 1971**, and the law was amended in **2021** to allow termination up to 20 weeks on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner, and between 20 and 24 weeks for specified categories of women with the opinion of two. MTPs are considered relatively safe during the **first trimester** (up to 12 weeks). Unsafe abortions by unqualified people are dangerous and can be fatal. Misuse of tests for female foeticide is illegal. (Textbook editions may describe the amendment differently — follow current law.)

steps.title: Solved: which method protects against STIs?
steps.body:
Step 1: pills, IUDs and surgery prevent pregnancy but do nothing to stop infections passing between partners.
Step 2: condoms create a physical barrier.
Step 3: so **condoms** are the method that also reduces the risk of STIs including HIV.

steps.title: Solved: why is lactational amenorrhoea unreliable long-term?
steps.body:
Step 1: intense breastfeeding suppresses ovulation.
Step 2: as feeding reduces and the baby grows, ovulation returns — often before the first period.
Step 3: so it is effective only up to about 6 months after birth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking emergency contraception can be used as a regular method — it is for emergencies only.
- Calling vasectomy and tubectomy temporary.
- Confusing hormone-releasing IUDs (LNG-20) with copper IUDs (CuT).

This is general education, not medical advice; choices should be made with a qualified doctor.

activity.prompt: Classify the contraceptive method

options: suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity
quiz.why: Copper ions released by CuT suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperm, which prevents fertilisation.
