quiz.q: Emergency contraception should be used within
quiz.why: Emergency contraceptives are most effective if taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse.
Condoms are barriers that also lower the risk of sexually transmitted infections. Pills, CuT and tubectomy do not protect against STIs.

quiz.q: MTP is considered relatively safe up to
quiz.why: Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) is considered relatively safe up to the first trimester (12 weeks). Later it becomes riskier.
Vasectomy is male sterilisation in which the vas deferens is cut and tied, so sperm cannot reach the semen.
Progestasert and LNG-20 are intrauterine devices that release hormones (progestogens), unlike copper-releasing IUDs.

scenes.text: A teenager reads scary, conflicting messages online about infections. He asks his school counsellor what is true.
The counsellor gives him clear facts: what STIs are, how they spread, how to prevent them and why early treatment matters.

steps.title: What and which
steps.body:
**STIs** (also called venereal diseases or reproductive tract infections) are transmitted mainly through sexual contact. Examples: **gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis B and HIV/AIDS**.

Hepatitis B and HIV can also spread by sharing injection needles, surgical instruments, transfusion of infected blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus. Except **genital herpes, hepatitis B and HIV**, the others are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

steps.title: Why early care matters
steps.body: Early symptoms are often minor (itching, discharge, slight pain, swellings) and may be absent, so infections go undetected. Social stigma also stops people from seeking help. Untreated STIs can cause **pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)**, abortions, still births, **ectopic pregnancy**, infertility and even cancer of the reproductive tract. Incidence is reported to be very high among people aged **15–24 years**.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body:
- Avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners
- Always use condoms during intercourse
- In case of doubt, go to a qualified doctor for early detection and complete treatment
- Never share needles or razors; ensure blood transfusions are screened

steps.title: Solved: which STIs are not completely curable?
steps.body: From the list, **genital herpes, hepatitis B and HIV infection** cannot be completely cured (they can be managed; hepatitis B can be prevented with a vaccine).

steps.title: Solved: case reasoning
steps.body:
Q: A person with a curable STI ignores mild symptoms because they fade. Why is this risky?

Step 1: fading symptoms don't mean the infection is gone.
Step 2: untreated infection can spread to partners and cause PID or infertility.
Step 3: correct action: visit a doctor, complete treatment, and inform partners so they are treated too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing an STI always shows symptoms.
- Assuming the oral pill protects from STIs.
- Thinking HIV spreads by touching, hugging or sharing food — it does not.

This is general education, not medical advice; consult a qualified doctor or government health centre.

activity.prompt: Questions students hesitate to ask

items.q: Can you tell if someone has an STI by looking at them?
items.a: No. Many infections have no visible signs. Only testing by a health professional can tell.

items.q: Does HIV spread through hugging, sharing utensils or mosquito bites?
items.a: No. HIV spreads through sexual contact with an infected person, infected blood, shared needles, or from an infected mother to her child.
Yes — there is a safe vaccine; ask a doctor about vaccination.

items.q: Where can I get confidential help in India?
items.a: Government hospitals and health centres provide testing and counselling. For emotional support, Tele-MANAS is 14416; for emergencies dial 112.

quiz.q: Which STI is completely curable when treated early?
quiz.why: Gonorrhoea is a bacterial STI and can be cured when treated with antibiotics early. HIV, hepatitis B and genital herpes are viral and cannot be completely cured.
Untreated STIs can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and infertility.

quiz.q: Age group with high reported STI incidence
quiz.why: Reported STI cases are highest in the 15–24 year age group.

quiz.q: Hepatitis B can also spread by
quiz.why: Hepatitis B is blood-borne, so besides sexual contact it can also spread by sharing contaminated needles. Casual contact such as shaking hands does not spread it.

quiz.q: Best single method to reduce STI risk during intercourse
quiz.why: Using condoms consistently is the best single method listed to cut the risk of STIs during intercourse, as it acts as a barrier.
An ectopic pregnancy is one in which the embryo implants outside the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube.

scenes.text: After years of trying, a couple visits a fertility specialist. Tests check both partners — infertility can be due to either.
Depending on the cause, doctors may suggest IUI, IVF with embryo transfer, GIFT or ICSI.

steps.title: Infertility
steps.body: Couples unable to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual co-habitation are infertile. Causes may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological, and can lie in **either partner**. In India the blame is often wrongly placed on the woman; specialised clinics diagnose and treat both.

steps.title: Assisted reproductive technologies (ART)
steps.body:
- **IVF–ET** ('test-tube baby'): ova from the wife/donor and sperm from the husband/donor fuse in the lab; the embryo is transferred.
  - **ZIFT**: zygote or early embryo (**up to 8 blastomeres**) transferred into the **fallopian tube**.
  - **IUT**: embryo with **more than 8 blastomeres** transferred into the **uterus**.
- Embryos formed by in-vivo fertilisation can also be transferred to assist women who cannot conceive.
- **GIFT**: transfer of an **ovum** from a donor into the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation.
- **ICSI**: a sperm is **injected directly into the ovum** in the lab.
- **Artificial insemination (AI)**: semen from the husband or a donor is introduced into the vagina or uterus (**IUI**) — used when the male partner cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count.

ART needs specialised professionals and is costly; emotional, religious and social factors also matter. Adoption is another loving path to parenthood. In India, ART clinics are regulated by the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021.

steps.title: Solved: choose the technique
steps.body:
Q: A woman produces no ova but has healthy fallopian tubes. Which technique?

Step 1: she needs an ovum from a donor.
Step 2: fertilisation can occur inside her body if the ovum is placed in the tube.
Step 3: **GIFT**.

steps.title: Solved: ZIFT vs IUT
steps.body:
Q: An embryo with 16 blastomeres is ready for transfer. Where and which technique?

More than 8 blastomeres → transferred into the **uterus** → **IUT**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping ZIFT (≤ 8 blastomeres, fallopian tube) and IUT (> 8, uterus).
- Thinking GIFT transfers an embryo — it transfers a gamete (ovum).
- Assuming infertility is always the woman's problem.

activity.prompt: Match the technique to its description
pairs: Embryo up to 8 blastomeres into fallopian tube
Embryo with more than 8 blastomeres into uterus

quiz.why: ICSI stands for intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection: a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum.

options: outside the body in the lab
quiz.why: IVF (in vitro fertilisation) means fertilisation outside the body in a laboratory ('in glass').

quiz.q: A low sperm count may be treated by
quiz.why: A low sperm count can be helped by artificial insemination (IUI), in which semen is collected and introduced into the female tract.
GIFT (gamete intra-fallopian transfer) transfers an ovum (gamete) collected from a donor into the fallopian tube.
Infertility can be due to a problem in either partner, so both should be examined.

questions.q: Reproductive health means
options: total well-being in all aspects of reproduction
questions.why: Reproductive health means total well-being in all aspects of reproduction, physical, emotional, behavioural and social, not just the absence of disease.

questions.q: Which is a barrier method?
questions.why: A condom is a barrier method, as it physically stops sperm from reaching the egg. CuT is an IUD, Saheli a pill and vasectomy a surgery.

questions.q: Which STI is not completely curable?
questions.why: Genital herpes is a viral STI, so it cannot be completely cured. Syphilis, trichomoniasis and gonorrhoea are curable if treated early.

questions.q: Hormone-releasing IUD
questions.why: LNG-20 is a hormone-releasing IUD (it releases levonorgestrel). Cu7, Multiload 375 and Lippes loop are copper-releasing or non-medicated.

questions.q: Lactational amenorrhoea is effective up to about
questions.why: Lactational amenorrhoea (no menstruation during intense breast-feeding) works as a contraceptive only for about six months after birth.

questions.q: Tubectomy is performed in
questions.why: Tubectomy is female sterilisation in which the fallopian tubes are cut and tied. In males it is called vasectomy.

questions.q: Assertion: Condoms reduce the risk of STIs. Reason: Condoms prevent contact of body fluids between partners.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. A condom prevents contact of body fluids and skin between partners, so it lowers the risk of many infections.

questions.q: Embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred by
questions.why: An embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus (intra-uterine transfer, IUT). Earlier embryos go into the fallopian tube (ZIFT).

questions.q: Case: A man's sperm count is very low. Which technique is first suggested?
questions.why: For a low sperm count, artificial insemination (IUI) is suggested first: semen is collected and introduced into the female tract.

questions.q: Pills inhibit
questions.why: Contraceptive pills inhibit ovulation and implantation, and also change the cervical mucus so sperm entry is hindered.

questions.q: MTP in India was first legalised in
questions.why: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act was passed in 1971 and legalised MTP in India under certain conditions.

questions.q: Emergency contraceptives should be taken within
questions.why: Emergency contraceptives should be taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse to be effective.

questions.q: Copper-releasing IUDs act by
questions.why: Copper-releasing IUDs release copper ions that suppress sperm motility and fertilising ability.

questions.q: Case: A woman cannot produce ova but can support fertilisation and pregnancy. Best option
questions.why: If a woman cannot produce ova but can support fertilisation and pregnancy, a donor ovum can be transferred into her fallopian tube by GIFT.

questions.q: Which statement about STIs is correct?
options: Early symptoms are often minor or absent
questions.why: Early STI symptoms are often minor or absent, so infected people may not realise it. That is why regular check-ups matter.

questions.q: Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination aims to
questions.why: The legal ban on prenatal sex determination is meant to prevent female foeticide and the imbalance in the sex ratio.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: In ICSI a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum. In the other options, the transfers are swapped: ZIFT is zygote into the fallopian tube, IUT is embryo into the uterus.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Principles of Inheritance and Variation
courses.summary: Mendel's laws with monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, deviations (incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, pleiotropy, polygenic traits), chromosomal theory, linkage, sex determination, mutation, pedigree analysis and genetic disorders.
outcomes: Learners can solve monohybrid, dihybrid and test crosses with Punnett squares
Learners can explain deviations from Mendelian ratios with examples
Learners can explain linkage, recombination and the chromosomal theory
Learners can compare sex-determination systems
Learners can analyse pedigrees and describe Mendelian and chromosomal disorders

lessons.title: Mendel's monohybrid cross: dominance and segregation

story.title: A monk and his pea garden

scenes.text: Between 1856 and 1863, Gregor Mendel crossed garden peas in a monastery garden and counted thousands of offspring.
His secret weapon was statistics: large samples, true-breeding lines, and careful ratios like 3 : 1.

steps.title: Why peas, and what Mendel did
steps.body: Mendel used **true-breeding** lines (which show stable trait inheritance over several generations) and chose **14 true-breeding varieties** differing in **seven pairs of contrasting traits** (e.g. tall/dwarf stem, round/wrinkled seed, yellow/green seed, violet/white flower). He did artificial pollination, followed the **F₁** and **F₂** generations, and applied mathematical logic. He published in 1865; his work was rediscovered in 1900 by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak.

steps.title: Monohybrid cross
steps.body:
Tall (TT) × dwarf (tt) → **F₁ all tall (Tt)**. Selfing F₁ → **F₂**: phenotype **3 tall : 1 dwarf**; genotype **1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt**.

Terms: **gene/factor** – unit of inheritance; **alleles** – alternative forms (T, t); **homozygous** (TT, tt), **heterozygous** (Tt); **genotype** vs **phenotype**. The **Punnett square** (by Reginald C. Punnett) shows gametes and offspring.

**Law of Dominance**: characters are controlled by paired factors; in a dissimilar pair one (dominant) expresses itself. **Law of Segregation**: alleles do not blend; the two alleles of a pair separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets only one.

steps.title: Test cross
steps.body:
To find whether a dominant-phenotype organism is TT or Tt, cross it with the **recessive parent** (tt).

- All offspring dominant → organism was **TT**
- 1 dominant : 1 recessive → organism was **Tt**

steps.title: Solved: Punnett square for Tt × Tt
steps.body:
Gametes: T, t from each parent.

Offspring: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

Genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1; phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Probability that an F₂ tall plant is heterozygous = 2/3.

steps.title: Solved: test-cross result
steps.body:
Q: A violet-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant; 52 violet and 48 white offspring appear. Genotype of the violet parent?

Ratio ≈ 1 : 1 ⇒ the violet parent was **heterozygous (Ww)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the F₂ genotype ratio as 3 : 1 (that's the phenotype ratio).
- Testing with a dominant plant in a 'test cross' — always use the homozygous recessive.
- Saying the recessive allele 'disappears' in F₁ — it is present but not expressed; it reappears in F₂.

activity.prompt: In a monohybrid F₂ of 800 plants, how many are expected to be homozygous dominant?

quiz.q: F₂ phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross with complete dominance
quiz.why: In a monohybrid cross with complete dominance, the F₂ generation shows a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio (3 dominant to 1 recessive).

quiz.q: A test cross is a cross with
quiz.why: A test cross is a cross of an individual of unknown genotype with the homozygous recessive parent, to find out its genotype.

quiz.q: Mendel studied how many pairs of contrasting traits?
quiz.why: Mendel studied seven pairs of contrasting traits in the garden pea.
Alleles are alternative forms of the same gene, found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

quiz.q: Fraction of F₂ tall plants that are TT
quiz.why: The tall F₂ plants are TT : Tt in 1 : 2, so among the tall ones, 1 in 3 is TT (homozygous).

quiz.q: The law based on gamete formation having one allele
quiz.why: The law of segregation says that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele.

lessons.title: Incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles and pleiotropy

scenes.text: Red snapdragon × white snapdragon gives… pink! Did Mendel get it wrong?
No — dominance isn't always complete. And ABO blood groups show two alleles can both be fully expressed.

steps.title: Incomplete dominance
steps.body:
The F₁ shows an **intermediate** phenotype. Snapdragon (*Antirrhinum*): RR (red) × rr (white) → Rr **pink**. F₂: **1 red : 2 pink : 1 white** — phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same.

Explaining dominance: an allele usually codes for a functional enzyme; a modified allele may make a non-functional enzyme or none. If one normal allele makes enough product, it appears dominant.

steps.title: Codominance and multiple alleles: ABO blood groups
steps.body:
Gene **I** has three alleles: **Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i**. Iᴬ and Iᴮ make slightly different forms of a sugar on the red-cell surface; i makes none. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are **codominant** (both expressed in IᴬIᴮ → group AB), and both are dominant over i.

- Group A: IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi
- Group B: IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi
- Group AB: IᴬIᴮ
- Group O: ii

Six genotypes, four phenotypes. A gene with more than two alleles in a population is a case of **multiple alleles** (an individual still has only two).

steps.title: Pleiotropy and polygenic inheritance
steps.body:
**Pleiotropy**: one gene affects several phenotypic traits. Example: in **phenylketonuria**, a single gene mutation causes intellectual disability and reduced hair and skin pigmentation. Starch synthesis in pea seeds is another example: BB gives large starch grains (round seeds), bb small grains (wrinkled), Bb round seeds but intermediate-sized grains — so for grain size it shows incomplete dominance.

**Polygenic inheritance**: traits like human **skin colour** and height are controlled by **three or more genes** with additive effects plus environment, giving a continuous range of phenotypes.

steps.title: Solved: parents with blood groups A and B have a child with group O
steps.body:
Step 1: child ii, so each parent gave i.
Step 2: parents must be **Iᴬi** and **Iᴮi**.
Step 3: possible children: IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O) — each 1/4.

steps.title: Solved: pink × pink snapdragons, 200 offspring
steps.body: Expected 1 : 2 : 1 ⇒ **50 red, 100 pink, 50 white**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling AB blood group 'incomplete dominance' — it is **codominance** (both fully expressed).
- Thinking a person can carry all three ABO alleles.
- Mixing pleiotropy (one gene → many traits) with polygenic (many genes → one trait).

activity.prompt: Match the pattern to its example
pairs: Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i in a population

quiz.why: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote looks intermediate, so the F₂ phenotypic ratio matches the genotypic ratio, 1 : 2 : 1.
The ABO system has three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) giving six genotypes: IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi, IᴬIᴮ and ii.
The genotype ii has neither A nor B antigen, so the blood group is O.
When a single gene affects several traits, it is called pleiotropy.
AB (IᴬIᴮ) × O (ii) gives children Iᴬi (group A) or Iᴮi (group B), so only A or B.
Human skin colour is controlled by several genes acting together, so it is polygenic.

lessons.title: Dihybrid cross, independent assortment, linkage and the chromosomal theory

scenes.text: Mendel crossed round-yellow peas with wrinkled-green ones. F₁ were all round-yellow; F₂ gave four kinds in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
Decades later, Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit flies showed that genes on the same chromosome don't always assort independently.

steps.title: Dihybrid cross
steps.body:
RRYY (round yellow) × rryy (wrinkled green) → F₁ **RrYy** (round yellow). F₁ gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry (each 1/4). F₂ (16 boxes): **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**.

**Law of Independent Assortment**: when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair is independent of the other.

steps.title: Chromosomal theory of inheritance
steps.body: Mendel's work was ignored until 1900 partly because 'factors' were abstract and his maths was unusual for biology then. Microscopy later showed chromosomes pair and separate in meiosis exactly as Mendel's factors would. **Sutton and Boveri** proposed that genes lie on chromosomes and their pairing and separation explain Mendel's laws (chromosomal theory). **Thomas Hunt Morgan** experimentally verified it using *Drosophila melanogaster* — easy to grow on simple medium, a life cycle of about two weeks, many progeny, clear sex differences and many visible hereditary variations.

steps.title: Linkage and recombination
steps.body: Morgan found that some gene pairs (e.g. yellow body–white eye) produced parental combinations far more often than expected; the genes were on the same (X) chromosome. **Linkage** = physical association of genes on a chromosome; **recombination** = generation of non-parental combinations. Tightly linked genes show low recombination (e.g. ~1.3%), loosely linked genes higher (~37.2% for white–miniature wing). **Alfred Sturtevant** used recombination frequencies between gene pairs to map their positions on chromosomes — the basis of genetic maps.

steps.title: Solved: proportions in a dihybrid F₂
steps.body:
Q: Out of 160 F₂ plants, how many are expected to be round green, and what fraction of all F₂ is homozygous for both genes?

Round green = 3/16 × 160 = **30**.
Homozygous for both: RRYY, RRyy, rrYY, rryy = 4/16 = **1/4**.

steps.title: Solved: dihybrid test cross
steps.body: RrYy × rryy → RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy in **1 : 1 : 1 : 1** (if genes assort independently). A big excess of parental types would suggest **linkage**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing F₁ gametes as Rr and Yy — gametes carry one allele of **each** gene (RY, Ry, rY, ry).
- Assuming independent assortment for genes on the same chromosome.
- Confusing recombination frequency with distance units incorrectly — higher frequency means genes are farther apart.

activity.prompt: In a dihybrid F₂ of 320 plants, how many are expected to show both recessive traits?

quiz.q: F₂ ratio of a dihybrid cross
quiz.why: In a dihybrid cross, the F₂ phenotypic ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, showing independent assortment of the two genes.

quiz.q: Number of gamete types from RrYy
quiz.why: RrYy produces gametes RY, Ry, rY and ry. That is 2² = 4 types.

quiz.q: Who verified the chromosomal theory with Drosophila?
quiz.why: Thomas Hunt Morgan used Drosophila to give experimental proof for the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
Genes that lie close together on a chromosome are tightly linked and are rarely separated by crossing over, so they show low recombination.

quiz.q: Genetic maps were first made by
quiz.why: Alfred Sturtevant used the recombination frequencies as a measure of the distance between genes, and made the first genetic maps.
A dihybrid test cross (RrYy × rryy) gives four phenotypes in equal numbers, 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, when the genes assort independently.

scenes.text: In 1891 Henking noticed a nuclear structure in some insect sperm and called it the X body.
It turned out to be a sex chromosome — and different animals use very different systems to decide sex.

steps.title: Systems
steps.body:
- **XX–XO** (e.g. grasshopper): all eggs carry X; half the sperm carry X, half none. Females XX, males XO.
- **XX–XY** (humans, *Drosophila*): males XY, females XX. Males are **heterogametic** (two kinds of sperm).
- **ZW–ZZ** (birds): **females are heterogametic (ZW)**, males ZZ — the egg decides the sex.
- **Haplodiploidy** (honey bee): an offspring from a fertilised egg (union of sperm and egg) is female (queen or worker, diploid, 32 chromosomes); an unfertilised egg develops into a male (drone, haploid, 16 chromosomes) by parthenogenesis. Drones produce sperm by mitosis, have no father and cannot have sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

steps.title: Humans
steps.body: 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes. Each child gets an X from the mother; from the father either X (→ girl) or Y (→ boy), in equal chance. So it is the **father's sperm** that determines sex, and each pregnancy has about a 50% chance of either.

steps.title: Solved: honey bee drone chromosome number
steps.body:
Step 1: workers and queens (diploid) have 32.
Step 2: drones develop from unfertilised (haploid) eggs ⇒ **16**.
Step 3: since drones are already haploid, they produce sperm by **mitosis**.

steps.title: Solved: probability puzzle
steps.body:
Q: A couple has three daughters. Probability that the fourth child is a son?

Each birth is independent ⇒ **1/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the female decides sex in humans — in humans it's the male; in birds the female.
- Thinking honey bee males have a father.
- Believing previous births change the next child's chance.

activity.prompt: Match the organism to its sex-determination system

quiz.q: In birds the heterogametic sex is
quiz.why: In birds the female is heterogametic (ZW), while the male is homogametic (ZZ).
Drone honey bees develop from unfertilised eggs, so they are haploid with 16 chromosomes (queens and workers have 32).
In grasshoppers the male has an XO sex-determination type, with only one X chromosome and no Y.

quiz.q: Number of autosome pairs in humans
quiz.why: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes (44 chromosomes) plus one pair of sex chromosomes, making 46.

quiz.q: In humans, sex of the child is decided by
quiz.why: The mother's egg always carries X, but sperm carry X or Y, so the sperm decides the child's sex.

lessons.title: Mutation, pedigree analysis and Mendelian disorders

story.title: A family tree at the clinic

scenes.text: A genetic counsellor draws a family tree with squares and circles, shading those who have a condition.
From the pattern she can tell whether a trait is dominant or recessive, autosomal or X-linked.

steps.title: Mutation and pedigree
steps.body:
**Mutation**: a change in the DNA sequence causing changes in genotype and phenotype. **Point mutation** changes a single base (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia); **frameshift** mutations from insertion/deletion of bases. Chemical and physical agents that cause mutations are **mutagens** (e.g. UV radiation).

Pedigree symbols: square = male, circle = female, shaded = affected, horizontal line between = mating, a double line = consanguineous mating, vertical line to offspring. Since controlled crosses are impossible in humans, pedigree analysis traces traits through generations.

steps.title: Mendelian disorders (single-gene)
steps.body:
- **Haemophilia** – X-linked recessive; a protein of the blood-clotting cascade is affected, so a small cut may bleed for long. A heterozygous female is a carrier; females are very rarely affected (requires carrier mother and haemophilic father). Queen Victoria's family pedigree shows many affected descendants.
- **Sickle-cell anaemia** – autosomal recessive; HbˢHbˢ is affected. A single base change GAG → GUG substitutes **glutamic acid with valine at the 6th position** of the β-globin chain. Under low oxygen, mutant haemoglobin polymerises and red cells become sickle-shaped. Hbᴬ Hbˢ are carriers (usually healthy).
- **Phenylketonuria** – autosomal recessive; lacks the enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine and its derivatives accumulate and cause intellectual disability; also excreted in urine.
- **Colour blindness** – X-linked recessive; defects in red or green cone function. Occurs in about 8% of males and only about 0.4% of females.
- **Thalassemia** – autosomal recessive blood disorder; reduced synthesis of α or β globin chains causes abnormal haemoglobin and anaemia. α-thalassemia: genes HBA1, HBA2 on **chromosome 16**; β-thalassemia: gene HBB on **chromosome 11**. Thalassemia is a **quantitative** problem (too few globin chains), sickle-cell a **qualitative** one (wrong globin).

steps.title: Solved: haemophilia cross
steps.body:
Carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) × normal father (XᴴY).

Daughters: XᴴXᴴ (normal), XᴴXʰ (carrier). Sons: XᴴY (normal), XʰY (haemophilic).

Probability that a **son** is affected = **1/2**; probability any child is affected = 1/4.

steps.title: Solved: sickle-cell carriers
steps.body: Hbᴬ Hbˢ × Hbᴬ Hbˢ → 1/4 HbᴬHbᴬ (normal), 1/2 carriers, **1/4 affected (HbˢHbˢ)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling colour blindness autosomal.
- Saying sickle-cell is caused by a frameshift — it's a **point** mutation (substitution).
- Writing that a son inherits his X chromosome from his father — sons get X from the mother.

activity.prompt: Classify the disorder

options: glutamic acid by valine at position 6
quiz.why: In sickle-cell anaemia a single base change (GAG to GUG) replaces glutamic acid with valine at the 6th position of the β-globin chain.
Haemophilia is X-linked recessive, since the gene is on the X chromosome and males with one affected X show the disease.

quiz.q: Colour blindness occurs in about what % of males?
quiz.why: Red–green colour blindness, an X-linked recessive trait, occurs in about 8% of males and far fewer females.

quiz.q: β-thalassemia gene HBB lies on chromosome
quiz.why: The β-globin gene (HBB), whose defects cause β-thalassemia, is on chromosome 11. The α-globin genes are on chromosome 16.

quiz.q: In pedigree charts a shaded circle means
quiz.why: In pedigree charts circles stand for females and squares for males. A shaded symbol means affected, so a shaded circle is an affected female.
In phenylketonuria the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine is missing or defective.

scenes.text: A lab technician photographs chromosomes from a blood sample and arranges them in pairs — a karyotype.
One extra or missing chromosome can change development; the karyotype reveals it.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Chromosomal disorders come from the absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of chromosomes. Failure of chromatids to separate in cell division (**non-disjunction**) gives gain or loss of a chromosome — **aneuploidy**. Failure of cytokinesis after telophase gives a whole extra set — **polyploidy** (often seen in plants).

steps.title: Three important syndromes
steps.body:
- **Down syndrome**: **trisomy 21** (47 chromosomes). First described by Langdon Down (1866). Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, a broad palm with a characteristic palm crease; physical, psychomotor and mental development is delayed.
- **Klinefelter syndrome**: **47, XXY** (extra X in a male). Overall masculine development, but may show feminine development such as breast development (gynaecomastia); individuals are usually sterile.
- **Turner syndrome**: **45, X0** (one X missing in a female). Sterile, ovaries rudimentary, lack of other secondary sexual characters.

People with these conditions deserve respect, inclusion and support; many live full lives with appropriate care.

steps.title: Solved: identify from karyotype
steps.body:
Q: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes with three copies of chromosome 21 in a female. Diagnosis?

Step 1: extra autosome 21 → trisomy 21.
Step 2: **Down syndrome** (can occur in either sex).

steps.title: Solved: how non-disjunction gives XXY
steps.body:
Step 1: in meiosis, the X chromosomes fail to separate in the mother, producing an XX egg.
Step 2: the XX egg is fertilised by a Y sperm.
Step 3: the zygote is **47, XXY** → Klinefelter syndrome.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Turner as 47, XXY or Klinefelter as 45, X0 — memorise: **Turner = one X, Klinefelter = extra X**.
- Calling Down syndrome sex-linked — it is an autosomal trisomy.

activity.prompt: Match the syndrome to its karyotype

quiz.why: Trisomy 21, an extra copy of chromosome 21, causes Down syndrome.
Turner syndrome has only one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome: 45, X0 (a female).
Non-disjunction, the failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis, leads to gain or loss of single chromosomes, called aneuploidy.
Klinefelter syndrome is 47, XXY: males with an extra X chromosome.
Polyploidy results from failure of cytokinesis after chromosome replication, so the whole chromosome set is doubled.

questions.q: F₂ phenotypic ratio in a monohybrid cross
questions.why: A monohybrid cross with complete dominance gives a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio in the F₂.

questions.q: Blood group AB shows
questions.why: In AB blood group both alleles (Iᴬ and Iᴮ) are fully expressed, so it is an example of codominance.

questions.q: Down syndrome is
questions.why: Down syndrome is trisomy 21 (an extra chromosome 21), so the person has 47 chromosomes.

questions.q: Snapdragon pink × pink gives red : pink : white
questions.why: With incomplete dominance (snapdragon), pink × pink gives red : pink : white in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: Number of gamete types from AaBbCc
questions.why: AaBbCc produces 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 types of gametes.

questions.q: Honey bee drones are
questions.why: Drones develop from unfertilised eggs by parthenogenesis, so they are haploid males.

questions.q: Assertion: A test cross reveals the genotype of a dominant-phenotype plant. Reason: the recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Crossing with the recessive parent, which gives only recessive alleles, makes the offspring's phenotypes show the gametes of the unknown parent, revealing its genotype.

questions.q: Parents A (Iᴬi) and B (Iᴮi): probability of an O child
questions.why: Parents Iᴬi × Iᴮi: a child is ii (group O) only if it gets i from both parents, probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.q: Carrier mother × normal father for haemophilia: probability a son is affected
questions.why: A carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) × normal father (XᴴY): sons get an X from the mother, so half the sons get Xʰ and are affected: 1/2.

questions.q: Case: In a dihybrid F₂ of 480 plants, the number expected to be round green (R_yy)
questions.why: Round green (R_yy) is 3/16 of the F₂, so 3/16 × 480 = 90 plants.

questions.q: Sickle-cell anaemia is due to
questions.why: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a point mutation, a single base change GAG to GUG, which makes valine replace glutamic acid.

questions.q: Low recombination frequency between two genes indicates
questions.why: Genes with a low recombination frequency are rarely separated by crossing over, which means they lie close together, tightly linked.

questions.q: A colour-blind man marries a woman homozygous normal. Their daughters will be
questions.why: A colour-blind man (XᶜY) and a homozygous normal woman (XX): each daughter gets his Xᶜ and her normal X, so all daughters are carriers.

questions.q: Case: A pedigree shows a trait in sons of unaffected mothers, skipping generations, and never passed father-to-son. Most likely
questions.why: A trait appearing in sons of unaffected mothers, skipping generations and never passing from father to son, fits X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.q: A dihybrid test cross gives 42% AB, 42% ab, 8% Ab, 8% aB. Recombination frequency
questions.why: Recombinants are the non-parental types Ab and aB: 8% + 8% = 16% recombination frequency.

questions.q: Phenylketonuria is an example of
questions.why: Phenylketonuria is due to one defective gene (enzyme) that has many effects on the body, so it is an example of pleiotropy.

questions.q: Klinefelter syndrome karyotype
questions.why: Klinefelter syndrome is 47, XXY, a male with an extra X chromosome.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Molecular Basis of Inheritance
courses.summary: DNA structure and packaging, the experiments that identified DNA as genetic material, replication, transcription and processing, the genetic code and translation, the lac operon, the Human Genome Project and DNA fingerprinting.
outcomes: Learners can describe the double helix and nucleosome packaging
Learners can explain the Griffith, Avery and Hershey–Chase experiments
Learners can explain semi-conservative replication and Meselson–Stahl
Learners can describe transcription, RNA processing and translation
Learners can explain the lac operon, HGP features and DNA fingerprinting

story.title: Two metres in a tiny nucleus

scenes.text: If you stretched out the DNA from one human cell, it would be about 2.2 metres long — yet it fits in a nucleus about 10⁻⁶ m across.
Cells pack DNA around protein spools called histones, like thread wound on bobbins.

steps.title: The polynucleotide chain
steps.body: A **nucleotide** = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate. Bases: purines **adenine (A), guanine (G)**; pyrimidines **cytosine (C), thymine (T)** in DNA, **uracil (U)** replacing T in RNA. Base + sugar (N-glycosidic bond) = **nucleoside**; adding phosphate (phosphoester bond) = nucleotide. Nucleotides join by **3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds**. DNA sugar is deoxyribose; RNA sugar is ribose (with a 2′-OH).

steps.title: The double helix (Watson & Crick, 1953)
steps.body:
Based on X-ray diffraction data from Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin.

- Two polynucleotide chains, sugar-phosphate backbone outside, bases inside
- Chains are **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′)
- Base pairing: **A=T (two H-bonds)**, **G≡C (three H-bonds)** — a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, giving uniform width
- Right-handed coil; pitch **3.4 nm**, about **10 bp per turn**, so ~**0.34 nm** between adjacent bp
- **Chargaff's rule**: in double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C, so (A + G) = (T + C)

Genome sizes: bacteriophage ϕX174 has 5386 nucleotides; phage λ 48,502 bp; *E. coli* 4.6 × 10⁶ bp; human haploid DNA about 3.3 × 10⁹ bp.

steps.title: Packaging
steps.body:
Prokaryotes: negatively charged DNA is held with positively charged proteins in a region called the **nucleoid**.

Eukaryotes: positively charged **histones** (rich in lysine and arginine) form an **octamer**; negatively charged DNA wraps around it → **nucleosome** (~200 bp). Repeating nucleosomes form 'beads-on-string' chromatin, which coils further into chromatin fibres and then into chromosomes (with **non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins**). Loosely packed, lightly stained, transcriptionally **active** chromatin = **euchromatin**; densely packed, darkly stained, **inactive** = **heterochromatin**.

steps.title: Solved: Chargaff calculation
steps.body:
Q: A double-stranded DNA has 20% adenine. Find the % of G.

Step 1: A = T = 20% ⇒ A + T = 40%.
Step 2: G + C = 60% and G = C ⇒ **G = 30%**.

steps.title: Solved: length of human DNA
steps.body:
Q: Estimate DNA length for 6.6 × 10⁹ bp (diploid).

Length = bp × 0.34 nm = 6.6 × 10⁹ × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m ≈ **2.2 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying A pairs with G — purines pair with **pyrimidines** (A–T, G–C).
- Writing three H-bonds for A=T.
- Saying heterochromatin is active — it is mostly inactive.

activity.prompt: A DNA molecule has 1000 base pairs. If 300 of its bases are thymine, how many guanine bases are there?

quiz.q: Distance between adjacent base pairs in B-DNA
quiz.why: In B-DNA, adjacent base pairs are 0.34 nm apart (3.4 nm per turn of 10 bp).

quiz.q: G≡C pairs have how many hydrogen bonds?
quiz.why: A G≡C base pair is held by 3 hydrogen bonds, whereas A=T has 2.
Histones are basic proteins rich in the positively charged amino acids lysine and arginine, which bind the negatively charged DNA.
A nucleosome has about 200 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.

quiz.q: If a DNA has 30% G, then A is

quiz.why: Euchromatin is loosely packed and transcriptionally active. Heterochromatin is densely packed and inactive.

lessons.title: The search for the genetic material

scenes.text: In 1928 Frederick Griffith injected mice with bacteria. Heat-killed deadly bacteria plus harmless live ones killed the mice — something had 'transformed' the harmless strain.
Over the next 25 years, scientists proved that the transforming substance — the genetic material — is DNA.

steps.title: Griffith's transformation (1928)
steps.body:
*Streptococcus pneumoniae*: **S strain** (smooth, capsule, virulent) and **R strain** (rough, no capsule, non-virulent).

- S → mouse dies
- R → mouse lives
- Heat-killed S → mouse lives
- Heat-killed S + live R → **mouse dies**; live S bacteria recovered

Conclusion: some 'transforming principle' from dead S bacteria converted R into S — but its chemical nature was unknown.

steps.title: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933–44); Hershey and Chase (1952)
steps.body:
Avery and colleagues purified biochemicals from heat-killed S cells: **DNA alone** transformed R bacteria; **proteases and RNases did not stop** transformation, but **DNase did** ⇒ DNA is the transforming principle.

Hershey and Chase grew bacteriophages with **radioactive ³²P** (labels DNA) or **³⁵S** (labels protein). After infection, blending and centrifugation, bacteria infected with ³²P-phage were radioactive; those with ³⁵S-phage were not ⇒ **DNA enters the bacterium; DNA is the genetic material** (unequivocal proof).

steps.title: Properties of genetic material; RNA world
steps.body:
Genetic material must: replicate; be chemically and structurally **stable**; allow slow change (mutation) for evolution; express itself as Mendelian characters.

DNA is more stable than RNA: RNA's **2′-OH** makes it reactive and easily degraded; DNA has **thymine** instead of uracil (adding stability), and double-strandedness allows repair. RNA is better for expression (it can catalyse reactions directly). Evidence suggests **RNA was the first genetic material** (RNA world); DNA evolved from it with chemical changes for stability. Some viruses (e.g. TMV, QB bacteriophage) still use RNA as genetic material.

steps.title: Solved: interpret an enzyme experiment
steps.body:
Q: Heat-killed S extract + DNase + live R → injected. Result?

Step 1: DNase destroys DNA.
Step 2: no transforming principle remains.
Step 3: R stays R; **mouse lives**.

steps.title: Solved: why use ³²P and ³⁵S?
steps.body:
Step 1: DNA contains phosphorus but not sulphur.
Step 2: proteins contain sulphur (in methionine, cysteine) but little/no phosphorus.
Step 3: so each isotope labels only one molecule type, allowing them to be tracked separately.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Griffith proved DNA is the genetic material — he only showed transformation.
- Swapping isotopes: ³²P labels **DNA**, ³⁵S labels **protein**.
- Claiming RNA is never genetic material.

activity.prompt: Put the discoveries in order

events.text: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identify DNA as the transforming principle
Hershey and Chase confirm DNA is the genetic material using phages
Watson and Crick propose the double helix
Meselson and Stahl show semi-conservative replication

quiz.why: Griffith worked with the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae (the S and R strains) in his transformation experiments.

quiz.q: Which enzyme blocked transformation in Avery's work?
quiz.why: In Avery, MacLeod and McCarty's work, DNase destroyed the DNA and blocked transformation, showing DNA is the transforming material.
³⁵S labels sulphur, which is found in proteins (e.g. cysteine), but not in DNA. So it labels the protein coat.

quiz.q: RNA is less stable because of
quiz.why: The 2′-OH group on the ribose makes RNA chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

quiz.q: Which virus has RNA as genetic material?
quiz.why: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has RNA as its genetic material. T2 phage, ϕX174 and λ phage are DNA viruses.

quiz.q: Hershey–Chase showed that what enters bacteria is
quiz.why: Hershey and Chase showed that radioactive ³²P (DNA) entered the bacteria while the ³⁵S (protein) stayed outside, so DNA is the genetic material.

scenes.text: In 1958 Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), then switched them to normal ¹⁴N.
Spinning DNA in a caesium chloride gradient, they saw one hybrid band after one generation — proof that each new DNA keeps one old strand.

steps.title: Semi-conservative replication
steps.body:
Watson and Crick proposed that the two strands separate and each acts as a **template** for a new complementary strand; each daughter DNA has one parental and one new strand — **semi-conservative**.

**Meselson–Stahl**: *E. coli* grown on ¹⁵NH₄Cl for many generations had heavy DNA (¹⁵N). Moved to ¹⁴N and sampled every 20 minutes (one generation). In **CsCl density gradient centrifugation**: after 1 generation all DNA was **hybrid** (intermediate density); after 2 generations **equal hybrid and light**. Taylor and colleagues showed the same in *Vicia faba* chromosomes using radioactive thymidine.

steps.title: Machinery
steps.body:
- Main enzyme: **DNA-dependent DNA polymerase**; it polymerises only in the **5′ → 3′** direction, very fast (~2000 bp/s in *E. coli*) and with high accuracy. Energy comes from deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates.
- Replication starts at an **origin of replication (ori)**; a small opening — the **replication fork** — forms.
- On the template with 3′ → 5′ polarity, synthesis is **continuous** (leading strand); on the other, **discontinuous** (lagging strand) as short pieces (Okazaki fragments) joined by **DNA ligase**.
- In eukaryotes replication occurs in the **S-phase** of the cell cycle; failure of cell division after replication leads to polyploidy.

steps.title: Solved: Meselson–Stahl after 3 generations
steps.body:
Step 1: generation 1 → 2 hybrid molecules.
Step 2: generation 2 → 2 hybrid + 2 light.
Step 3: generation 3 → 2 hybrid + 6 light ⇒ hybrid : light = **1 : 3** (25% hybrid).

steps.title: Solved: why lagging strand is discontinuous
steps.body:
Step 1: polymerase only adds nucleotides at the 3′ end (works 5′ → 3′).
Step 2: the fork opens in one direction, so one new strand grows towards the fork (continuous) while the other must grow away from it.
Step 3: that strand is made in short pieces, later joined by ligase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying replication is conservative or dispersive.
- Writing that polymerase works 3′ → 5′.
- Forgetting that ligase joins the discontinuous fragments.

activity.prompt: Starting with one ¹⁵N DNA molecule in ¹⁴N medium, how many molecules are fully light after 4 generations?

quiz.why: DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule has one old and one new strand, as shown by Meselson and Stahl.
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in heavy nitrogen, ¹⁵N, then in ¹⁴N, to separate old from new DNA by density.
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5′ → 3′ direction.
DNA ligase joins the discontinuous (Okazaki) fragments on the lagging strand.

quiz.q: In eukaryotes DNA replicates in the
quiz.why: In eukaryotes DNA replicates during the S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle.

quiz.q: After 2 generations in ¹⁴N, hybrid : light DNA =
quiz.why: After two generations in ¹⁴N, half the DNA molecules are hybrid (¹⁵N–¹⁴N) and half are light (¹⁴N–¹⁴N), i.e. 1 : 1.

story.title: Copying one recipe from the cookbook

scenes.text: A cook doesn't carry the whole cookbook to the stove — she copies one recipe onto a card.
Cells do the same: they copy one gene into RNA (transcription), then edit it before use.

steps.title: Transcription unit
steps.body:
Transcription copies genetic information from one DNA strand into RNA (with U instead of T). Only **one strand** is copied in a given region.

- **Template strand**: polarity 3′ → 5′; read by RNA polymerase.
- **Coding strand**: 5′ → 3′; same sequence as the RNA (T in place of U); not copied.
- A transcription unit has a **promoter** (upstream, towards the 5′ end of the coding strand; binding site for RNA polymerase), the **structural gene**, and a **terminator** (downstream).
- Coding sequences = **exons**; intervening non-coding sequences = **introns** (in eukaryotes; split genes). Cistron ≈ segment coding a polypeptide; in bacteria transcription units are often **polycistronic**, in eukaryotes **monocistronic**.

steps.title: Process in bacteria
steps.body: One **DNA-dependent RNA polymerase** makes all RNAs (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA). It binds the promoter with an initiation factor (**σ, sigma**) to start (**initiation**), extends RNA (**elongation**), and stops at the terminator with a termination factor (**ρ, rho**). In bacteria, mRNA needs no processing and **translation can start while transcription is still going on** (both in the cytoplasm).

steps.title: Eukaryotes: polymerases and processing
steps.body:
- **RNA pol I** → rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S)
- **RNA pol II** → precursor mRNA, the **heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA)**
- **RNA pol III** → tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs

hnRNA processing: **splicing** (introns removed, exons joined), **capping** (methyl guanosine triphosphate added to the 5′ end), **tailing** (200–300 adenylate residues added to the 3′ end, template-independent). The processed mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm for translation.

steps.title: Solved: write the mRNA
steps.body:
Q: Coding strand 5′-ATGCGTAC-3′. Give the mRNA.

Step 1: mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand.
Step 2: replace T with U ⇒ **5′-AUGCGUAC-3′**.
(Template strand is 3′-TACGCATG-5′.)

steps.title: Solved: why can't bacteria-style co-transcriptional translation happen in eukaryotes?
steps.body:
Step 1: in eukaryotes transcription occurs in the nucleus.
Step 2: hnRNA must be spliced, capped and tailed, then exported.
Step 3: translation happens in the cytoplasm, so the two processes are separated in space and time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing mRNA complementary to the coding strand — it's complementary to the **template** strand.
- Saying RNA pol III makes rRNAs 28S/18S — that's pol I.
- Forgetting that the poly-A tail is added without a DNA template.

activity.prompt: Write the mRNA for the coding strand 5′-TACG-3′.

quiz.q: The strand with 3′ → 5′ polarity used for transcription
quiz.why: The strand with 3′ → 5′ polarity serves as the template for transcription, giving an RNA complementary to it.
In bacteria, the sigma factor helps RNA polymerase recognise the promoter and start (initiate) transcription.
In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase II transcribes precursor mRNA (hnRNA).
Capping adds methyl guanosine triphosphate to the 5′ end of hnRNA.
Introns are intervening non-coding sequences in the gene that are removed during splicing. Exons are the coding parts.

options: can be translated while being transcribed
quiz.why: In bacteria, transcription and translation occur in the same cell compartment and mRNA needs no processing, so translation can start while transcription is still going on.

scenes.text: George Gamow reasoned that 4 bases must code for 20 amino acids. Pairs give only 16 combinations; triplets give 64 — enough.
Har Gobind Khorana, Marshall Nirenberg and Severo Ochoa then decoded which triplet means which amino acid.

steps.title: Features of the genetic code
steps.body:
- **Triplet**: 3 bases = 1 codon; 64 codons, **61 code for amino acids**, **3 are stop codons** (UAA, UAG, UGA)
- **Unambiguous and specific**: one codon → one amino acid
- **Degenerate**: some amino acids have more than one codon
- Read in a contiguous fashion — **no punctuation** (commaless)
- Nearly **universal** (with some exceptions, e.g. in mitochondrial codes and some protozoans)
- **AUG** has dual function: codes for **methionine** and acts as the **start codon**

Khorana developed chemical methods to synthesise RNA of defined base combinations (homopolymers and copolymers); Nirenberg's cell-free system helped; Ochoa's enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) polymerised RNA without a template.

steps.title: Mutations and the code; tRNA
steps.body:
Insertion or deletion of **one or two** bases shifts the reading frame (**frameshift**), changing all downstream codons; insertion/deletion of **three** bases adds/removes one amino acid without a frameshift. A single-base substitution (point mutation) changes one codon (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia).

**tRNA** is the **adapter molecule**: it has an **anticodon loop** (pairs with the codon) and an **amino acid acceptor end**. Secondary structure looks like a **clover-leaf**; in 3-D it is an **inverted L**. There are specific tRNAs for each amino acid; stop codons have no tRNA.

steps.title: Translation
steps.body:
1. **Charging (aminoacylation)** of tRNA: amino acid activated using ATP and linked to its tRNA.
2. **Initiation**: the ribosome (small + large subunits) binds the mRNA at the start codon AUG, recognised by the initiator tRNA.
3. **Elongation**: the large subunit has two tRNA-binding sites; successive charged tRNAs pair with codons; peptide bonds form. The 23S rRNA in bacteria acts as the enzyme — a **ribozyme** — for peptide bond formation.
4. **Termination**: a **release factor** binds the stop codon and the polypeptide is released.

mRNA also has **untranslated regions (UTRs)** before the start codon (5′ UTR) and after the stop codon (3′ UTR), needed for efficient translation.

steps.title: Solved: count amino acids
steps.body:
Q: An mRNA reads 5′-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3′ (spaces for clarity). How many amino acids?

AUG (Met), UUU (Phe), GGC (Gly), UAA (stop) ⇒ **3 amino acids**.

steps.title: Solved: frameshift
steps.body: Sentence-model: RAM HAS RED CAP. Delete the first 'H' → RAM ASR EDC AP… every word after the deletion is garbled. Deleting three letters (HAS) → RAM RED CAP: one 'word' lost, rest fine. Bases behave the same way.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 64 codons code for amino acids — **61** do.
- Calling AUG a stop codon.
- Saying the code is ambiguous because it is degenerate — degeneracy (many codons → one amino acid) is different from ambiguity.

statements.s: UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
The genetic code is ambiguous.
statements.why: Each codon specifies only one amino acid.

statements.s: AUG codes for methionine and is the start codon.
Deleting three adjacent bases always causes a frameshift.
statements.why: It removes one codon; the frame is kept.

statements.s: 23S rRNA acts as a ribozyme in bacteria.

quiz.q: Number of codons that code for amino acids
quiz.why: There are 64 codons, of which 3 are stop codons, so 61 codons code for amino acids.
tRNA is the adapter that reads the mRNA codon with its anticodon and carries the matching amino acid.
tRNA looks like a clover-leaf in a two-dimensional diagram, but its actual three-dimensional shape is an inverted L.

quiz.q: Peptide bond formation in bacteria is catalysed by
quiz.why: In bacteria, 23S rRNA acts as a ribozyme and catalyses peptide bond formation.

quiz.q: One amino acid having several codons shows the code is
quiz.why: When one amino acid is coded by more than one codon, the genetic code is called degenerate.

quiz.q: mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UGA-3′ codes for how many amino acids?
quiz.why: AUG (Met) and GCU (Ala) code for two amino acids, and UGA is a stop codon, so there are 2 amino acids.

lessons.title: Regulation of gene expression: the lac operon

scenes.text: E. coli in your gut doesn't waste energy making lactose-digesting enzymes when there is no milk sugar around.
When lactose appears, a molecular switch — the lac operon — turns the genes on.

steps.title: Levels of regulation
steps.body: In eukaryotes, gene expression can be regulated at transcription (formation of primary transcript), processing (splicing), transport of mRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm, and translation. In prokaryotes, control of the **rate of transcription initiation** is the main site. Arrangement where a polycistronic structural gene is regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes is an **operon**.

steps.title: The lac operon (Jacob and Monod)
steps.body:
- **i gene** (regulator; 'i' from inhibitor): codes the **repressor**, made constitutively
- **z gene** → **β-galactosidase** (hydrolyses lactose to galactose + glucose)
- **y gene** → **permease** (increases cell permeability to β-galactosides)
- **a gene** → **transacetylase**

No lactose: repressor binds the **operator** → RNA polymerase can't transcribe → genes OFF.
Lactose (inducer; actually allolactose) present: inducer binds and inactivates the repressor → RNA polymerase transcribes → genes ON. When lactose is used up, repression returns. This is **negative regulation**. (The operon also has positive regulation, not detailed at this level.)

steps.title: Solved: predict the outcome
steps.body:
Q: A mutant *E. coli* makes a repressor that cannot bind the operator. What happens without lactose?

Step 1: the repressor can't block the operator.
Step 2: RNA polymerase transcribes z, y, a continuously.
Step 3: the enzymes are made **all the time (constitutively)**, wasting energy.

steps.title: Solved: why is lactose an inducer?
steps.body: Lactose (via allolactose) inactivates the repressor, **inducing** transcription — so the lac operon is an inducible operon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the i gene is part of the polycistronic mRNA with z, y, a — it has its own promoter.
- Thinking the repressor binds lactose to activate genes directly — it is **inactivated** by the inducer.
- Saying glucose is the inducer.

activity.prompt: Match lac operon parts with functions

quiz.q: The lac operon was proposed by
quiz.why: François Jacob and Jacques Monod proposed the lac operon model for gene regulation in 1961.
The z gene of the lac operon codes for β-galactosidase, the enzyme that splits lactose.
Lactose (as allolactose) is the inducer of the lac operon: it binds the repressor and inactivates it.
Without lactose, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription of the structural genes.

quiz.q: Regulation of lac operon by repressor is
quiz.why: The lac operon is regulated by a repressor that switches genes off, which is negative regulation.

lessons.title: Human Genome Project and DNA fingerprinting

scenes.text: Forensic scientists compare DNA from a crime scene with suspects' samples. No two people (except identical twins) share the same pattern of repeats.
The tools came from genomics: the Human Genome Project mapped our DNA, and DNA fingerprinting exploits its variable regions.

steps.title: Human Genome Project (HGP)
steps.body:
Launched in **1990**, completed in **2003**, coordinated by the US Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health, with contributions from the UK's Wellcome Trust and others. It used methods like **Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)** (identifying genes expressed as RNA) and **sequence annotation** (sequencing the whole genome, then assigning functions). DNA was cut into fragments, cloned in vectors such as **BAC** and **YAC**, and sequenced with automated sequencers (based on Frederick Sanger's method).

Salient features:
- About **3164.7 million bp**
- Average gene ~3000 bases; largest known human gene **dystrophin** ~2.4 million bases
- Estimated ~30,000 genes at that time (later studies suggest around 20,000 protein-coding genes)
- **99.9%** of bases are identical in all people
- Less than **2%** of the genome codes for proteins; repeated sequences make up a large part
- Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968), Y the fewest (231)
- About **1.4 million** locations with single-base DNA differences (**SNPs**)

steps.title: DNA fingerprinting
steps.body:
Developed by **Alec Jeffreys**. It compares **repetitive DNA** — especially **satellite DNA** (separates as small peaks in density gradient centrifugation). Satellite DNA classified as micro-satellite, mini-satellite etc.; these don't code for proteins and show high **polymorphism** (inheritable variation; if a variant occurs at a frequency > 0.01 in a population it is a polymorphism).

Steps: isolate DNA → digest with **restriction endonucleases** → separate fragments by **electrophoresis** → transfer to nitrocellulose/nylon membranes (**Southern blotting**) → hybridise with labelled **VNTR probes** → detect by **autoradiography**. VNTR (variable number of tandem repeats) size ranges from about 0.1 to 20 kb.

Uses: forensic science, paternity disputes, studying population and genetic diversity. Small amounts of DNA can be amplified by **PCR**.

steps.title: Solved: paternity reasoning
steps.body:
Q: A child's DNA bands: every band is found in either the mother or a man X. Interpretation?

Step 1: a child inherits half its bands from each biological parent.
Step 2: bands not from the mother must come from the father.
Step 3: if all such bands match X, the result supports X being the biological father (labs use many probes and statistics before concluding).

steps.title: Solved: why use repeats and not genes?
steps.body:
Step 1: coding genes are highly similar across people (99.9% identity overall).
Step 2: VNTRs vary greatly in repeat number between individuals.
Step 3: so they give individual-specific patterns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying VNTRs code for proteins.
- Confusing Southern blotting (DNA) with other blots.
- Saying the HGP found 99.9% difference between people — it's 99.9% **similarity**.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of DNA fingerprinting

quiz.why: The Human Genome Project began in 1990 and was completed in 2003.

quiz.q: Percentage of bases identical in all humans
quiz.why: About 99.9% of nucleotide bases are the same in all people. Only about 0.1% differ.
Dystrophin, which is linked to muscular dystrophy, is the largest known human gene with about 2.4 million bases.
Chromosome Y has the fewest genes, about 231, while chromosome 1 has the most.
Alec Jeffreys developed DNA fingerprinting, using VNTRs to tell individuals apart.
VNTRs (variable number of tandem repeats) belong to repetitive satellite DNA, which differs between individuals.

questions.q: Base pairing in DNA
questions.why: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine (A–T) and guanine with cytosine (G–C), as in Chargaff's rules. A–U is in RNA.

questions.q: Number of stop codons
questions.why: There are three stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA.

questions.q: DNA fingerprinting uses
questions.why: DNA fingerprinting uses VNTRs (repeated sequences), which vary from person to person.

questions.q: If DNA has 18% cytosine, adenine is
questions.why: By Chargaff's rule C = G = 18%, so G + C = 36% and A + T = 64%. Since A = T, adenine = 32%.

questions.q: Hershey and Chase used
questions.why: Hershey and Chase used radioactive ³²P to label DNA and ³⁵S to label protein.

questions.q: Okazaki fragments form on the
questions.why: Okazaki fragments are short pieces made on the lagging strand, which is synthesised discontinuously.

questions.q: Assertion: In bacteria translation can begin before transcription ends. Reason: bacterial mRNA needs no processing and both occur in the cytoplasm.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. In bacteria mRNA needs no processing and both processes occur in the same compartment, so translation can start before transcription is finished.

questions.q: RNA polymerase III makes
questions.why: RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs. Pol I makes the larger rRNAs and Pol II makes hnRNA.

questions.q: Meselson–Stahl: after 3 generations in ¹⁴N, % hybrid DNA
questions.why: In 3 generations in ¹⁴N there are 8 DNA molecules, of which 2 are hybrid (each with one old ¹⁵N strand), so 25%.

questions.q: Case: An mRNA 5′-AUG CCC AAA UGA-3′ is translated. Number of amino acids
questions.why: AUG, CCC and AAA code for three amino acids, and UGA is a stop codon, so 3 amino acids.

questions.q: Histone octamer + DNA forms
questions.why: DNA wrapped around a histone octamer forms a nucleosome, the basic unit of chromatin.

questions.q: A mutant repressor that can't bind the operator makes lac genes
questions.why: If the repressor cannot bind the operator, transcription is never blocked, so the lac genes are expressed constitutively (all the time).

questions.q: Deletion of a single base in a coding region usually causes
questions.why: Deleting one base shifts the reading frame of all the codons that follow, which is a frameshift mutation.

questions.q: Coding strand 5′-ATGGCA-3′; the template strand is
questions.why: The template strand is complementary and antiparallel to the coding strand 5′-ATGGCA-3′, so it is 3′-TACCGT-5′ (with T, not U, since it is DNA).

questions.q: Length of DNA with 5 × 10⁶ bp (approx.)
questions.why: Length = number of bp × 0.34 nm = 5 × 10⁶ × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1.7 × 10⁻³ m = 1.7 mm.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of the genetic code?
questions.why: The genetic code is triplet, degenerate and nearly universal, but not ambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid.

questions.q: Why is DNA preferred as genetic material over RNA?
options: it is more stable (no 2′-OH; has thymine)
questions.why: DNA is more stable than RNA because it has no reactive 2′-OH group and uses thymine, which helps repair, so it is better suited to storing genetic information.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Evolution
courses.summary: Origin of life, evidences for evolution, adaptive radiation, theories of Lamarck, Darwin and de Vries, Hardy–Weinberg principle and evolutionary forces, and a brief account of life's history and human evolution.
outcomes: Learners can describe theories of the origin of life and Miller's experiment
Learners can distinguish homologous and analogous organs with examples
Learners can compare Lamarckism, Darwinism and mutation theory
Learners can solve Hardy–Weinberg problems and classify selection types
Learners can outline human evolution with approximate dates

scenes.text: In 1953 Stanley Miller sealed methane, hydrogen, ammonia and water vapour in glass and passed electric sparks through it for days.
Amino acids appeared — evidence that life's building blocks could form from simple chemicals on the early Earth.

steps.title: From the universe to Earth
steps.body: The universe is very old — current scientific estimates put the Big Bang at about **13.8 billion years ago**. Earth formed about **4.5 billion years ago**. The early atmosphere had water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia released from molten mass; UV rays split water into H₂ and O₂. (Older textbooks give different figures; dates are revised as evidence improves.)

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Special creation**: all living things created as they are; Earth only a few thousand years old — not supported by evidence.
- **Panspermia**: units of life ('spores') transferred from other planets — still a speculative idea.
- **Spontaneous generation**: life arises from decaying matter. **Louis Pasteur** disproved it: pre-sterilised flasks stayed free of life, while flasks open to air developed microbes.
- **Oparin and Haldane**: the first forms of life came from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein), via **chemical evolution** — formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents — on a hot, reducing early Earth.

steps.title: Miller's experiment and first life
steps.body: Miller created electric discharge in a closed flask with **CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at about 800 °C** and observed formation of **amino acids**. Others later observed sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats. Analysis of meteorites also revealed similar compounds. The first non-cellular forms of life probably arose about 3 billion years ago (e.g. giant molecules like RNA, proteins, polysaccharides) and cellular life later in water. (Fossil evidence of microbial life is at least about 3.5 billion years old.)

steps.title: Solved: interpret Pasteur
steps.body:
Step 1: broth in a sealed, pre-sterilised flask stays clear.
Step 2: broth in a flask exposed to air becomes cloudy with microbes.
Step 3: conclusion: life comes from pre-existing life, not spontaneously from broth.

steps.title: Solved: what did Miller NOT show?
steps.body: He showed **amino acids** could form abiotically. He did not create a living cell; the step from molecules to self-replicating cells remains an open research question.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Miller created life — he made organic molecules.
- Including oxygen in the early reducing atmosphere of the experiment.
- Presenting panspermia as proven.

activity.prompt: Arrange in time order

events.text: Earliest fossil evidence of microbial life
Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species

quiz.why: Louis Pasteur showed with his flask experiments that life comes only from pre-existing life, disproving spontaneous generation.
Miller's apparatus simulated early Earth with CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour (a reducing atmosphere).
In Miller's experiment, electric discharges in that gas mixture produced amino acids.
Oparin and Haldane proposed that life began through chemical evolution of simple molecules into complex ones.
Panspermia is the idea that life came to Earth from outer space (other planets).

scenes.text: Before England's factories, most peppered moths were pale, matching lichen-covered trees. After industrialisation, soot darkened the bark and dark moths became common.
Birds ate the moths they could see. Nature 'selected' the camouflaged form — evolution observed within decades.

steps.title: Palaeontological and anatomical evidence
steps.body:
**Fossils** — remains of life forms in rocks — show that organisms in different rock layers differ; some forms became extinct; their age is estimated by **radioactive dating**.

- **Homologous organs**: same basic structure, different functions → **divergent evolution**. Forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and humans (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges); vertebrate hearts and brains; in plants, the **thorn of Bougainvillea** and **tendril of Cucurbita**.
- **Analogous organs**: different structure, similar function → **convergent evolution**. Wings of butterfly and bird; eyes of octopus and mammals; flippers of penguins and dolphins; sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification).

steps.title: Biochemical and observed evidence
steps.body:
Similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms indicate common ancestry.

**Industrial melanism** (*Biston betularia*): in collections before industrialisation (around 1850), white-winged moths outnumbered dark ones; after industrialisation the reverse held in polluted areas. In rural areas without pollution, dark moths remained rare. Predators spot moths against contrasting backgrounds — natural selection in action.

**Anthropogenic action** also drives evolution: excess use of herbicides, pesticides and antibiotics selects resistant weeds, insects and microbes in a few months or years.

steps.title: Solved: homologous or analogous?
steps.body:
Q: Wings of a bat and wings of a butterfly?

Step 1: bat wings are modified forelimbs with bones; butterfly wings are cuticle extensions with no bones.
Step 2: same function, different origin/structure ⇒ **analogous** (convergent evolution).

steps.title: Solved: why antibiotic courses must be completed
steps.body:
Step 1: in a bacterial population, a few cells may carry resistance mutations.
Step 2: an antibiotic kills susceptible cells; stopping early leaves the toughest survivors.
Step 3: they multiply, so the population becomes resistant — evolution by selection in real time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling potato and sweet potato homologous — they are **analogous** (stem vs root).
- Saying dark moths 'turned' dark because of soot — the frequency of an existing dark form increased.
- Mixing divergent (homology) and convergent (analogy) evolution.

activity.prompt: Homologous or analogous?

items.text: Forelimbs of whale, bat and human
