lessons.title: Adaptive radiation and theories of evolution

scenes.text: On the Galapagos Islands Darwin saw finches with very different beaks — seed-crushers, insect-eaters and more — all similar otherwise.
He concluded they had evolved from a common ancestor that reached the islands and spread into different niches.

steps.title: Adaptive radiation
steps.body:
Evolution of different species in a geographical area starting from one point and radiating to other habitats.

- **Darwin's finches** (Galapagos): from original seed-eaters, forms with altered beaks arose, becoming insectivorous and vegetarian finches.
- **Australian marsupials**: from an ancestral stock, many marsupials evolved (e.g. numbat, spotted cuscus, flying phalanger, bandicoot, kangaroo, koala, Tasmanian wolf…).
- When more than one adaptive radiation appears in an isolated area, it leads to **convergent evolution**: e.g. Australian marsupials and placental mammals elsewhere (Tasmanian wolf ↔ wolf; marsupial mole ↔ placental mole; sugar glider ↔ flying squirrel).

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Lamarck**: evolution driven by **use and disuse** of organs and inheritance of acquired characters (e.g. giraffes stretching necks). Not supported: acquired characters are not inherited genetically.
- **Darwin (and Wallace)**: **natural selection** — organisms vary; populations produce more offspring than can survive; those with heritable variations better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more (**fitness = reproductive fitness**). Over generations, new types arise. Darwin based this on his voyage on **HMS Beagle**; Alfred Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, reached similar conclusions.
- **Hugo de Vries** (working on evening primrose): proposed **mutations** — large, sudden variations — cause evolution, i.e. **saltation** (single-step large mutation), unlike Darwin's small, directional variations.

steps.title: Solved: Lamarck vs Darwin on giraffes
steps.body:
Lamarck: giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves; longer necks were passed on.

Darwin: giraffes varied in neck length; those with longer necks reached more food, survived and left more offspring, so the trait's frequency increased.

steps.title: Solved: spot convergent evolution
steps.body:
Q: Australian sugar glider and North American flying squirrel look alike. Why?

They belong to different lineages (marsupial vs placental) but adapted to similar gliding lifestyles — **convergent evolution**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Darwin's fitness means physical strength — it is **reproductive success**.
- Attributing mutation theory to Darwin.
- Calling adaptive radiation 'convergent' — radiation is divergent from one ancestor; convergence arises when separate radiations produce similar forms.

activity.prompt: Match the idea to the scientist
pairs: Use and disuse; inheritance of acquired characters

quiz.why: Darwin's finches on the Galapagos, with beaks adapted to different foods from one ancestor, show adaptive radiation.
In Darwin's theory, fitness means reproductive fitness: the ability to leave more surviving offspring, not strength or size.
Hugo de Vries worked on the evening primrose (Oenothera) and proposed the mutation theory.
The Tasmanian wolf and the placental wolf look similar but come from different lineages, so this is convergent evolution.

options: acquired characters are not genetically inherited
quiz.why: Lamarck's idea that acquired characters are inherited is rejected, since changes acquired during life are not passed on through genes.

lessons.title: Mechanism of evolution and Hardy–Weinberg principle

scenes.text: In a large population of beetles, scientists count alleles for colour every year. If nothing disturbs the population, the frequencies stay the same.
When they do change — by migration, drift, mutation, recombination or selection — evolution is happening.

steps.title: Hardy–Weinberg principle
steps.body:
In a population, allele frequencies are stable and constant from generation to generation — **genetic equilibrium** — if the population is large, mating is random, and there is no mutation, migration or selection.

With allele frequencies p and q: p + q = 1 and genotype frequencies **p² + 2pq + q² = 1** (AA, Aa, aa). A measured deviation from these values indicates the extent of **evolutionary change**.

steps.title: Factors that disturb equilibrium
steps.body:
- **Gene migration (gene flow)**: genes move between populations
- **Genetic drift**: chance changes, strongest in small populations; when a small group founds a new population with very different allele frequencies it is the **founder effect**
- **Mutation**
- **Genetic recombination** during gamete formation
- **Natural selection**: makes heritable variations enabling better survival and reproduction more common. It can be **stabilising** (more individuals acquire the mean character), **directional** (more acquire a value other than the mean) or **disruptive** (more individuals at both extremes).

steps.title: Solved: Hardy–Weinberg calculation
steps.body:
Q: In a population, 16% show a recessive trait (aa). Find p, q and carrier frequency.

Step 1: q² = 0.16 ⇒ q = 0.4.
Step 2: p = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6.
Step 3: carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = **0.48 (48%)**; AA = p² = 0.36.

steps.title: Solved: identify the type of selection
steps.body:
Q: Over generations, a bird population's beak sizes cluster at both very small and very large, with fewer medium beaks.

Both extremes favoured ⇒ **disruptive selection**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking q = 0.16 directly from 16% affected — 16% is **q²**.
- Saying drift is important in large populations — it matters most in small ones.
- Confusing stabilising (favours mean) with directional (shifts mean).

activity.prompt: If the frequency of allele A is 0.7 in a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of heterozygotes (Aa)?

quiz.why: The Hardy–Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1, giving the genotype frequencies for two alleles.

quiz.q: Founder effect is a type of
quiz.why: The founder effect, in which a small founding group has different allele frequencies, is a type of genetic drift.
Disruptive selection favours both extremes of a trait and selects against the average, giving two peaks.

options: random mating with no mutation, migration or selection
quiz.why: Allele frequencies stay constant only in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, with random mating and no mutation, migration, selection or drift.
If p = 0.6, the frequency of AA is p² = 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36.

lessons.title: A brief account of evolution and the origin of humans

story.title: A walk through the fossil gallery

scenes.text: In a natural history museum, Mira walks past skulls arranged by age — larger braincases appear as she moves towards the present.
Human evolution was not a straight ladder but a branching bush, with Africa at its root.

steps.title: Broad sequence of life (simplified)
steps.body: Life began in water. Over hundreds of millions of years, plants and animals moved to land; jawless fish → fish with jaws → lobefins (ancestors of amphibians; e.g. *Coelacanth*, thought extinct, was found in 1938 off South Africa) → amphibians → reptiles → mammals and birds. Reptiles such as dinosaurs dominated before their extinction about 65 million years ago; mammals then diversified. In plants: seaweeds → bryophytes → pteridophytes → gymnosperms → angiosperms (simplified).

steps.title: Human evolution (approximate dates)
steps.body:
- About **15 million years ago**: hairy, ape-like *Dryopithecus* and *Ramapithecus* walked like gorillas and chimpanzees (Ramapithecus more man-like)
- About **2 million years ago**: **Australopithecines** probably lived in East African grasslands, hunted with stone weapons, ate mainly fruit
- **Homo habilis** ('handy man'): brain about **650–800 cc**; probably did not eat meat
- About **1.5 million years ago**: **Homo erectus**, brain about **900 cc**, probably ate meat
- **Neanderthal man**: brain about **1400 cc**, lived in the near east and central Asia between about 1,00,000 and 40,000 years ago; used hides for protection and buried their dead
- **Homo sapiens** arose in Africa and moved across continents; modern Homo sapiens arose during the ice age between about 75,000 and 10,000 years ago
- Pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago (e.g. **Bhimbetka** rock shelters, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh); agriculture began about 10,000 years ago

Dates are estimates and are revised as new fossils are found.

steps.title: Solved: order by brain size
steps.body: Homo habilis (650–800 cc) < Homo erectus (~900 cc) < Neanderthal (~1400 cc). Brain size increased over hominin evolution (modern human average ~1350 cc).

steps.title: Solved: why is Coelacanth special?
steps.body:
Step 1: lobefins are thought to be ancestors of the first amphibians.
Step 2: Coelacanth, a lobefin, was considered extinct.
Step 3: it was caught alive in 1938 off South Africa — a 'living fossil'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying humans evolved from modern chimpanzees — humans and chimpanzees share a **common ancestor**.
- Mixing up brain sizes of H. habilis and H. erectus.
- Treating approximate dates as exact.

quiz.why: Homo erectus had a brain capacity of about 900 cc, bigger than Homo habilis (650–800 cc) but smaller than the Neanderthal (about 1400 cc).

The coelacanth is a lobe-finned fish once thought extinct, a 'living fossil'.
Humans and chimpanzees did not evolve from each other: they share a common ancestor and then diverged.

questions.why: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium needs no selection, mutation or migration (and a large population with random mating).

questions.q: Darwin's finches are an example of
questions.why: Darwin's finches evolved varied beaks from a common ancestor, which is adaptive radiation.

questions.q: Saltation was proposed by
questions.why: Saltation, a sudden large mutation, was proposed by Hugo de Vries as the basis of speciation.

questions.q: Founder effect causes
questions.why: The founder effect is a case of genetic drift: a small group's chance allele frequencies differ from the original population.

questions.why: Both are true. Potato (a stem) and sweet potato (a root) have different origins but a similar storage function, so they are analogous.

questions.why: If q² = 0.09 then q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Carriers = 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42.

questions.why: Mosquitoes that already had resistance survived DDT and multiplied, which is natural selection caused by human activity.

questions.why: After industrialisation, soot darkened tree bark, so dark moths were better camouflaged and survived more, so they increased.

questions.why: A brain capacity of about 1400 cc belongs to the Neanderthal.

questions.why: In directional selection, the population's mean shifts toward one extreme of the trait.

questions.why: The Tasmanian wolf (marsupial) and the wolf (placental) look alike because they evolved separately in similar niches, which is convergent evolution.

questions.why: q = 0.2, so q² = 0.04. The expected number of aa individuals = 0.04 × 1000 = 40.

options: It showed life comes from pre-existing life

questions.why: The heterozygote frequency is 2pq. With p = 0.5, q = 0.5, so 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.5.

questions.why: The thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita are both modified stems with a different function, so they are homologous structures (the textbook example).

scenes.text: Every monsoon, a district hospital fills with fever patients — typhoid from unsafe water, malaria and dengue from mosquitoes.
Knowing which pathogen causes which disease, and how it spreads, tells us exactly how to prevent it.

steps.title: Health and pathogens
steps.body: **Health** is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease. Diseases that pass from one person to another are **infectious**. Disease-causing organisms are **pathogens**: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, helminths.

steps.title: Bacterial and viral diseases
steps.body:
- **Typhoid** – *Salmonella typhi*; enters the small intestine via contaminated food and water, can spread to other organs through blood. Sustained high fever (39–40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache, loss of appetite; intestinal perforation and death in severe cases. Confirmed by the **Widal test**. A famous carrier, Mary Mallon ('Typhoid Mary'), a cook, spread it for years without falling ill herself.
- **Pneumonia** – *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae*; infects alveoli, which fill with fluid. Fever, chills, cough, headache; in severe cases lips and fingernails turn grey to bluish. Spread by droplets/aerosols and sharing utensils.
- **Common cold** – **rhinoviruses**; infect the nose and respiratory passage, **not the lungs**. Nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache, tiredness, lasting 3–7 days. Spread by droplets and contaminated objects.

steps.title: Protozoan, helminth and fungal diseases
steps.body:
- **Malaria** – *Plasmodium* (*P. vivax*, *P. malariae*, *P. falciparum*; falciparum malaria is the most serious, can be fatal). Female *Anopheles* injects **sporozoites** → multiply in **liver cells** → attack **red blood cells** and rupture them → release of the toxin **haemozoin** causes chills and high fever recurring every 3–4 days. Gametocytes develop in RBCs; a biting mosquito takes them up; fertilisation and development occur in the mosquito's gut; sporozoites move to its **salivary glands**. The mosquito is the **definitive host** (sexual stage) and humans the intermediate host.
- **Amoebiasis** – *Entamoeba histolytica* in the large intestine; constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, stools with excess mucus and blood clots. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers.
- **Ascariasis** – roundworm *Ascaris*; internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, intestinal blockage. Eggs pass in faeces and contaminate soil, water and plants.
- **Filariasis (elephantiasis)** – *Wuchereria bancrofti* and *W. malayi*; chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs (and genital organs), gross deformities. Spread by female mosquito vectors.
- **Ringworm** – fungi *Microsporum*, *Trichophyton*, *Epidermophyton*; dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp with intense itching. Favoured by heat and moisture (skin folds); spread via soil or shared towels, clothes, combs.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Personal hygiene (clean body, clean drinking water and food); public hygiene (proper disposal of waste and excreta, periodic cleaning of water reservoirs, standard practices in public catering). For vector-borne diseases (malaria, filariasis, dengue, chikungunya by *Aedes*): avoid stagnant water, regular cleaning of coolers, mosquito nets, door/window screens, introduce larvae-eating fish like *Gambusia*, spray insecticides in drains and ditches. Vaccination has controlled polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus, and **eradicated smallpox**.

steps.title: Solved: identify the disease
steps.body:
Q: A patient has fever with chills recurring every 3 days after travelling to a mosquito-prone area. Blood smear shows parasites in RBCs.

Step 1: recurring fever + RBC parasites → malaria.
Step 2: vector → female *Anopheles*; toxin → haemozoin.

steps.title: Solved: why is typhoid tested by Widal?
steps.body: The Widal test detects **antibodies** against *Salmonella typhi* in the patient's blood serum, confirming typhoid infection.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying common cold infects lungs.
- Writing the male *Anopheles* as the vector — only **females** bite and transmit.
- Calling ringworm a worm — it's a **fungal** infection.

This is general education, not medical advice — see a doctor for fever lasting more than a day or two.

activity.prompt: Match the disease with its pathogen

quiz.why: The Widal test detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi in the blood and is used to confirm typhoid.
When Plasmodium ruptures the red blood cells, the toxic substance haemozoin is released and causes the chills and high fever of malaria.

quiz.q: Fish used to control mosquito larvae
quiz.why: The fish Gambusia feeds on mosquito larvae, so it is used to control mosquitoes.
Elephantiasis (filariasis) is caused by the filarial worm Wuchereria and results in swelling of limbs.

quiz.q: Sporozoites of Plasmodium are stored in the mosquito's
quiz.why: The sporozoites of Plasmodium are stored in the salivary glands of the female Anopheles mosquito and are injected when it bites.

quiz.q: Which disease has been eradicated by vaccination?
quiz.why: Smallpox was eradicated globally through vaccination. Polio is nearly eliminated but not eradicated, and typhoid and malaria still occur.

story.title: The second chickenpox that never came

scenes.text: Dev had chickenpox at age six. Years later, his sister catches it, but he doesn't — his body 'remembers'.
That memory is acquired immunity, built by lymphocytes and antibodies.

steps.title: Innate immunity (present at birth, non-specific)
steps.body:
- **Physical barriers**: skin; mucus coating of respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts traps microbes
- **Physiological barriers**: acid in stomach, saliva in mouth, tears in eyes
- **Cellular barriers**: leukocytes — polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), monocytes, natural killer lymphocytes — and macrophages phagocytose and destroy microbes
- **Cytokine barriers**: virus-infected cells secrete **interferons**, protecting non-infected cells

steps.title: Acquired immunity (specific, with memory)
steps.body:
First encounter → low-intensity **primary response**; later encounter → highly intensified **secondary (anamnestic) response**, thanks to memory.

- **B-lymphocytes** produce **antibodies** (immunoglobulins) — **humoral immunity**. An antibody has four peptide chains, two light and two heavy (H₂L₂). Types: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG.
- **T-lymphocytes** help B cells and mediate **cell-mediated immunity (CMI)** — responsible for **graft rejection**; hence tissue and blood-group matching and lifelong immunosuppressants after transplants.

**Active immunity**: body makes its own antibodies (after infection or vaccination) — slow but long-lasting. **Passive immunity**: ready-made antibodies given — fast, temporary. Examples: **colostrum** has IgA for the infant; the foetus receives IgG through the placenta; injections of preformed antibodies or antitoxins (e.g. for tetanus, or snake antivenom).

steps.title: Vaccination, allergy, autoimmunity and lymphoid organs
steps.body:
**Vaccination**: inactivated/weakened pathogen or its antigenic proteins prime the immune system to make memory B and T cells. Recombinant DNA technology produces antigenic polypeptides in bacteria or yeast (e.g. **hepatitis B vaccine from yeast**).

**Allergy**: exaggerated response to allergens (dust mites, pollen, animal dander). Antibodies of the **IgE** type; mast cells release **histamine and serotonin**. Symptoms: sneezing, watery eyes, running nose, difficulty breathing. Drugs: anti-histamines, adrenaline, steroids.

**Autoimmunity**: immune system attacks self cells (e.g. **rheumatoid arthritis**).

**Lymphoid organs**: **primary** — bone marrow and thymus (where lymphocytes are produced/mature); **secondary** — spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine, appendix. **MALT** (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) is about 50% of the lymphoid tissue in the body.

steps.title: Solved: active or passive?
steps.body:
- Polio vaccine → **active** (body makes antibodies).
- Anti-tetanus serum after a deep wound → **passive** (ready-made antibodies, quick protection).
- Mother's milk antibodies to baby → **passive (natural)**.

steps.title: Solved: why do transplant patients take immunosuppressants?
steps.body:
Step 1: T-lymphocytes recognise the graft as 'non-self'.
Step 2: cell-mediated immunity attacks it (graft rejection).
Step 3: immunosuppressants damp this response; matching tissue types also reduces risk.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling vaccines 'passive' immunity.
- Saying IgG mediates allergy — it is **IgE**.
- Listing spleen as a primary lymphoid organ — it is **secondary**.

activity.prompt: Innate or acquired?

quiz.why: An antibody molecule is made of four peptide chains, two heavy and two light, written H₂L₂.
IgE antibodies are responsible for allergic reactions.
Colostrum, the mother's first milk, is rich in IgA antibodies that protect the infant, giving passive immunity.
Graft rejection is caused by cell-mediated immunity, in which T cells attack the foreign tissue.
The primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes are produced and mature, are the bone marrow and the thymus.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease: the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue.

scenes.text: On World AIDS Day (1 December), a school holds an assembly. Students list myths: 'You get HIV from hugging', 'mosquitoes spread it'.
A doctor explains how HIV actually spreads, what it does to the immune system and how to prevent it.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: **AIDS** = Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome — deficiency of the immune system acquired during life. First reported in **1981**. Caused by **HIV** (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), a **retrovirus** with an RNA genome.

steps.title: Transmission and who is at risk
steps.body:
HIV spreads by:

- sexual contact with an infected person
- transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products
- sharing infected needles (e.g. among intravenous drug users)
- from an infected mother to her child through the placenta

It does **not** spread by mere touch or physical contact — only through body fluids. Those at higher risk include people with multiple sexual partners, drug addicts who take drugs intravenously, individuals who require repeated blood transfusions and children born to HIV-infected mothers.

steps.title: How HIV damages immunity
steps.body:
1. HIV enters **macrophages**; its RNA is copied into viral DNA by **reverse transcriptase**.
2. Viral DNA integrates into the host DNA; infected cells produce virus particles — the macrophage acts like an **HIV factory**.
3. HIV enters **helper T-lymphocytes (T_H)**, replicates and produces progeny viruses, which attack more T_H cells. T_H numbers fall progressively.
4. Infected persons get repeated fever, diarrhoea, weight loss, and **opportunistic infections** (e.g. *Mycobacterium*, viruses, fungi, parasites like *Toxoplasma*).

There is often a **time-lag of a few months to many years (usually 5–10 years)** between infection and symptoms. Diagnosis: **ELISA** (Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay), confirmed by other tests. **Antiretroviral drugs** are only partially effective: they prolong life but cannot cure AIDS.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: India's **NACO** (National AIDS Control Organisation) and NGOs educate people. Measures: ensure safe blood from blood banks; use of only disposable needles and syringes in hospitals; free distribution of condoms; control of drug abuse; advocating safe sex; regular check-ups for susceptible populations. Help infected people with care and dignity — stigma stops people from getting tested.

steps.title: Solved: why is AIDS called a syndrome?
steps.body: It is not a single disease but a group of symptoms and opportunistic infections resulting from the destruction of helper T cells.

steps.title: Solved: why does HIV need reverse transcriptase?
steps.body:
Step 1: HIV's genome is RNA.
Step 2: to integrate into host DNA it must first become DNA.
Step 3: reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the RNA template.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying HIV spreads through hugging, sharing food or mosquito bites.
- Calling HIV a DNA virus.
- Thinking antiretroviral drugs cure AIDS.

This is general education, not medical advice. Free, confidential testing is available at government health centres.

statements.s: HIV is a retrovirus.
HIV can spread by shaking hands.
ELISA is used to diagnose HIV infection.
Antiretroviral drugs completely cure AIDS.
HIV reduces helper T cells.

quiz.why: AIDS was first reported in 1981.
HIV mainly infects and destroys helper T cells (T_H), which weakens the immune system.

quiz.q: Enzyme that copies HIV RNA into DNA
quiz.why: Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA of HIV into DNA, which then integrates into the host genome.
Macrophages can make new virus particles without being destroyed quickly, so they act as an 'HIV factory'.
ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) is the standard test to detect HIV infection (antibodies).

quiz.q: Time-lag between infection and symptoms is usually
quiz.why: The period between HIV infection and the appearance of AIDS symptoms is usually 5–10 years, and can vary.

scenes.text: A doctor explains a biopsy: under the microscope, a lump's cells are growing without control and invading nearby tissue.
Understanding what cancer is — and isn't — helps families make calm, informed decisions.

steps.title: What goes wrong
steps.body:
Normal cells show **contact inhibition**: contact with other cells stops their division. Cancer cells lose it, divide uncontrollably and form masses called **tumours**.

- **Benign** tumours stay confined, cause little damage.
- **Malignant** tumours proliferate, invade surrounding tissue and spread via blood to distant sites — **metastasis** — the most feared property.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body:
Transformation of normal cells into neoplastic cells is induced by physical, chemical or biological agents — **carcinogens**.

- Physical: ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays) and non-ionising (UV) radiation damage DNA
- Chemical: e.g. those in **tobacco smoke** (major cause of lung cancer)
- Biological: **oncogenic viruses** carrying viral oncogenes; cellular **proto-oncogenes (c-onc)** in normal cells, when activated under certain conditions, can cause transformation

steps.title: Detection and treatment
steps.body:
- **Detection**: **biopsy** and **histopathological** studies; blood and bone-marrow tests (increased cell counts in leukaemias); radiography (X-rays), **CT** (computed tomography, 3-D image), **MRI** (strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation); antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular techniques to detect cancer-related genes in individuals with inherited susceptibility.
- **Treatment**: surgery, **radiation therapy**, **chemotherapy** (many drugs have side-effects such as hair loss and anaemia), and **immunotherapy** — patients may be given **biological response modifiers such as α-interferon**, which activate the immune system to destroy the tumour. Most treatments combine methods.

steps.title: Solved: benign vs malignant
steps.body:
Q: A tumour stays in a capsule and doesn't invade or spread. Which type?

**Benign**. If it invaded and spread to lymph nodes or distant organs it would be malignant (metastasis).

steps.title: Solved: why are tumour cells hard for the immune system to fight?
steps.body: Tumour cells can avoid detection and destruction by the immune system; immunotherapy with α-interferon helps activate immune responses against them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all tumours are cancerous — benign tumours are not malignant.
- Calling MRI an X-ray technique — it uses magnetic fields.
- Thinking cancer is contagious between people — it is not (though some viruses that raise risk can spread).

This is general education, not medical advice — any unexplained lump, bleeding or persistent symptom should be checked by a doctor.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Normal cells stop dividing on contact
Spread of cancer cells to distant sites
Normal cellular gene that can become cancer-causing

quiz.why: Normal cells stop dividing on touching neighbours (contact inhibition). Cancer cells lose this property, which leads to uncontrolled growth.

quiz.q: Spread of cancer to distant sites
quiz.why: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the original site to other parts of the body, a feature of malignant tumours.

quiz.q: Which is a non-ionising radiation carcinogen?
quiz.why: Of the choices, UV rays are non-ionising radiation. Gamma rays, X-rays and alpha particles are ionising.
α-Interferon is a biological response modifier that boosts the immune system and is used in cancer immunotherapy.

quiz.q: Leukaemia is detected by increased cell counts in
quiz.why: Leukaemia, cancer of the blood-forming tissue, is detected by raised white cell counts in blood and bone marrow.
Oncogenic viruses carry viral oncogenes, which can transform normal cells into cancerous cells.

lessons.title: Drugs, alcohol and tobacco: effects and help

scenes.text: At a party, someone offers 16-year-old Arjun a 'harmless' pill. His friends watch to see what he'll do.
Knowing exactly what drugs do to the body — and having a ready reply — makes it easier to say no and to help friends who are struggling.

steps.title: Commonly abused drugs (what they are, what they do)
steps.body:
- **Opioids**: bind specific opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gut. **Heroin** ('smack', diacetylmorphine) is obtained by acetylation of **morphine**, extracted from the latex of poppy (*Papaver somniferum*). It is a **depressant** and slows body functions.
- **Cannabinoids**: interact with cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain. From the inflorescences of *Cannabis sativa* — marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja. Affect the cardiovascular system.
- **Coca alkaloid (cocaine)**: from *Erythroxylum coca* (native to South America); interferes with transport of the neurotransmitter **dopamine**; stimulates the CNS, causing euphoria and increased energy; excessive doses cause hallucinations. Other plants with hallucinogenic properties: *Atropa belladonna* and *Datura*.
- Medicines like **barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines** and others are used to treat mental illnesses like depression and insomnia, but are often abused. Morphine is a very effective sedative and painkiller used medically.
- **Tobacco**: contains **nicotine**, an alkaloid that stimulates the adrenal gland to release **adrenaline and noradrenaline**, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking is associated with cancers of lung, urinary bladder and throat, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease and gastric ulcer. Chewing tobacco is associated with oral cancer. Smoking raises **carbon monoxide** in blood and reduces haem-bound oxygen.

steps.title: Why young people start and the warning signs
steps.body:
Adolescence (about 12–18 years) is a period of change and vulnerability. Reasons people start: curiosity, need for adventure and excitement, experimentation, peer pressure, stress (e.g. academic pressure), and the perception that drugs/alcohol are 'cool'.

**Danger signs** of misuse: drop in academic performance, unexplained absence from school, lack of interest in personal hygiene, withdrawal, isolation, depression, fatigue, aggressive and rebellious behaviour, deteriorating relationships, loss of interest in hobbies, changes in sleeping and eating habits, fluctuating weight and appetite.

steps.title: Effects of abuse
steps.body: Repeated use leads to **dependence** — the body's tendency to manifest a characteristic, unpleasant **withdrawal syndrome** if use is abruptly stopped (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating), sometimes severe and life-threatening, needing medical supervision. Other effects: reckless behaviour, vandalism and violence; coma and death from overdose; **HIV and hepatitis B** from shared needles; liver damage (**cirrhosis**) from chronic alcohol use; alcohol or drugs during pregnancy can harm the foetus. Misuse of **anabolic steroids** in sports causes serious side-effects (in females: masculinisation, mood swings, abnormal menstrual cycles, excessive hair growth; in males: acne, aggressiveness, reduced testicle size and sperm production, breast enlargement, kidney and liver dysfunction, premature closure of growth centres of long bones in adolescents).

steps.title: Prevention and getting help
steps.body:
- **Avoid undue peer pressure**; every child has a right to their own choices and pace
- **Education and counselling** to handle problems, stress and disappointment
- **Seek help from parents and peers**; trusted adults can guide and support
- **Look for danger signs** in friends and tell an adult who can help
- **Seek professional and medical help**: qualified psychologists, psychiatrists, and de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes. Recovery is possible.

Help in India: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (mental health support), **1098** Childline (under 18), **112** for emergencies. This is general education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Solved: classify the effect
steps.body:
Q: A drug blocks dopamine transport and makes a person feel energetic and euphoric. Which drug class?

Step 1: dopamine transport interference + stimulation → **cocaine** (coca alkaloid).
Step 2: contrast: heroin is a depressant; cannabinoids act on cannabinoid receptors.

steps.title: Solved: why smoking reduces oxygen supply
steps.body:
Step 1: smoke contains carbon monoxide (CO).
Step 2: CO binds haemoglobin more strongly than O₂.
Step 3: less haem-bound oxygen reaches tissues — breathlessness and heart strain follow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling heroin a stimulant — it is a **depressant**.
- Saying nicotine lowers blood pressure — it **raises** BP and heart rate via adrenaline/noradrenaline.
- Believing 'just once' is risk-free — dependence and overdose can follow quickly with some drugs.

a.text: At a party, an older student offers you a pill and says, 'Everyone's trying it — don't be boring.' What do you do?

choices.label: Say 'No thanks, I'm good' and move to your friends
choices.feedback: A short, confident refusal works. You don't owe an explanation.

choices.label: Take it so you don't look boring
choices.feedback: Peer pressure is real, but unknown pills can cause overdose or dependence.

b.text: Later you see a friend looking very drowsy and confused after taking something. What now?

choices.label: Stay with them, tell a trusted adult and call 112 if they are hard to wake or breathing oddly
choices.feedback: Correct — getting help fast can save a life.

choices.label: Leave them to sleep it off alone
choices.feedback: Never leave someone alone in that state; overdose can be fatal.

c.text: You start to feel unwell and dizzy.

choices.label: Tell a friend and a trusted adult immediately; call 112 if symptoms are serious
choices.feedback: Asking for help is the right move — you won't be judged for staying safe.

end1.text: You chose safety and got help. Talking to a counsellor or calling Tele-MANAS (14416) can help with pressure or worries.

end2.text: This could have ended badly. If someone may have overdosed, stay with them and call 112.

quiz.why: Heroin (smack) is made by acetylating morphine, which is obtained from the latex of the poppy plant.
Cocaine blocks the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine, causing a stimulant effect.
Nicotine stimulates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and noradrenaline, which raise blood pressure and heart rate.

quiz.q: Chronic alcohol use damages the liver causing
quiz.why: Chronic heavy alcohol use damages the liver, and can cause cirrhosis (scarring) of the liver.

quiz.q: A danger sign of drug misuse
quiz.why: Withdrawal and isolation are warning signs of drug misuse. Anyone who notices this should offer support and encourage seeking help from a trusted adult or a doctor.
The Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline in India is 14416. It gives free, confidential support and anyone who is struggling should feel free to call.

questions.why: Acne, aggression and reduced sperm count are known side effects of misusing anabolic steroids to improve performance. Anyone worried about this should talk to a doctor.

questions.why: Proto-oncogenes are normal cellular genes (c-onc) which can turn into oncogenes when activated, and can lead to cancer.

questions.why: In malaria, the gametocytes taken up by the female Anopheles fuse in the mosquito's gut, where sexual reproduction occurs. The mosquito is the definitive host.

questions.why: Cannabinoids (from Cannabis) mainly affect the cardiovascular system, as per the syllabus.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Microbes in Human Welfare
courses.summary: Microbes in household foods and industrial products (beverages, antibiotics, enzymes, bioactive molecules), sewage treatment, biogas, biocontrol and biofertilisers.
outcomes: Learners can link microbes to household and industrial products
Learners can explain primary and secondary sewage treatment and BOD
Learners can describe biogas production and biocontrol agents
Learners can describe types of biofertilisers

lessons.title: Microbes in household and industrial products

scenes.text: Priya's breakfast: idli, curd and bread. Her biology teacher says, 'Tiny cooks made all of that!'
From curd to antibiotics and cholesterol-lowering drugs, microbes are workers in kitchens and factories.

steps.title: Household products
steps.body:
- **Curd**: *Lactobacillus* and other **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)** produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins; LAB also increase **vitamin B₁₂** and check disease-causing microbes in the stomach.
- **Dosa/idli dough** is fermented by bacteria; puffing is due to CO₂.
- **Bread** dough is fermented by baker's yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*.
- **Toddy**, a traditional drink of parts of southern India, is made by fermenting palm sap.
- **Cheese**: large holes in Swiss cheese come from CO₂ produced by *Propionibacterium sharmanii*; Roquefort cheese is ripened by specific fungi.

steps.title: Industrial products
steps.body:
Microbes are grown in very large **fermentors**.

- **Beverages**: *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (brewer's yeast) ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to make ethanol. Wine and beer are made without distillation; whisky, brandy and rum by distillation of fermented broth.
- **Antibiotics**: **penicillin** was the first discovered — **Alexander Fleming** noticed a mould (*Penicillium notatum*) stopping *Staphylococci* growth; its full potential was established by **Ernest Chain and Howard Florey**. The three shared the Nobel Prize in 1945. Antibiotics greatly reduced deaths from plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.
- **Chemicals/enzymes**: *Aspergillus niger* (fungus) → citric acid; *Acetobacter aceti* (bacterium) → acetic acid; *Clostridium butylicum* → butyric acid; *Lactobacillus* → lactic acid; yeast → ethanol. **Lipases** in detergents remove oily stains; **pectinases and proteases** clarify bottled juices.
- **Bioactive molecules**: **streptokinase** from *Streptococcus* (modified by genetic engineering) acts as a 'clot buster' for heart-attack patients; **cyclosporin A** from the fungus *Trichoderma polysporum* is an immunosuppressant for organ transplants; **statins** from the yeast *Monascus purpureus* lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis.

steps.title: Solved: why does idli batter rise?
steps.body:
Step 1: bacteria ferment the batter overnight.
Step 2: fermentation releases CO₂.
Step 3: trapped CO₂ makes the batter puff up (and gives a slightly sour taste).

steps.title: Solved: match drug to source
steps.body:
Q: A transplant patient takes a fungal product to prevent rejection. Which?

**Cyclosporin A** from *Trichoderma polysporum*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing *Aspergillus niger* for acetic acid — it gives **citric** acid.
- Saying statins come from bacteria — from the yeast *Monascus purpureus*.
- Thinking all alcoholic drinks are distilled.

activity.prompt: Match the microbe to the product

quiz.why: Lactic acid bacteria in curd increase its nutritional quality, particularly vitamin B₁₂.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin after noticing that a mould (Penicillium) killed Staphylococci on his culture plate.
Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus, dissolves blood clots, so it is called a clot buster.

quiz.q: Which drink is made by distillation?
quiz.why: Whisky is made by distilling fermented juice. Wine, beer and toddy are fermented drinks that are not distilled.

options: competitive inhibition of cholesterol synthesis enzyme
quiz.why: Statins, from Monascus yeast, competitively inhibit the enzyme that makes cholesterol, so they lower blood cholesterol.
Pectinases and proteases are used to clarify bottled juices by breaking down pectin and proteins that cloud them.

story.title: Where does the drain water go?

scenes.text: A city produces huge amounts of wastewater every day. Releasing it untreated into rivers would spread disease and kill aquatic life.
In a sewage treatment plant (STP), microbes do the heavy lifting of cleaning it.

steps.title: Primary treatment (physical)
steps.body: Physical removal of particles: sequential **filtration** removes floating debris; **sedimentation** removes grit (soil, small pebbles). Settled solids form **primary sludge**; the supernatant is the **effluent**, which goes to secondary treatment.

steps.title: Secondary (biological) treatment
steps.body:
Effluent passes into large **aeration tanks**, constantly agitated mechanically with air pumped in. Useful aerobic microbes grow into **flocs** (masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments in mesh-like structures). They consume the major part of the organic matter, reducing the **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand — the amount of oxygen consumed if all organic matter in 1 litre of water were oxidised by bacteria). BOD is a measure of organic matter: **the greater the BOD, the more polluting** the water.

When BOD is reduced sufficiently, effluent goes to a **settling tank**, where flocs sediment as **activated sludge**. A small part is pumped back into the aeration tank as **inoculum**; most goes to large **anaerobic sludge digesters**, where anaerobic bacteria digest bacteria and fungi in the sludge, producing **biogas** (methane, hydrogen sulphide, CO₂). The treated effluent is released into natural water bodies.

steps.title: Rivers in India
steps.body: The Ministry of Environment and Forests initiated the **Ganga Action Plan** and **Yamuna Action Plan** to save these major rivers from pollution, planning to build many sewage treatment plants so that only treated sewage reaches rivers.

steps.title: Solved: compare two samples
steps.body:
Q: Sample A has BOD 300 mg/L; sample B 20 mg/L. Which is more polluted?

Higher BOD = more organic matter ⇒ **sample A**.

steps.title: Solved: why pump back some activated sludge?
steps.body:
Step 1: activated sludge is rich in active flocs.
Step 2: returning it seeds the aeration tank with microbes.
Step 3: treatment starts faster and stays efficient.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying primary treatment is biological — it is **physical**.
- Thinking higher BOD means cleaner water — it's the opposite.
- Saying sludge digesters are aerobic — they are **anaerobic**.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of sewage treatment
items: Effluent aerated; microbes form flocs and reduce BOD
Part of sludge returned as inoculum
Rest digested anaerobically to give biogas

quiz.why: Primary treatment of sewage is physical: filtration and sedimentation remove floating and settling solids.

options: masses of bacteria with fungal filaments
quiz.why: Flocs are masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments that grow in aeration tanks and digest organic matter.
High BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) means a lot of biodegradable organic matter, and so more polluted water.

quiz.q: Biogas from sludge digesters contains mainly
quiz.why: Anaerobic digestion of sludge gives biogas, mainly methane, with H₂S and CO₂.

quiz.q: Ganga Action Plan was started by the Ministry of
quiz.why: The Ganga Action Plan was started by the Ministry of Environment and Forests to clean the river.
After aeration, the effluent goes to a settling tank, where the flocs settle as activated sludge.

scenes.text: In a village, cow dung fills a covered pit; a pipe carries gas to the kitchen stove.
In the field nearby, ladybird beetles quietly eat aphids — no chemical spray needed.

steps.title: Biogas
steps.body:
Biogas is a mixture of gases, predominantly **methane**, produced by microbial activity; it is inflammable and used as fuel. **Methanogens** (e.g. *Methanobacterium*) grow anaerobically on cellulosic material. They are found in anaerobic sludge and in the **rumen of cattle**, where they help break down cellulose; cattle dung (gobar) is rich in them.

A biogas plant: a concrete tank (10–15 feet deep) receiving bio-wastes and slurry of dung, a floating cover that rises as gas forms, an outlet pipe for gas, and another outlet for spent slurry (used as fertiliser). Biogas technology in India was developed mainly through the efforts of **IARI** (Indian Agricultural Research Institute) and **KVIC** (Khadi and Village Industries Commission).

steps.title: Biocontrol
steps.body:
**Biocontrol** = using biological methods to control plant diseases and pests, reducing dependence on toxic chemicals that harm humans, animals and the environment. Organic farmers aim for a balanced system where pests are kept at manageable levels by natural predators rather than eliminated.

- **Ladybird beetle** (red-and-black) → aphids; **dragonflies** → mosquitoes
- *Bacillus thuringiensis* (**Bt**): dried spores sprayed on plants (e.g. cabbage); caterpillars eat them and the toxin kills them in the gut, without harming other insects
- *Trichoderma* fungi: free-living in root ecosystems; control several plant pathogens
- **Baculoviruses** (genus *Nucleopolyhedrovirus*): attack insects and arthropods; species-specific, narrow-spectrum, no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects — useful in **integrated pest management (IPM)** and ecologically sensitive areas

steps.title: Solved: why is methane produced in cattle?
steps.body:
Step 1: the rumen is anaerobic and full of cellulose.
Step 2: methanogens digest cellulose anaerobically.
Step 3: methane is a by-product, released as gas and present in dung.

steps.title: Solved: why prefer baculoviruses to broad insecticides?
steps.body:
Step 1: chemical insecticides kill useful insects too.
Step 2: baculoviruses are species-specific.
Step 3: they control the pest while conserving beneficial insects — ideal for IPM.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling methanogens aerobic — they are **anaerobic**.
- Saying organic farmers try to eradicate all insects.
- Thinking Bt toxin harms all insects equally.

activity.prompt: Biogas or biocontrol?

quiz.why: Methane is the main gas in biogas. It burns easily and is used as fuel.
Methanogens are anaerobic bacteria found in the rumen of cattle, where they also help break down cellulose.

quiz.q: Biogas technology in India was developed by
quiz.why: Biogas technology in India was developed mainly by IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute) and KVIC (Khadi and Village Industries Commission).
Ladybird beetles are predators of aphids, so they are used for biological pest control.
Baculoviruses attack only specific insects and arthropods, so they are species-specific and safe for non-target organisms.
The fungus Trichoderma is a biocontrol agent against plant pathogens.

story.title: Healthy soil without bags of urea

scenes.text: A farmer grows pulses one season and paddy the next, adding blue-green algae to his paddy fields.
His soil stays fertile with less chemical fertiliser, thanks to nitrogen-fixing microbes.

steps.title: What biofertilisers are
steps.body: **Biofertilisers** are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil — mainly bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria. They reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers, which pollute.

steps.title: Main groups
steps.body:
- **Symbiotic bacteria**: *Rhizobium* in root nodules of leguminous plants fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms usable by plants.
- **Free-living bacteria** in soil: *Azospirillum* and *Azotobacter* fix nitrogen.
- **Fungi (mycorrhiza)**: symbiosis of fungi (many of the genus *Glomus*) with plant roots; the fungus absorbs **phosphorus** from soil and passes it to the plant; plants also gain resistance to root-borne pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought, and overall growth improves.
- **Cyanobacteria**: autotrophic microbes in aquatic and terrestrial environments; many fix atmospheric nitrogen, e.g. *Anabaena*, *Nostoc*, *Oscillatoria*. In **paddy fields** they are important biofertilisers; blue-green algae also add organic matter to soil.

In India many commercial biofertilisers are available, and farmers use them regularly to replenish soil nutrients.

steps.title: Solved: crop rotation with legumes
steps.body:
Step 1: legume roots carry *Rhizobium* nodules.
Step 2: nitrogen fixed in nodules enriches the soil when residues decompose.
Step 3: the following cereal crop needs less nitrogen fertiliser.

steps.title: Solved: which biofertiliser for a phosphorus-poor soil?
steps.body: **Mycorrhizal fungi (e.g. Glomus)** — they absorb phosphorus for the plant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling *Azotobacter* symbiotic — it is **free-living**.
- Saying mycorrhiza fixes nitrogen — its main role is **phosphorus** uptake.
- Forgetting cyanobacteria's importance in **paddy** fields.

activity.prompt: Match the biofertiliser to its feature
pairs: Symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume nodules
Cyanobacterium fixing N₂ in paddy fields

quiz.why: Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes (like pea and beans) and fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
Mycorrhizal fungi help plants absorb phosphorus from soil.
Nostoc is a cyanobacterium (blue-green alga) that fixes nitrogen, so it is used as a biofertiliser.
Azotobacter is a free-living nitrogen-fixing soil bacterium. Rhizobium is symbiotic.
Biofertilisers supply nutrients naturally, so they reduce the need for chemical fertilisers.

questions.why: The main gas in biogas is methane, which is used as fuel.

questions.q: Citric acid is produced by
questions.why: Citric acid is produced industrially by the fungus Aspergillus niger.

questions.q: Free-living N₂-fixing bacterium

questions.why: Cyclosporin A, from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, is an immunosuppressant used in organ transplants.

questions.q: Assertion: A high BOD indicates heavily polluted water. Reason: BOD measures the oxygen needed by microbes to oxidise organic matter.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. BOD measures the oxygen microbes need to oxidise organic matter, and more organic pollution gives a higher BOD, so R explains A.

questions.q: Large holes in Swiss cheese are due to
questions.why: The large holes in Swiss cheese are made by CO₂ released by Propionibacterium sharmanii.

questions.q: Case: A farmer wants to control cabbage caterpillars without harming bees. Best choice
questions.why: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spores make a toxin that kills specific caterpillars and does not harm bees, unlike broad insecticides.

questions.q: Flocs are formed in
questions.why: Flocs form in the aeration tanks during secondary (biological) sewage treatment, where aerobic microbes grow.

questions.q: Statins come from
questions.why: Statins, which lower blood cholesterol, are produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus.

questions.q: Mycorrhizal plants show
options: phosphorus uptake, drought and salinity tolerance
questions.why: Mycorrhizal association helps plants take up phosphorus and gives resistance to drought, salinity and root pathogens.

questions.q: Penicillin's potential as an antibiotic was established by
questions.why: Ernst Chain and Howard Florey established the effectiveness of penicillin as an antibiotic, and shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming.

questions.q: Case: An STP's anaerobic digester produces gas that is piped for cooking. Which microbes are responsible?
questions.why: Methanogens are anaerobic archaea that produce methane in the digester, which can be used as fuel gas.

questions.q: Baculoviruses are useful in IPM because they
options: are species-specific with no effect on non-targets
questions.why: Baculoviruses are species-specific and narrow-spectrum, so they affect only the target insect and not other organisms, which suits integrated pest management.

questions.q: Which pair is mismatched?
questions.why: Aspergillus niger produces citric acid, not lactic acid, so that pair is wrong. Lactic acid comes from Lactobacillus.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Biotechnology: Principles and Processes
courses.summary: Principles of genetic engineering, restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis, cloning vectors and selection, competent hosts, DNA isolation, PCR, bioreactors and downstream processing.
outcomes: Learners can explain the principles and steps of recombinant DNA technology
Learners can explain how restriction enzymes and gel electrophoresis work
Learners can describe vector features and selection of recombinants
Learners can explain PCR and large-scale production

scenes.text: In 1972 Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer cut a piece of DNA carrying an antibiotic-resistance gene and joined it to a plasmid.
Put into E. coli, it replicated with the bacterium — the first recombinant DNA. Modern biotechnology was born.

steps.title: Definition and two core techniques
steps.body:
**Biotechnology** deals with techniques of using live organisms or their enzymes to produce products and processes useful to humans. The **European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB)** defines it as 'the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services'.

Two core techniques of modern biotechnology:
- **Genetic engineering**: altering the chemistry of genetic material (DNA/RNA), introducing it into host organisms and changing their phenotype
- **Bioprocess engineering**: maintaining sterile (contamination-free) conditions to grow only the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities for manufacturing antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes, etc.

steps.title: Why vectors and an origin of replication
steps.body:
A piece of DNA introduced alone into an organism usually cannot multiply. It must be linked to a sequence called the **origin of replication (ori)**, where replication starts; any DNA linked to it can replicate in the host — this is **cloning** (many identical copies).

Cohen and Boyer linked an antibiotic-resistance gene to a native plasmid of *Salmonella typhimurium*, using restriction enzymes to cut and **DNA ligase** to join, then transferred it into *E. coli*.

Three basic steps of genetically modifying an organism:
1. Identify DNA with desirable genes
2. Introduce the identified DNA into the host
3. Maintain the introduced DNA in the host and transfer it to its progeny

steps.title: Solved: why is genetic engineering better than conventional breeding for a single trait?
steps.body:
Step 1: conventional hybridisation brings in many genes — undesirable ones too.
Step 2: genetic engineering isolates and introduces only the desired gene.
Step 3: so a specific trait can be added without disturbing the rest.

steps.title: Solved: role of ori
steps.body:
Q: A gene is put into a host without an ori. What happens?

It will not be replicated as the cells divide and will be lost — hence it is joined to a vector carrying an ori.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering.
- Saying ligase cuts DNA — it **joins** DNA.
- Forgetting that a gene needs an ori to replicate in a host.

activity.prompt: Arrange the basic steps of genetically modifying an organism
items: Identify DNA with the desirable gene
Join it to a vector with an ori using DNA ligase
Introduce the recombinant DNA into the host
Maintain the DNA and transfer it to progeny

quiz.q: First recombinant DNA was made by
quiz.why: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer made the first recombinant DNA in 1972 by linking an antibiotic-resistance gene to a plasmid.
DNA ligase joins DNA fragments, acting as molecular glue. Restriction enzymes cut DNA.

lessons.title: Tools I: restriction enzymes and gel electrophoresis

story.title: Molecular scissors with a reading habit

scenes.text: EcoRI scans DNA until it finds GAATTC — then it cuts, leaving short single-stranded overhangs.
Fragments are then sorted by size in a gel, glowing orange under UV light.

steps.title: Restriction enzymes
steps.body:
In 1963 two enzymes restricting bacteriophage growth in *E. coli* were isolated — one adds methyl groups to DNA, the other (a **restriction endonuclease**) cuts DNA. The first restriction endonuclease, **Hind II**, always cuts at a specific six-base-pair sequence — its **recognition sequence**. Today more than 900 restriction enzymes are known from over 230 bacterial strains.

Naming, e.g. **EcoRI**: E = genus *Escherichia*, co = species *coli*, R = strain RY13, I = first enzyme isolated from that strain.

- **Exonucleases** remove nucleotides from the ends; **endonucleases** cut at specific positions within DNA.
- Recognition sites are **palindromes** — the sequence reads the same on the two strands when read in the same direction (5′→3′): 5′-GAATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAAG-5′.
- Cutting slightly away from the centre (between the same two bases on opposite strands) leaves single-stranded overhangs — **sticky ends** — which form hydrogen bonds with complementary sticky ends; **DNA ligase** then seals them. Cutting the vector and the source DNA with the **same enzyme** gives matching sticky ends.

steps.title: Gel electrophoresis
steps.body: DNA fragments are negatively charged, so in an electric field they move towards the **anode** through a matrix, most commonly **agarose** (a natural polymer from sea weeds). Smaller fragments move farther (sieving effect). DNA is stained with **ethidium bromide** and seen as bright **orange bands** under UV light. Bands are cut out of the gel and extracted — **elution** — and the purified DNA is used to make recombinant DNA.

steps.title: Solved: is it palindromic?
steps.body: Q: 5′-GGATCC-3′. Complementary strand read 5′→3′: GGATCC. Same ⇒ **palindrome** (it is the BamHI site).

steps.title: Solved: read a gel
steps.body:
Q: Fragments of 500 bp, 2000 bp and 1000 bp are loaded together. Order from the well (top) down?

Largest moves least: **2000 bp (top), 1000 bp, 500 bp (farthest)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DNA moves to the cathode — it moves to the **anode** (positive).
- Writing EcoRI's 'R' as 'restriction' — it stands for the strain RY13.
- Thinking larger fragments travel farther.

activity.prompt: Complete the palindrome.
activity.text: If one strand is 5′-GAATTC-3′, the other strand read 5′→3′ is ___ .

quiz.why: In EcoRI, E stands for the genus Escherichia and 'co' for the species coli, R for the strain RY13, and I for the order of discovery.
Hind II, which always cuts DNA at a specific six-base-pair sequence, was the first restriction endonuclease isolated.

Agarose, the gel matrix used in electrophoresis, is a natural polymer obtained from seaweeds.

quiz.why: Smaller fragments pass through the gel pores more easily, so they move farther in the same time.

lessons.title: Tools II: cloning vectors and competent hosts

scenes.text: A student plates bacteria on a dish with a special chromogenic substrate. Some colonies turn blue, some stay white.
The white ones carry the inserted gene — insertional inactivation made the selection easy.

steps.title: Features of a cloning vector
steps.body:
- **Origin of replication (ori)**: starts replication; also controls **copy number**
- **Selectable marker**: helps identify and eliminate **non-transformants** and selectively permit growth of **transformants** — commonly genes for resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin (normal *E. coli* lack these)
- **Cloning sites**: to link alien DNA, the vector should have very few, preferably **single**, recognition sites for commonly used restriction enzymes
- **Vectors for plants and animals**: *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* (a plant pathogen) delivers a piece of DNA ('T-DNA') via its **Ti plasmid**, transforming plant cells into tumours; it has been modified into a non-pathogenic vector. **Retroviruses** in animals have been disarmed and are used to deliver genes into animal cells.

In plasmid **pBR322**, inserting foreign DNA at the BamHI site of the **tetracycline-resistance gene** inactivates it: recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline.

steps.title: Insertional inactivation (blue–white screening)
steps.body: Because replica plating on two antibiotics is cumbersome, alternative markers distinguish recombinants by colour. Foreign DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of the enzyme **β-galactosidase**. With a chromogenic substrate, **non-recombinant** colonies (enzyme active) appear **blue**; **recombinant** colonies (enzyme gene inactivated) stay **white**.

steps.title: Making hosts competent
steps.body:
DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass through cell membranes by itself.

- Bacteria are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as **calcium**, then incubated with recombinant DNA on **ice**, given a brief **heat shock at 42 °C**, and returned to ice — the DNA enters.
- **Micro-injection**: DNA injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell
- **Biolistics (gene gun)**: plant cells bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of **gold or tungsten** coated with DNA
- **Disarmed pathogen vectors**: infect the cell and transfer recombinant DNA

steps.title: Solved: pBR322 selection
steps.body:
Foreign DNA inserted at BamHI (within tetᴿ). Transformed cells are plated:

- grow on ampicillin and tetracycline → no insert (non-recombinant)
- grow on ampicillin but **not** tetracycline → **recombinant**
- no growth on ampicillin → not transformed

steps.title: Solved: colour of colonies
steps.body:
Q: After cloning into the lacZ (β-galactosidase) region, which colonies do you pick?

Pick **white** colonies — the insert disrupted β-galactosidase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Picking blue colonies as recombinants.
- Saying selectable markers help make DNA — they help **select** transformants.
- Forgetting the ice–heat-shock–ice sequence.

quiz.why: A gene gun (biolistics) shoots DNA-coated gold or tungsten particles into cells, and is mainly used with plant cells.

quiz.why: The BamHI site in pBR322 lies inside the tetracycline-resistance gene (tetᴿ). Inserting DNA there inactivates it.

lessons.title: Processes: isolation, amplification (PCR), bioreactors and downstream processing

scenes.text: A biotech company wants a human protein in large amounts. First it must isolate and copy the gene, then grow modified cells in giant vessels.
Finally the protein is purified, formulated and tested before it ever reaches a patient.

steps.title: Isolation and cutting
steps.body: Cells are broken open with enzymes — **lysozyme** (bacteria), **cellulase** (plant cells), **chitinase** (fungi). DNA is freed from RNA, proteins, lipids and polysaccharides with **ribonuclease** and **protease**. Purified DNA precipitates as fine threads when chilled **ethanol** is added. It is then cut with restriction enzymes, checked by agarose electrophoresis, and the desired fragment ligated into a vector cut with the same enzyme.

steps.title: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
steps.body:
PCR amplifies a gene of interest *in vitro* using two sets of **primers** (small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA) and a DNA polymerase. Each cycle:

1. **Denaturation** at high temperature — strands separate
2. **Annealing** — primers bind
3. **Extension** — **Taq polymerase** (from the thermophilic bacterium *Thermus aquaticus*, stays active at high temperatures) extends primers

Repeated many times, the DNA doubles each cycle: about a billion copies after ~30 cycles (2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹).

steps.title: Obtaining the product
steps.body:
Cells with the recombinant gene are grown in culture; for large-scale production **bioreactors** (100–1000 litres) are used. A **stirred-tank** bioreactor is usually cylindrical with a curved base to help mixing; it has an agitator, oxygen delivery (sparging) system, and systems to control temperature, pH, foam, and a sampling port. A **continuous culture** removes used medium and adds fresh medium to keep cells in their physiologically most active log phase, giving more biomass and product.

**Downstream processing**: separation and purification of the product, then **formulation** with suitable preservatives and strict **quality control** testing (clinical trials for drugs) before marketing.

steps.title: Solved: PCR copy number
steps.body:
Q: Starting with 1 DNA molecule, how many copies after 10 cycles?

2¹⁰ = **1024** copies (assuming perfect doubling).

steps.title: Solved: why Taq polymerase?
steps.body:
Step 1: denaturation needs about 94 °C every cycle.
Step 2: most enzymes are destroyed at that temperature.
Step 3: Taq, from a hot-spring bacterium, is **thermostable**, so it survives repeated cycles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the PCR order as annealing → denaturation → extension.
- Saying lysozyme breaks plant cell walls (that's cellulase).
- Forgetting downstream processing and quality control.

items: Add primers, nucleotides and Taq polymerase

quiz.why: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, so chitinase is used to break them open.
Chilled ethanol makes DNA precipitate out as fine threads that can be spooled out.

quiz.why: PCR doubles DNA each cycle, so after 5 cycles there are 2⁵ = 32 copies from one molecule.
Continuous culture keeps the cells in the log (exponential) phase by adding fresh medium and removing used medium.
Downstream processing includes separation, purification and formulation of the product after fermentation, together with quality control.

questions.why: Treating E. coli with Ca²⁺ and then a brief heat shock makes the cell wall more permeable, so the cells become competent and take up DNA.

questions.why: Elution is the step of cutting out the DNA bands from the agarose gel and extracting the fragments.

questions.q: Two enzymes isolated in 1963 in E. coli were responsible for
questions.why: Two enzymes isolated in E. coli in 1963, a methylase and a restriction endonuclease, restricted the growth of bacteriophages.

questions.why: A gene gun (biolistics) shoots DNA-coated gold or tungsten particles into plant cells and needs no vector.

questions.why: The same restriction enzyme leaves the same complementary sticky ends on the source DNA and the vector, so they can base-pair and be joined by ligase.

questions.why: The origin of replication (ori) determines how many copies of the plasmid are present in a cell.

questions.why: PCR amplification of the gene is done before and during cloning, not as part of the downstream processing. Downstream processing is for purifying the product.

lessons.title: Biotechnology in agriculture: Bt crops and RNAi

scenes.text: Cotton farmers lose crops to bollworms. A gene from a soil bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis, gives cotton plants their own insecticidal protein.
In tobacco, scientists silenced a nematode's gene using RNA interference — the worm couldn't survive on the roots.

steps.title: Genetically modified (GM) plants
steps.body: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are **genetically modified organisms (GMOs)**. GM plants have been useful in: making crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat); reducing reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops); reducing post-harvest losses; increasing efficiency of mineral usage; enhancing nutritional value (e.g. vitamin-A-enriched rice); and creating tailor-made plants for alternative resources like starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.

steps.title: Bt toxin — how it kills pests
steps.body:
*Bacillus thuringiensis* makes proteins that kill certain insects — lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes). The protein exists as an **inactive protoxin** in crystals inside the bacterium, so it doesn't harm the bacterium.

When an insect eats it, the **alkaline pH of the gut** solubilises the crystals and the protoxin becomes **active toxin**. It binds to the surface of **midgut epithelial cells** and creates **pores**, causing cell swelling, lysis and the insect's death.

The toxin is coded by **cry** genes. Proteins encoded by **cryIAc and cryIIAb** control **cotton bollworms**; **cryIAb** controls the **corn borer**.

steps.title: Pest-resistant plants by RNA interference
steps.body: The nematode *Meloidogyne incognita* infects tobacco roots, reducing yield. **RNA interference (RNAi)** — a cellular defence in all eukaryotes — silences a specific mRNA when a complementary **dsRNA** binds and prevents its translation. Using *Agrobacterium* vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into tobacco so that both sense and anti-sense RNA formed; these made dsRNA, which silenced the parasite's mRNA. The parasite could not survive in the transgenic host — the plant was protected.

steps.title: Solved: why doesn't Bt toxin kill the bacterium or humans?
steps.body:
Step 1: it is stored as an inactive protoxin.
Step 2: activation needs the alkaline gut pH of specific insects and binding to their gut receptors.
Step 3: the bacterium isn't affected and the toxin is specific to target insect groups.

steps.title: Solved: choose the gene
steps.body:
Q: Which cry genes would you introduce to protect cotton from bollworms?

**cryIAc and cryIIAb**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Bt toxin acts in an acidic gut — it is **alkaline**.
- Calling 'cry' genes 'crystal-forming enzymes' — they code the toxin proteins (cry = crystal protein).
- Saying RNAi adds a toxic protein — it **silences** an mRNA.

activity.prompt: Order the steps by which Bt toxin kills an insect
items: Insect eats plant tissue containing protoxin
Alkaline gut pH solubilises the crystals
Protoxin is converted to active toxin
Toxin binds to midgut epithelial cells
Pores form; cells swell and lyse

quiz.why: cryIAb controls the corn borer (a maize pest). cryIAc and cryIIAb act on cotton bollworms.
The Bt protoxin is inactive until it reaches the alkaline gut of the insect, where it is activated.
RNA interference (RNAi) silences a gene by using complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) that blocks the mRNA.
The nematode Meloidogyne incognita infects the roots of tobacco plants and reduces yield.

quiz.why: Agrobacterium vectors were used to introduce nematode-specific genes into tobacco cells.

lessons.title: Biotechnology in medicine: insulin, gene therapy and diagnosis

scenes.text: Insulin for diabetes once came from pancreases of slaughtered cattle and pigs, and some patients reacted to it.
In 1983 Eli Lilly made human insulin chains in E. coli — the first of many safe, recombinant medicines.

steps.title: Genetically engineered insulin
steps.body:
Human insulin has two short polypeptide chains, **A and B**, linked by **disulphide bridges**. In mammals it is made as a **pro-hormone (pro-insulin)** containing an extra stretch, the **C peptide**, which is removed during maturation.

In 1983 the American company **Eli Lilly** prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B, introduced them into **plasmids of *E. coli***, produced the chains separately, extracted them and combined them by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin. Recombinant therapeutics are safer and more effective — they don't induce unwanted immune responses as products from non-human sources can.

steps.title: Gene therapy
steps.body:
**Gene therapy** corrects a gene defect diagnosed in a child/embryo by inserting a normal gene into the person's cells or tissues to compensate for the non-functional gene.

The first clinical gene therapy was given in **1990** to a 4-year-old girl with **adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency** (ADA is crucial for the immune system). Lymphocytes from the patient's blood were grown in culture; a functional ADA cDNA was introduced using a **retroviral vector**; the cells were returned to the patient. Because these cells are not immortal, the patient needs periodic infusions. Treatment options also include bone-marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy. A permanent cure may be possible if the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at **early embryonic stages**.

steps.title: Molecular diagnosis
steps.body:
Conventional methods (serum and urine analysis) can't detect infections early, when pathogen numbers are very low.

- **Recombinant DNA technology, PCR and ELISA** allow early diagnosis.
- **PCR** detects very low amounts of a pathogen's DNA/RNA by amplification — used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and mutations in genes of suspected cancer patients.
- A single-stranded DNA/RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule (**probe**) hybridises to its complement in a clone; detected by **autoradiography** — a clone with a mutated gene won't appear on the film.
- **ELISA** is based on antigen–antibody interaction; infection can be detected by the presence of antigens or of antibodies made against the pathogen.

steps.title: Solved: why remove the C peptide?
steps.body:
Step 1: pro-insulin contains A, B and C chains.
Step 2: mature insulin has only A and B, joined by disulphide bridges.
Step 3: making A and B separately and joining them avoids having to remove C peptide.

steps.title: Solved: why periodic infusions in ADA gene therapy?
steps.body:
Step 1: genetically engineered lymphocytes are returned to the patient.
Step 2: lymphocytes are not immortal and die over time.
Step 3: so the patient needs repeated infusions — unlike an embryonic-stage correction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the 1990 gene therapy used an adenovirus — it used a **retroviral** vector.
- Saying insulin's chains are joined by peptide bonds — by **disulphide** bridges.
- Thinking ELISA detects only DNA — it uses antigens/antibodies.

scenes.text: In 1997, a transgenic cow named Rosie produced milk enriched with a human protein.
Most transgenic animals, though, are mice — models that help us understand diseases and test medicines safely.

steps.title: What and why
steps.body:
Animals whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are **transgenic animals**. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, though **over 95% of all existing transgenic animals are mice**.

Uses:
- **Normal physiology and development**: studying how genes are regulated and affect body functions (e.g. insulin-like growth factor)
- **Study of disease**: models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's disease
- **Biological products**: e.g. human protein **α-1-antitrypsin** used to treat **emphysema**; attempts for phenylketonuria and cystic fibrosis treatments. In **1997**, the first transgenic cow, **Rosie**, produced human-protein-enriched milk (**2.4 g per litre**) containing **human alpha-lactalbumin**, nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk
- **Vaccine safety**: transgenic mice are being developed to test vaccine safety before human use (e.g. polio vaccine)
- **Chemical safety testing (toxicity testing)**: animals made more sensitive to toxic substances give results faster

steps.title: Solved: why use transgenic mice for vaccine testing?
steps.body:
Step 1: some vaccines (e.g. polio) need testing for safety before use in humans.
Step 2: transgenic mice carrying human-like susceptibility give relevant results.
Step 3: this could replace the use of monkeys for some tests.

steps.title: Solved: why was Rosie's milk special?
steps.body: It contained **human alpha-lactalbumin** (2.4 g/L), making it nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying most transgenic animals are cows — over 95% are **mice**.
- Attributing α-1-antitrypsin to diabetes treatment — it is used for **emphysema**.
- Confusing transgenic (foreign gene) with cloned (identical copy) animals.

Transgenic cow: milk with human alpha-lactalbumin, 2.4 g/L
Human protein used to treat emphysema

quiz.why: Transgenic mice are used to test the safety of vaccines, such as the polio vaccine, before use in humans.
