lessons.title: Ethical issues: GEAC, patents and biopiracy

scenes.text: Farmers in India and Pakistan have grown basmati rice for centuries. In 1997, a foreign company obtained a patent related to basmati-derived rice lines.
The episode raised big questions: who owns traditional knowledge, and how should GM organisms be regulated?

steps.title: Regulation in India
steps.body: Manipulating living organisms can have unpredictable effects when GMOs are released into ecosystems. Ethical standards are therefore needed. The Indian Government set up the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)**, which makes decisions about the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services.

steps.title: Patents and biopiracy
steps.body:
Companies have been granted patents on products and technologies that use genetic materials, plants and other biological resources long identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a region or country.

- **Basmati rice**: India has a huge diversity of rice varieties, including many documented basmati varieties with a unique aroma and flavour. In 1997 an American company got patent rights (through the US Patent and Trademark Office) relating to new basmati-derived lines, which caused major controversy.
- Attempts have also been made to patent uses of traditional Indian herbal medicines such as **turmeric** and **neem**.

**Biopiracy** = the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment. Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge; developing nations are rich in both. There is growing realisation of injustice and inadequate compensation, so countries are developing laws to prevent unauthorised exploitation. The Indian Parliament has amended the Patents law to address such issues, including emergency provisions and research and development initiatives.

steps.title: Solved: is it biopiracy?
steps.body:
Q: A company collects a medicinal plant used by a tribal community, patents a drug from it and shares no benefit with the community or country.

Step 1: uses bio-resource and traditional knowledge.
Step 2: no authorisation, no benefit sharing.
Step 3: this fits the definition of **biopiracy**.

steps.title: Solved: role of GEAC
steps.body: Before a GM crop is grown commercially in India, GEAC appraises the research data on its safety for humans, animals and the environment and decides on approval.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing GEAC as an international body — it is set up by the **Government of India**.
- Thinking biopiracy refers to illegal copying of software.
- Saying all patents on biological material are biopiracy — biopiracy is use **without authorisation or fair compensation**.

activity.prompt: Common questions on biotech ethics

items.a: Each GM product is assessed case by case for safety; in India GEAC appraises GM organisms before release. Scientific assessments look at toxicity, allergenicity and environmental impact.

items.q: Why does biopiracy matter to India?
items.a: India is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge; without protection, others can profit from them without permission or fair benefit sharing.

items.q: Can a plant variety be patented?
items.a: Patent and plant-variety laws differ between countries; patents are usually granted on new inventions, which is why claims on traditional resources are challenged.
Learn the science, respect communities' knowledge, and support documentation of traditional knowledge so it can be protected.

It binds midgut epithelial cells and makes pores

courses.title: Ch 11 · Organisms and Populations
courses.summary: Population attributes, growth models (exponential and logistic), life history variation, population interactions (mutualism, competition, predation, parasitism, commensalism, amensalism), plus enrichment on responses to abiotic factors and adaptations.
outcomes: Learners can calculate birth/death rates and read age pyramids
Learners can apply exponential and logistic growth equations
Learners can classify population interactions with examples
Learners can describe responses and adaptations to abiotic stress

scenes.text: Forest officials estimate tigers from pugmarks and camera traps — nobody can count every animal directly.
What they track are population attributes: density, birth and death rates, sex ratio and age structure.

steps.title: What a population is
steps.body: A **population** is a group of individuals of the same species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources, and potentially interbreeding. Individuals have births and deaths; populations have **birth rates and death rates** — per capita rates.

steps.title: Key attributes
steps.body:
- **Birth rate (natality)**: number of births per individual per unit time. E.g. if a pond has 20 lotus plants and 8 new ones form in a year, birth rate = 8/20 = **0.4 per lotus per year**.
- **Death rate (mortality)**: e.g. 4 of 40 fruit flies die in a week → 0.1 per fly per week.
- **Sex ratio**: e.g. 60% females, 40% males.
- **Age distribution**: plotting the proportion in pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive groups gives an **age pyramid** — **expanding** (triangular, growing), **stable** (bell-shaped) or **declining** (urn-shaped).
- **Population density (N)**: number per unit area. Sometimes **percent cover** or **biomass** is a better measure (e.g. one huge banyan tree vs 200 carrot grass plants). Indirect estimates are also used — e.g. tiger census based on **pugmarks and faecal pellets**.

steps.title: Solved: birth rate
steps.body:
Q: A pond has 20 frogs; next year there are 28 because of births only. Birth rate?

(28 − 20)/20 = 8/20 = **0.4 per frog per year**.

steps.title: Solved: read the pyramid
steps.body:
Q: A country's age pyramid has a very broad base of children and a narrow top. Trend?

Many pre-reproductive individuals → **expanding (growing) population**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving birth *numbers* when the question asks for *rate* (divide by population).
- Confusing urn-shaped (declining) and bell-shaped (stable) pyramids.
- Assuming population size always means numbers — biomass or cover may be more meaningful.

activity.prompt: In a pond of 50 water lilies, 10 die in a year. What is the death rate per lily per year?

quiz.q: Population density can be measured as
quiz.why: Population density can be expressed as the number of individuals, percent cover or biomass, depending on the organism.
A bell-shaped age pyramid has roughly equal pre-reproductive and reproductive groups, which indicates a stable population.
An urn-shaped pyramid has a narrow base (few young), so the population is declining.
Tiger numbers are estimated by using pugmarks and faecal pellets, as counting every tiger is not practical.
Natality is the birth rate, the number of births per unit population per unit time.

quiz.q: If 4 of 40 flies die in a week, death rate per week
quiz.why: Death rate = number of deaths/population = 4/40 = 0.1 per week.

scenes.text: In a nutrient-rich flask, bacteria double rapidly. Then food runs out and the growth curve levels off.
The first phase is exponential (J-shaped); the full curve is logistic (S-shaped) — limited by carrying capacity.

steps.title: What changes population size
steps.body:
Density changes through **natality (B)**, **immigration (I)** (increase) and **mortality (D)**, **emigration (E)** (decrease):

**Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]**

Usually births and deaths are most important; immigration matters when a new habitat is being colonised.

steps.title: Growth models
steps.body:
- **Exponential growth** (unlimited resources): dN/dt = (b − d)N = **rN**, where r is the **intrinsic rate of natural increase**. Integrated: **Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ**. Gives a **J-shaped** curve. Examples of r: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12; for India's human population in 1981, r was 0.0205.
- **Logistic growth** (limited resources): **dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K]**, where **K** is the **carrying capacity**. Phases: lag, acceleration, deceleration, then an asymptote at K. Gives a **sigmoid (S-shaped)** curve — the **Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth**. It is considered more realistic because resources eventually become limiting.

steps.title: Life history variation
steps.body: Populations evolve to maximise reproductive fitness (Darwinian fitness, high r). Some organisms breed **once** in their lifetime (Pacific salmon, bamboo); others breed **many times** (most birds and mammals). Some produce **many small offspring** (oysters, pelagic fishes); others a **few large offspring** (birds, mammals). Ecologists suggest life-history traits evolve in relation to the constraints of the habitat's abiotic and biotic components.

steps.title: Solved: logistic growth rate
steps.body:
Q: r = 0.1 per day, K = 1000, N = 500. Find dN/dt.

dN/dt = 0.1 × 500 × (1000 − 500)/1000 = 50 × 0.5 = **25 individuals/day**. (Growth is fastest at N = K/2.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the logistic curve J-shaped (it is S-shaped).
- Forgetting immigration and emigration in Nₜ₊₁.
- Saying growth is maximum when N = K — at K growth is zero.

activity.prompt: J-shaped (exponential) or S-shaped (logistic)?

quiz.why: The carrying capacity, the maximum population size that the environment can sustain, is denoted by K.
Exponential growth, with unlimited resources, is given by dN/dt = rN.
The logistic growth curve is S-shaped (sigmoid), levelling off at the carrying capacity K.
The Pacific salmon breeds only once in its lifetime and dies soon after (semelparous).
In the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, at N = K the factor (K − N) is 0, so growth stops.

quiz.q: Intrinsic rate r of India in 1981
quiz.why: The intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) of the human population in India in 1981 was 0.0205.

scenes.text: Each fig species is pollinated by one partner wasp species, which lays eggs inside the fig's fruit. Neither can complete its life cycle alone.
Elsewhere, a cuckoo lays its eggs in a crow's nest — the crow raises the cuckoo's chick. Nature has many kinds of relationships.

steps.title: Kinds of interactions
steps.body:
| Interaction | Species A | Species B |

- **Mutualism**: + / +
- **Competition**: − / −
- **Predation**: + / −
- **Parasitism**: + / −
- **Commensalism**: + / 0
- **Amensalism**: − / 0

Predation, parasitism and commensalism share a feature: the interacting species live closely together.

steps.title: Predation and competition
steps.body:
**Predation** transfers energy to higher trophic levels, keeps prey populations in check and maintains species diversity by reducing competition among prey. When prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s spread uncontrollably, it was brought under control by introducing a **cactus-feeding moth** from its natural habitat. Prey defences: camouflage (frogs, insects), poison — the **monarch butterfly** is distasteful because, as a caterpillar, it feeds on a poisonous weed; plants defend with thorns (*Acacia*, cactus) and chemicals — *Calotropis* produces highly poisonous **cardiac glycosides**; nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium are plant defences against grazers.

**Competition** occurs when closely related (or even unrelated) species compete for the same limiting resources. Examples: in some South American lakes visiting flamingos and resident fishes compete for zooplankton; the **Abingdon tortoise** of the Galapagos became extinct within a decade after **goats** were introduced. **Connell's** experiments on Scotland's rocky coast: the larger barnacle *Balanus* dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller *Chthamalus*. **Gause's competitive exclusion principle**: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the competitively inferior one is eliminated. Species can coexist by **resource partitioning** — MacArthur showed five closely related warbler species coexisting on the same tree by foraging in different parts.

steps.title: Parasitism, commensalism and mutualism
steps.body:
- **Parasitism**: parasites are often host-specific, lose unnecessary organs, have adhesive organs and high reproductive capacity; may need intermediate hosts (the human **liver fluke** needs a snail and a fish). *Cuscuta* is a parasitic plant on hedges. Ectoparasites (lice, ticks), endoparasites (tapeworm). **Brood parasitism**: the cuckoo (koel) lays eggs in the crow's nest; its eggs resemble the host's.
- **Commensalism**: orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch; barnacles on a whale's back; **cattle egret** foraging near grazing cattle (cattle stir up insects); **sea anemone and clown fish** (fish gets protection; anemone not obviously affected).
- **Mutualism**: **lichens** (fungus + photosynthesising alga/cyanobacterium); **mycorrhizae** (fungus + plant roots); plants and pollinators; **fig and wasp**; the Mediterranean orchid *Ophrys* uses **sexual deceit** — one petal resembles a female bee, so male bees 'pseudocopulate' with the flower and carry pollen.

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
Q: A clown fish lives among sea-anemone tentacles; the anemone neither gains nor loses noticeably.

Fish benefits (+), anemone unaffected (0) ⇒ **commensalism**.

steps.title: Solved: interpret Connell
steps.body:
Q: When *Balanus* is removed from rocks, *Chthamalus* spreads into the lower zone. What does this show?

*Chthamalus* was being excluded by competition from *Balanus* — evidence of **interspecific competition**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the cuckoo–crow relation commensalism — it is **brood parasitism**.
- Mixing amensalism (−/0) and commensalism (+/0).
- Saying predators only harm ecosystems — they keep prey populations in check and maintain diversity.

activity.prompt: Match the example to the interaction

quiz.q: Interaction where one benefits and the other is unaffected
quiz.why: In commensalism one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited (+/0).
Gause's principle (competitive exclusion) says that two closely related species competing for the same limited resources cannot coexist indefinitely.
Calotropis produces poisonous cardiac glycosides that make it unpalatable to grazers.
The Ophrys orchid mimics a female bee in colour and scent, so male bees try to mate with it, which is sexual deceit.
The liver fluke needs two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish, to complete its life cycle.

quiz.q: Abingdon tortoise became extinct after introduction of
quiz.why: On the Galápagos Abingdon Island, the Abingdon tortoise went extinct after goats were introduced, because the goats outcompeted it for food.

lessons.title: Responses to abiotic factors and adaptations (enrichment)

scenes.text: On a trip to a high mountain pass, tourists feel nausea, fatigue and heart palpitations. A few days later, they feel better.
Their bodies acclimatised — more red blood cells, faster breathing. Organisms have many ways to cope with harsh conditions.

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Some recent editions of the textbook focus this chapter on populations; this lesson on abiotic factors and adaptations is included as enrichment and for exams (like NEET) that may still test it. Check your syllabus.

steps.title: Responses to abiotic factors
steps.body:
Organisms facing stressful conditions may:

- **Regulate**: maintain homeostasis (e.g. birds and mammals keep body temperature constant by sweating, shivering)
- **Conform**: cannot maintain a constant internal environment (most animals and nearly all plants)
- **Migrate**: move temporarily to a more hospitable area (e.g. Siberian birds to Keoladeo National Park, Bharatpur, in winter)
- **Suspend**: bacteria/fungi form thick-walled spores; seeds go dormant; bears hibernate in winter; some snails and fish aestivate in summer; many zooplankton species enter **diapause**

steps.title: Adaptations
steps.body:
- **Kangaroo rat** (North American deserts) meets water needs by internal oxidation of fat (metabolic water) and can concentrate urine.
- Desert plants: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, **CAM** photosynthesis (stomata open at night), leaves reduced to spines (*Opuntia*) with photosynthesis in flattened stems.
- **Allen's rule**: mammals from colder climates have shorter ears and limbs to minimise heat loss.
- Seals have a thick layer of fat (**blubber**) below the skin as insulation.
- At high altitude, the body compensates for low O₂ by increasing red blood cell production, decreasing the binding affinity of haemoglobin, and increasing breathing rate.
- Some archaebacteria live in hot springs and deep-sea vents above 100 °C; many fish live in Antarctic waters below 0 °C.

steps.title: Solved: regulate or conform?
steps.body:
Q: A small animal like a shrew finds thermoregulation energetically expensive. Why are very small mammals rare in polar regions?

Small animals have a large surface area relative to volume, so they lose heat fast and must spend much energy to make heat through metabolism.

steps.title: Solved: identify the strategy
steps.body:
Q: Zooplankton in a lake under unfavourable conditions stop development. Strategy?

**Diapause** (a stage of suspended development) — a 'suspend' response.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying plants regulate body temperature like mammals.
- Mixing hibernation (winter) and aestivation (summer).
- Thinking acclimatisation at altitude is instant.

activity.prompt: Which response is this?

items.text: Most plants' temperature follows the environment

quiz.why: Allen's rule says mammals in colder climates have shorter ears and limbs, which reduces heat loss.
CAM plants open their stomata at night, when it is cooler, to lose less water.

quiz.q: Kangaroo rat gets water mainly from
quiz.why: The kangaroo rat of North America's deserts gets its water from the internal oxidation of fat, so it need not drink.
Hibernation is a dormant winter state in which animals, like bears, avoid cold and shortage of food.

quiz.q: At high altitude the body increases
quiz.why: At high altitude, there is less oxygen, so the body increases RBC production (and breathing rate) to cope.

questions.q: A population is a group of
questions.why: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in a given area.

questions.q: Mutualism is
questions.why: Mutualism is an interaction in which both species benefit (+/+).

questions.q: Logistic curve is
questions.why: A logistic growth curve is S-shaped (sigmoid).

questions.q: Birth rate when 8 new plants arise in a pond of 20
questions.why: Birth rate = new individuals/population = 8/20 = 0.4 per plant.

questions.q: Cuckoo laying eggs in crow's nest
questions.why: A cuckoo laying eggs in another bird's nest is brood parasitism, where the host raises the parasite's young.

questions.why: An expanding population has a broad base (many young), so its age pyramid is triangular.

options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. By Gause's competitive exclusion principle, the inferior competitor is eliminated, so closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely.

Case: Prickly pear cactus overran Australia and was controlled by a moth. This is
questions.why: The prickly pear cactus was controlled by the cactus-feeding moth, which acts as a predator (herbivore) of the plant. This is biological control.

questions.q: Five warbler species coexisting on one tree illustrates
questions.why: Five warbler species feeding in different parts of the same tree are an example of resource partitioning (MacArthur's work), which lets competing species coexist.

questions.q: Monarch butterfly is distasteful to predators because
options: it feeds on a poisonous weed as a caterpillar
questions.why: A monarch butterfly caterpillar feeds on a poisonous weed, so the adult tastes bad to predators.

questions.q: Growth rate in a logistic model is maximum at
questions.why: In logistic growth, the growth rate rN(1 − N/K) is greatest at N = K/2, the middle of the S-curve.

questions.q: Case: When Balanus is removed, Chthamalus expands to lower rocks. This demonstrates
questions.why: When Balanus is removed, Chthamalus spreads to the lower area. This shows that competition from Balanus had restricted it (Connell's study of interspecific competition).

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: An orchid growing on a mango tree is an epiphyte that gets support without harming the tree, which is commensalism.

questions.q: If r = 0.0205 per year, approximate doubling time (ln 2 ≈ 0.693)
questions.why: Doubling time = ln 2 / r = 0.693/0.0205 ≈ 33.8, about 34 years.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Ecosystem
courses.summary: Ecosystem structure and function, productivity (GPP and NPP), decomposition, energy flow, food chains and the 10% law, and ecological pyramids with their limitations.
outcomes: Learners can describe ecosystem structure using a pond as example
Learners can calculate NPP and explain decomposition steps and factors
Learners can apply the 10% law to food chains
Learners can draw and interpret pyramids of number, biomass and energy

scenes.text: Class 12 students seal pond water, plants, snails and mud in a jar on the windowsill. Weeks later it is still alive.
Producers, consumers and decomposers keep energy flowing and materials recycling — a tiny ecosystem.

steps.title: What an ecosystem is
steps.body: An **ecosystem** is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with their physical environment. Size ranges from a small pond to a large forest or sea. Broad categories: **terrestrial** (forest, grassland, desert) and **aquatic** (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary). Crop fields and aquaria are **man-made** ecosystems.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Abiotic** components: light, temperature, water, soil, inorganic nutrients
- **Biotic**: producers (autotrophs), consumers (herbivores, carnivores), decomposers
- **Species composition** and **stratification** — vertical distribution of species at different levels (trees in the top layer, shrubs next, herbs and grasses at the bottom)

Four basic functions: **productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling**.

In a **pond**: abiotic water, dissolved inorganic and organic substances, and rich soil deposits at the bottom; producers — phytoplankton, some algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants; consumers — zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms; decomposers — fungi, bacteria and flagellates, especially abundant at the bottom.

steps.title: Solved: classify components of a pond
steps.body: Phytoplankton → producer; zooplankton → primary consumer; small fish → secondary consumer; bacteria in mud → decomposer; sunlight and dissolved minerals → abiotic.

steps.title: Solved: why is a crop field called man-made?
steps.body: Humans decide its species composition, inputs (water, fertiliser) and removal of biomass at harvest, so it is maintained artificially.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving decomposers out of ecosystem structure.
- Calling stratification horizontal — it is **vertical** layering.
- Thinking ecosystems must be large.

activity.prompt: Biotic or abiotic?

quiz.q: Vertical distribution of species in layers is
quiz.why: Stratification is the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels (layers) in an ecosystem.
A crop field is man-made (managed by humans). Forests, oceans and deserts are natural ecosystems.
Phytoplankton photosynthesise, so they are the main producers in a pond.

quiz.q: Number of basic ecosystem functions listed
quiz.why: The four basic ecosystem functions are productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling.

quiz.q: Decomposers in a pond are abundant
quiz.why: Decomposers are most abundant at the bottom of a pond, in the mud, where dead matter settles.

scenes.text: Leaves pile up every autumn on a forest floor, yet the floor never fills up.
Earthworms, fungi and bacteria break the litter down, returning nutrients to the soil — decomposition.

steps.title: Productivity
steps.body:
- **Primary production**: amount of biomass (organic matter) produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis; expressed as weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²).
- **Productivity**: the **rate** of biomass production, e.g. g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹.
- **Gross primary productivity (GPP)**: rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. A considerable part is used by plants in **respiration (R)**.
- **Net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP − R**: biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs.
- **Secondary productivity**: rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

Primary productivity depends on the plant species, environmental factors, nutrient availability and photosynthetic capacity. The annual NPP of the whole biosphere is about **170 billion tons** (dry weight) of organic matter; despite covering about 70% of the surface, the **oceans contribute only about 55 billion tons**.

steps.title: Decomposition
steps.body:
Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like CO₂, water and nutrients. Dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead animal remains including faecal matter form **detritus**.

Steps:
1. **Fragmentation** — detritivores (e.g. earthworm) break detritus into smaller particles
2. **Leaching** — water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil and get precipitated as unavailable salts
3. **Catabolism** — bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances
4. **Humification** — accumulation of a dark, amorphous substance, **humus**, highly resistant to microbial action; it decomposes very slowly and acts as a reservoir of nutrients
5. **Mineralisation** — humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients

Rate depends on: **chemical composition** of detritus — slower if rich in **lignin and chitin**, quicker if rich in **nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars**; and **climate** — **warm and moist** conditions favour decomposition, while low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it, causing build-up of organic material. Decomposition is largely an **oxygen-requiring** process.

steps.title: Solved: NPP
steps.body:
Q: GPP of a field = 2500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹; respiration = 1000. NPP?

2500 − 1000 = **1500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹**.

steps.title: Solved: where is decomposition faster?
steps.body:
Q: Tropical rainforest or tundra?

Warm and moist tropical forest → **faster**; cold tundra → slow, organic matter accumulates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing NPP = GPP + R.
- Saying humus decomposes quickly — it is very resistant.
- Thinking lignin-rich wood decays faster than nitrogen-rich leaves.

activity.prompt: A forest has GPP of 4000 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ and plant respiration of 1500 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. NPP?

quiz.why: Net primary productivity = gross primary productivity − respiratory losses (NPP = GPP − R).

quiz.q: Annual NPP of the biosphere is about
quiz.why: The annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter.
Decomposition begins with fragmentation of detritus into smaller pieces by detritivores like earthworms.
Humus is dark, highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes very slowly, serving as a nutrient reservoir.

quiz.q: Decomposition is faster in detritus rich in
quiz.why: Detritus rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars decomposes faster. Lignin, chitin and wax slow it down.
Low temperature and anaerobic (oxygen-poor) conditions slow the microbes that cause decomposition.

scenes.text: Sunlight falls on a grassland. Grass captures a little of it; grasshoppers eat the grass; frogs eat the grasshoppers; snakes eat the frogs.
At every step only about one-tenth of the energy passes up. That's why food chains are short.

steps.title: Sunlight and producers
steps.body:
Except for deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems. Of the incident solar radiation, **less than 50%** is **photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)**. Plants and photosynthetic bacteria capture only **2–10% of the PAR**, and this small amount sustains the entire living world.

Energy flows **unidirectionally**: sun → producers → consumers. Ecosystems obey the **second law of thermodynamics**: they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise molecules and counteract increasing disorder.

steps.title: Food chains and trophic levels
steps.body:
- **Grazing food chain (GFC)**: Grass → Goat → Man; producers are the base.
- **Detritus food chain (DFC)**: begins with dead organic matter; made of decomposers (saprotrophs — fungi, bacteria) that secrete digestive enzymes and absorb the products. In aquatic ecosystems GFC is the major conduit for energy flow; in terrestrial ecosystems a much larger fraction of energy flows through the DFC.
- Food chains interconnect to form a **food web**.
- **Trophic levels**: producers (1st), herbivores/primary consumers (2nd), primary carnivores (3rd), secondary carnivores (4th). The amount of living material at a trophic level at a particular time is the **standing crop** (biomass or number per unit area).
- **10 per cent law** (Lindeman): only about **10% of the energy** is transferred to each next trophic level, which limits the number of trophic levels.

steps.title: Solved: 10% law
steps.body:
Q: Producers fix 10,000 J. How much reaches the tertiary consumer (4th trophic level)?

10,000 → 1000 (herbivore) → 100 (primary carnivore) → **10 J** (secondary carnivore / 4th level).

steps.title: Solved: PAR captured
steps.body:
Q: If 1000 J of sunlight falls on a leaf, roughly how much is PAR and how much may be captured?

PAR < 500 J; captured 2–10% of PAR ⇒ about **10–50 J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy cycles in ecosystems — it **flows** one way; nutrients cycle.
- Applying the 10% law to sunlight rather than between trophic levels.
- Forgetting that the detritus food chain is the major pathway on land.

activity.prompt: If 20,000 J is fixed by producers, how much energy reaches the primary carnivores (10% law)?

quiz.q: Plants capture what fraction of PAR?
quiz.why: Plants capture only 2–10% of the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).
PAR (photosynthetically active radiation) is less than 50% of the incident solar radiation.
Energy flows in one direction only: from the sun to producers to consumers, and it is not recycled.
Raymond Lindeman stated the 10 per cent law, which says that about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.

quiz.q: Major energy pathway in terrestrial ecosystems
quiz.why: In terrestrial ecosystems, the detritus food chain is the major conduit of energy flow; in aquatic ecosystems, it is the grazing food chain.

options: living material at a trophic level at a time
quiz.why: Standing crop is the mass of living organisms at a trophic level at a particular time.

story.title: A single tree full of insects

scenes.text: One banyan tree hosts thousands of insects, which feed a few birds.
Drawing numbers as a pyramid gives a strange shape — inverted in the middle. Energy pyramids, though, are always upright.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
The base of each pyramid represents producers (first trophic level); the apex the top carnivores. Three types: **number**, **biomass** and **energy**. Calculations must include all organisms at a trophic level.

- **Pyramid of numbers** — grassland: upright (many grass plants, fewer herbivores, still fewer carnivores). In a tree ecosystem it may be **inverted or spindle-shaped** (one tree supports many insects).
- **Pyramid of biomass** — usually upright on land; **inverted in the sea** because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton at a given time (phytoplankton reproduce very fast).
- **Pyramid of energy** — **always upright**, because energy is lost as heat at each step; it can never be inverted.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- Ecological pyramids don't take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels.
- They assume a simple food chain, which almost never exists in nature; they don't accommodate a food web.
- **Saprophytes are not given any place** in ecological pyramids, even though they play a vital role.

steps.title: Solved: predict the pyramid
steps.body:
Q: Pyramid of biomass in a sea: phytoplankton 4 kg, zooplankton 21 kg, fish 50 kg (per unit area). Shape?

Biomass increases upwards ⇒ **inverted pyramid of biomass**.

steps.title: Solved: why can't an energy pyramid be inverted?
steps.body:
Step 1: each trophic level receives energy only from the level below.
Step 2: about 90% is lost (respiration, heat) at each transfer.
Step 3: so each higher level always has less energy ⇒ always upright.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all pyramids are always upright — only the energy pyramid is.
- Putting saprophytes in pyramids.
- Forgetting the tree case for inverted pyramid of numbers.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Biodiversity and Conservation
courses.summary: Levels and numbers of biodiversity, India's share, latitudinal and species–area patterns, importance of species richness, causes of biodiversity loss, and in situ and ex situ conservation.
outcomes: Learners can describe genetic, species and ecological diversity with examples
Learners can explain latitudinal gradients and the species–area relationship
Learners can explain the 'evil quartet' causes of biodiversity loss
Learners can compare in situ and ex situ conservation strategies

scenes.text: Scientists have described well over a million species, yet estimates of the true total run to several millions.
India, with only 2.4% of the world's land, holds about 8.1% of its recorded species — one of the 12 megadiversity countries.

steps.title: Levels of biodiversity (term popularised by Edward Wilson)
steps.body:
- **Genetic diversity**: within a species, e.g. the medicinal plant *Rauwolfia vomitoria* growing in different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency and concentration of the chemical **reserpine**. India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and about 1,000 varieties of mango.
- **Species diversity**: e.g. the Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.
- **Ecological diversity**: India's deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows give much greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

steps.title: How many species?
steps.body:
According to the IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than **1.5 million**. **Robert May** estimated global species diversity at about **7 million**. More than **70%** of all recorded species are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) are no more than 22%. Among animals, **insects** are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70% of all animals.

India has only **2.4%** of the world's land area but a share of **8.1%** of global species diversity — one of **12 mega diversity countries**. Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many animals have been recorded from India.

steps.title: Solved: which level?
steps.body:
Q: Different populations of *Rauwolfia* produce different amounts of reserpine. Which level of biodiversity?

Variation **within** one species ⇒ **genetic diversity**.

steps.title: Solved: animal share
steps.body:
Q: Of 100 recorded species, roughly how many are animals and how many of those are insects?

Animals > 70; insects > 70% of animals ≈ **about 50 of the 100**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the Western Ghats example 'ecological diversity' — it is **species** diversity.
- Saying plants outnumber animals in recorded species.
- Confusing described (≈1.5 million) with estimated (≈7 million) species.

lessons.title: Patterns of biodiversity and its importance

scenes.text: Colombia, near the equator, has nearly 1,400 bird species; Greenland, near the pole, only 56.
Biodiversity changes with latitude and with area — and ecosystems with more species tend to be more stable.

steps.title: Latitudinal gradients
steps.body:
Diversity generally **decreases from the equator towards the poles**. Tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas. Bird species: Colombia ~1,400; New York (41° N) 105; Greenland (71° N) 56; India, with much of its land in the tropics, more than 1,200. The **Amazonian rain forest** has the greatest biodiversity on Earth — more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 fishes, 1,300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, 378 reptiles and more than 1,25,000 invertebrates.

Why tropics are richer (hypotheses): they remained relatively **undisturbed for millions of years** (temperate regions had frequent glaciations), giving a long time for speciation; tropical environments are **less seasonal** and more constant and predictable; more **solar energy** is available, contributing to higher productivity.

steps.title: Species–area relationship
steps.body:
**Alexander von Humboldt** observed that within a region species richness increased with explored area, but only up to a limit. On a log scale the relationship is a straight line:

**log S = log C + Z log A** (S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope/regression coefficient, C = Y-intercept).

Z typically lies between **0.1 and 0.2**, regardless of taxonomic group or region. For very large areas like whole continents, the slope is much steeper (**Z ≈ 0.6 to 1.2**); for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, Z = 1.15.

steps.title: Why biodiversity matters
steps.body:
Communities with more species tend to be more stable — less year-to-year variation in productivity, more resistance to occasional disturbance, and more resistance to invasion by alien species. **David Tilman's** long-term outdoor plot experiments found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.

**Rivet popper hypothesis** (Paul Ehrlich): an ecosystem is like an aeroplane and species are the rivets; losing a few rivets may not affect flight, but as more are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak — and losing rivets on key parts (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is a more serious threat.

steps.title: Solved: species–area
steps.body:
Q: On log-log axes, Z = 0.2. If area increases 10 times, by what factor does species richness grow?

S ∝ A^Z ⇒ 10^0.2 ≈ **1.58 times**.

steps.title: Solved: why so many species in the tropics?
steps.body: 1. Not glaciated — long undisturbed evolutionary time. 2. Less seasonal climate allows niche specialisation. 3. More solar energy → higher productivity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the species–area equation as S = Z + A.
- Saying Z for continents is 0.1–0.2 (it's steeper, 0.6–1.2).
- Thinking the rivet popper hypothesis says all species are equally important.

lessons.title: Loss of biodiversity: the evil quartet

story.title: The fish that vanished from Lake Victoria

scenes.text: Lake Victoria in East Africa once had hundreds of unique cichlid fish. The introduction of the Nile perch led to the extinction of more than 200 of them.
Alien species, habitat loss, over-exploitation and co-extinctions — the 'evil quartet' — drive today's extinctions.

steps.title: How serious is it?
steps.body:
The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the **extinction of 784 species** in the last 500 years (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants). Recent extinctions include the **dodo** (Mauritius), **quagga** (Africa), **thylacine** (Australia), **Steller's sea cow** (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger (**Bali, Javan, Caspian**). In the last twenty years alone, 27 species have disappeared. Many more are threatened (e.g. 12% of birds, 23% of mammals, 32% of amphibians and 31% of gymnosperms). Current extinction rates are estimated to be **100 to 1,000 times faster** than in pre-human times — a possible **sixth mass extinction**, caused by human activities.

Consequences of loss: decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought, and increased variability in ecosystem processes such as productivity, water use and pest and disease cycles.

steps.title: Causes — the evil quartet
steps.body:
1. **Habitat loss and fragmentation** — the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14% of the Earth's land surface and now cover no more than 6%. The Amazon rain forest ('lungs of the planet') is being cut and cleared for cultivating **soya beans** or conversion to grasslands for raising **beef cattle**. Fragmentation hurts animals needing large territories and migratory species.
2. **Over-exploitation** — many species extinct in the last 500 years (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon) were over-exploited by humans; many marine fish populations are over-harvested.
3. **Alien species invasions** — the **Nile perch** in Lake Victoria caused extinction of more than 200 cichlid species; invasive weeds like carrot grass (*Parthenium*), *Lantana* and water hyacinth (*Eichhornia*) threaten native species; the illegal introduction of the African catfish *Clarias gariepinus* for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.
4. **Co-extinctions** — when a species becomes extinct, plant and animal species associated with it obligatorily also become extinct (e.g. a host fish and its unique parasites; plant–pollinator mutualisms).

steps.title: Solved: name the cause
steps.body:
Q: Forest cleared for a soybean farm; a forest bird disappears. Cause?

**Habitat loss and fragmentation**.

steps.title: Solved: co-extinction
steps.body:
Q: A fig species dies out in an area. What happens to its specific pollinating wasp?

It depends obligatorily on the fig, so it also disappears — **co-extinction**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking over-exploitation is the most important cause — **habitat loss** is.
- Calling *Parthenium* a native species.
- Confusing co-extinction with competition.

scenes.text: In the Khasi and Jaintia Hills, some forest patches have been protected for generations as sacred groves — no tree is cut.
Today they shelter rare plants and animals. Along with national parks, seed banks and zoos, they are part of conserving biodiversity.

steps.title: Why conserve?
steps.body:
- **Narrowly utilitarian**: humans derive direct economic benefits — food, firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicines. More than 25% of drugs currently sold worldwide are derived from plants, and about 25,000 plant species contribute to traditional medicines used by native peoples. **Bioprospecting** — exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance.
- **Broadly utilitarian**: ecosystem services — forests supply oxygen through photosynthesis and regulate climate; pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasures.
- **Ethical**: every species has intrinsic value; we have a moral duty to care for their well-being and pass on our biological legacy to future generations.

steps.title: In situ (on-site) conservation
steps.body:
- **Biodiversity hotspots** (Norman Myers): regions with very high species richness and high endemism, under threat. Initially 25 were identified; now **34**. Three cover India's rich regions: the **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka**, **Indo-Burma** and the **Himalaya**. Together the hotspots cover less than 2% of the Earth's land area, yet protecting them could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by up to about 30%.
- **Protected areas** in India: **biosphere reserves**, **national parks** and **wildlife sanctuaries** (their numbers grow over time — check current official figures).
- **Sacred groves**: tracts of forest set aside and protected by communities — e.g. **Khasi and Jaintia Hills** (Meghalaya), **Aravalli Hills** (Rajasthan), **Western Ghats** regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and **Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar** areas (central India). In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for many rare and threatened plants.

steps.title: Ex situ (off-site) conservation and global efforts
steps.body:
Threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and protected in **zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks**. Gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods by **cryopreservation**; eggs can be fertilised **in vitro**; plants propagated by **tissue culture**; seeds of commercially important plants stored in **seed banks**.

Global: the **Earth Summit** in Rio de Janeiro (**1992**) called on all nations to take measures for conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (Convention on Biological Diversity). The **World Summit on Sustainable Development** in Johannesburg (**2002**) saw 190 countries pledge to achieve, by 2010, a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss.

steps.title: Solved: in situ or ex situ?
steps.body:
- National park → **in situ**
- Seed bank → **ex situ**
- Sacred grove → **in situ**
- Cryopreserved sperm of an endangered antelope → **ex situ**

steps.title: Solved: why are hotspots a priority?
steps.body:
Step 1: they hold exceptionally high species richness and endemism.
Step 2: they are under severe threat.
Step 3: protecting less than 2% of land could prevent a large share (up to ~30%) of predicted extinctions — high return for effort.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling zoos in situ conservation.
- Mixing up the Rio (1992) and Johannesburg (2002) summits.
- Saying India has only one hotspot — it has parts of **three** (Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya).

steps.title: Plants and humans
steps.body:
- Anther: 4 microsporangia; tapetum nourishes; exine = sporopollenin; pollen mostly shed 2-celled
- Embryo sac: 8-nucleate, 7-celled; monosporic; filiform apparatus on synergids
- Double fertilisation: syngamy (2n zygote) + triple fusion (3n PEN)
- Outbreeding: dioecy stops autogamy and geitonogamy; monoecy stops only autogamy
- Testes 2–2.5 °C cooler; Leydig → androgens; Sertoli nourish; FSH → Sertoli, LH → Leydig
- Oogenesis starts before birth; secondary oocyte released; meiosis II after sperm entry
- LH surge → ovulation; corpus luteum → progesterone; fertilisation in ampulla; hCG in pregnancy tests

steps.title: Reproductive health
steps.body:
- CuT/Cu7/Multiload: copper suppresses sperm motility; LNG-20/Progestasert hormonal IUDs
- Emergency contraception within 72 h; condoms also reduce STI risk
- MTP Act 1971 (amended 2021); safer in first trimester
- ZIFT ≤ 8 blastomeres → fallopian tube; IUT > 8 → uterus; GIFT ovum → tube; ICSI sperm into ovum

steps.title: Genetics
steps.body:
- Monohybrid F₂ 3 : 1 (1 : 2 : 1 genotype); dihybrid 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; test cross 1 : 1 or 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
- Incomplete dominance 1 : 2 : 1; ABO: codominance + multiple alleles (6 genotypes)
- Sex: XX–XO grasshopper, XX–XY human, ZW–ZZ birds (female heterogametic), haplodiploid bees
- Haemophilia, colour blindness X-linked recessive; sickle-cell (Glu→Val at 6), PKU, thalassemia autosomal recessive
- Down 47 (+21), Klinefelter 47 XXY, Turner 45 X0

steps.title: Molecular basis
steps.body:
- A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3); 0.34 nm/bp; 10 bp/turn; nucleosome ~200 bp
- Griffith 1928; Avery–MacLeod–McCarty 1944; Hershey–Chase 1952 (³²P DNA, ³⁵S protein); Meselson–Stahl 1958 (¹⁵N)
- RNA pol I: rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S); II: hnRNA; III: tRNA, 5S, snRNA
- 64 codons, 61 sense, 3 stop (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG start
- lac operon: i (repressor), z (β-gal), y (permease), a (transacetylase)
- HGP 1990–2003; 3164.7 million bp; 99.9% identical

quiz.why: Analogous organs have a similar function but a different origin. Bird wings and butterfly wings are an example (convergent evolution), while homologous organs share the same origin.
IgE antibodies, which sit on mast cells, are responsible for allergic reactions.
Citric acid is produced industrially by the fungus Aspergillus niger.

scenes.text: Ecology questions mix concepts with a handful of key numbers and examples.
Learn the equations and the famous examples — they come up every year.

steps.title: Populations
steps.body:
- Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]
- Exponential: dN/dt = rN; Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ (J-shaped)
- Logistic: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K (S-shaped, Verhulst–Pearl)
- Interactions: mutualism +/+, competition −/−, predation & parasitism +/−, commensalism +/0, amensalism −/0
- Examples: Abingdon tortoise vs goats; Balanus vs Chthamalus (Connell); Gause's principle; MacArthur's warblers; cuckoo brood parasitism; Ophrys sexual deceit; fig–wasp

steps.title: Ecosystem
steps.body:
- NPP = GPP − R; biosphere NPP ~170 billion t (oceans ~55)
- Decomposition: fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation; slow with lignin, chitin, cold, anaerobic
- PAR < 50% of sunlight; plants capture 2–10% of PAR; 10% law
- Energy pyramid always upright; biomass inverted in sea; numbers inverted in a tree

steps.title: Biodiversity
steps.body:
- India: 2.4% land, 8.1% species; 12 megadiverse countries
- log S = log C + Z log A; Z 0.1–0.2 (regions), 0.6–1.2 (continents)
- IUCN 2004: 784 extinctions in 500 years; evil quartet: habitat loss (main), over-exploitation, alien species, co-extinction
- 34 hotspots; India: Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya
- In situ: hotspots, protected areas, sacred groves; ex situ: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation
- Rio Earth Summit 1992; Johannesburg 2002

cards.back: log S = log C + Z log A

quiz.why: Commensalism is an interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither benefited nor harmed (+/0).
The 10% law, given by Lindeman, says that only about 10% of the energy passes from one trophic level to the next.
There are 34 biodiversity hotspots (originally identified by Norman Myers, with the number later raised from 25 to 34).

quiz.q: Inverted pyramid of biomass occurs in
quiz.why: In the sea, the pyramid of biomass is inverted because the small standing crop of fast-turning-over phytoplankton supports a larger biomass of consumers.
With unlimited resources a population grows exponentially, producing a J-shaped curve. A limited-resource growth gives an S-shaped curve.

quiz.q: The 7-celled embryo sac has how many nuclei?
quiz.why: A typical embryo sac is 7-celled but has 8 nuclei, because the two polar nuclei lie together in one central cell.

quiz.q: Pink × pink snapdragon gives white offspring with probability
quiz.why: Pink snapdragons are heterozygous (Rr), so pink × pink gives 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. White (rr) is 1/4 of the offspring.
Meselson and Stahl used the heavy isotope of nitrogen, ¹⁵N, to follow DNA replication.

Elephantiasis (filariasis) is caused by the filarial worm Wuchereria.

quiz.q: Taq polymerase is thermostable because it comes from
quiz.why: Taq polymerase is thermostable because it is obtained from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium living in hot springs.

quiz.q: Energy reaching the 3rd trophic level if producers fix 10,000 J
quiz.why: By the 10% law, the energy goes 10,000 J → 1,000 J (second level) → 100 J (third trophic level).

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: 8 questions, 25 minutes. Read each case carefully before looking at options.

steps.title: Assertion–reason method
steps.body: 1. Is A true? 2. Is R true? 3. Only if both are true: does R explain A? Write T/F next to each before choosing.

items: Scheduled a retake in a week

quiz.q: Assertion: Geitonogamy is genetically like autogamy. Reason: pollen comes from the same plant.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
quiz.why: Both are true. In geitonogamy the pollen comes from another flower of the same plant, so it has the same genotype as in autogamy.

quiz.q: Colour-blind man × carrier woman: probability a daughter is colour blind
quiz.why: The daughter always gets the father's X with the colour-blindness allele (Xᶜ). From the carrier mother she gets Xᶜ half the time, and then is colour blind: probability 1/2.

quiz.q: An mRNA 5′-AUG UUU UAG GGC-3′ codes for
quiz.why: AUG codes for Met and UUU for Phe, and UAG is a stop codon. So the chain has 2 amino acids and GGC is not translated.

quiz.q: Case: A patient's T_H cell count is falling steadily and opportunistic infections recur. Most likely
quiz.why: A steady fall in helper T cells with repeated opportunistic infections points to HIV infection, which destroys these cells.

quiz.q: In pBR322 with insert at BamHI, recombinants are sensitive to
quiz.why: An insert at the BamHI site inactivates the tetracycline-resistance gene, so recombinants are sensitive to tetracycline but still resistant to ampicillin.

quiz.q: Logistic growth: r = 0.5, K = 200, N = 100. dN/dt
Case: An area loses its only fig species; its pollinator wasp disappears too. This is
quiz.why: When a species goes extinct, species that depend on it, like an obligate pollinator wasp, also go extinct. This is co-extinction.
Aspergillus niger makes citric acid, not acetic acid (acetic acid comes from Acetobacter aceti), so that pair is mismatched.

questions.q: Exine of pollen is made of
questions.why: The outer wall of pollen, the exine, is made of the very tough polymer sporopollenin.

questions.q: Usual site of fertilisation in humans
questions.why: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the oviduct.

questions.q: Monohybrid F₂ phenotypic ratio
questions.why: A monohybrid cross with complete dominance gives a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio in F₂.

questions.q: Clot buster enzyme
questions.why: Streptokinase, from the bacterium Streptococcus, dissolves clots and is called the clot buster.

questions.q: Copper-releasing IUD
questions.why: CuT is a copper-releasing IUD. LNG-20 and Progestasert release hormones, and Saheli is a pill.

questions.q: Number of stop codons
questions.why: There are three stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA.

questions.q: Vector of malaria
questions.why: Malaria is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.q: Energy pyramid is
questions.why: The pyramid of energy is always upright because energy is lost at every trophic level.

questions.q: Assertion: Haemophilia is more common in males. Reason: it is X-linked recessive and males have one X.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Haemophilia is X-linked recessive, and males have a single X, so one affected allele is enough to show the disease. This explains why it is more common in males.

questions.q: In a dihybrid F₂ of 160, the number of double recessives
questions.why: In a dihybrid F₂ of 160 plants, the double recessive class is 1/16 × 160 = 10.

questions.q: DNA with 20% adenine has guanine
Case: A sewage sample's BOD falls from 300 to 30 mg/L after aeration. What caused this?
options: aerobic microbes in flocs consumed organic matter
questions.why: A big fall in BOD means organic matter was consumed. In secondary treatment, aerobic microbes in flocs in aeration tanks break down the organic matter.

questions.q: GPP 5000, R 1800 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹. NPP
questions.why: NPP = GPP − R = 5000 − 1800 = 3200 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.

questions.q: Meselson–Stahl after 2 generations in ¹⁴N
questions.why: After two generations in ¹⁴N, DNA is half hybrid (¹⁵N–¹⁴N) and half light (¹⁴N–¹⁴N), as replication is semi-conservative.

questions.q: Hardy–Weinberg: 1% show recessive trait. Carrier frequency ≈
questions.why: q² = 0.01 gives q = 0.1 and p = 0.9. Carrier frequency 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18.

questions.q: Case: A woman with blocked fallopian tubes but healthy uterus and ova. Most suitable ART
questions.why: With blocked fallopian tubes, the fertilisation is done in the lab and the embryo is placed directly into the uterus (IVF with IUT), bypassing the tubes. ZIFT and GIFT need functioning tubes.

questions.q: Bt toxin kills insects by
options: forming pores in midgut cells after activation in alkaline gut
questions.why: The Bt protoxin is activated in the alkaline gut of the insect. It then binds the midgut cells and forms pores, which kills the insect.

Which statement about the lac operon is correct?
options: Allolactose inactivates the repressor, switching genes on
Repressor binds the promoter only when lactose is present
questions.why: In the lac operon, allolactose (from lactose) binds the repressor and inactivates it, so the structural genes are switched on. The repressor binds the operator, and the i gene codes for the repressor.

questions.q: Klinefelter syndrome arises from
questions.why: Klinefelter syndrome arises from non-disjunction that gives an extra X chromosome, 47, XXY.
